# CRE Insurance Certificate Compliance Review

## 1. Opening Context

This skill produces a lawyer-grade compliance review of insurance certificates (typically ACORD 25 Certificates of Liability Insurance) and related policy endorsement evidence against the insurance and risk-transfer requirements in a commercial real estate (\

) Access Agreement (or similar site access, entry, license, or services agreement). In practice, these reviews are often the only gatekeeping mechanism before an owner, property manager, lender's consultant, contractor, vendor, or other \

is permitted on-site. Done well, the review reduces the client's loss exposure by confirming that the required coverages and limits are actually in place, the client is properly protected as an Additional Insured where required, and coverage will respond first and without erosion by the client's own insurance when \

status is required.\n\nExecution of this work product requires a high degree of precision because insurance deficiencies often remain hidden until a loss occurs. A certificate is merely a snapshot of coverage; it is not the policy itself, and in most jurisdictions it does not grant rights to the certificate holder. If an attorney or paralegal fails to identify that a certificate lacks an endorsement establishing Additional Insured status, omits required \
language, or misses a \

gap, the client may find its own insurance program responding to a claim that should have been covered by the Recipient. A competent review ensures that risk is properly shifted to the party performing the work or accessing the property, preserving the client's loss history and policy limits. Good execution looks like a disciplined comparison of the Access Agreement's insurance clause to what the Recipient has actually produced, a clear written deficiency notice identifying exactly what must be corrected, and a risk-based escalation when the documentation cannot prove compliance.

## 2. Understanding the Context and Purpose

In CRE operations, an Access Agreement shifts or allocates risk among the property-side parties (owner, landlord, lender, property manager, asset manager) and the accessing party (contractor, engineer, environmental consultant, broker, tenant contractor, telecom vendor, etc.). The insurance requirements are typically paired with indemnity obligations: the Recipient promises to defend and indemnify certain \
and insurance is intended to fund that promise and reduce coverage disputes.\n\nThe attorney's role is to ensure the \

section of the Agreement is not just boilerplate but an enforceable shield. You are looking for a precise match between the contractual requirement and the evidence of coverage. You must approach this with an adversarial mindset: assume the insurance carrier will look for any technicality to deny coverage to your client as an Additional Insured after a loss. Your goal is to close those technical loopholes before the first person steps onto the property.

The primary audience for the review output is the client's transaction or asset-management team, the property manager or site operations team, and sometimes the counterparty's risk manager or broker. Their expectations are pragmatic: a pass/fail conclusion, a short explanation of what is missing, and specific instructions that a broker can implement. Strategically, read the insurance clause as part of an integrated risk-transfer package: the Additional Insured requirement is only meaningful if it tracks the contract's indemnity scope; primary/non-contributory language matters most when multiple parties have overlapping policies; and waiver of subrogation is most valuable when the parties want to avoid insurer-versus-insurer litigation.

Scope boundary: this skill is designed for contract-driven certificate compliance reviews in CRE access and vendor contexts. It does not replace a full policy review, does not opine on the enforceability of indemnity provisions, and does not provide coverage opinions. Where a coverage position turns on policy wording, manuscript endorsements, or state-specific insurance law, the skill instructs the executing LLM to escalate and flag items for attorney verification.

## 3. Prerequisites and Information Gathering

Before beginning the substantive review, the following documents and data points must be obtained and organized. Do not proceed to a final compliance determination until these materials are available, as a partial review often leads to critical omissions.

At minimum, collect: (a) the executed Access Agreement (or the signature-ready final) including all exhibits, insurance schedules, and any insurance requirements rider or property rules incorporated by reference; (b) every certificate of insurance (COI) provided (typically ACORD 25 for CGL, and sometimes separate ACORD forms for auto, workers' compensation, umbrella/excess, professional liability, pollution legal liability, or builder's risk); (c) copies of Additional Insured endorsements (e.g., ISO Forms CG 20 10 and CG 20 37) and any primary/non-contributory endorsements if provided; (d) any waiver of subrogation endorsements if required; (e) the Recipient's insurer and broker contact details; and (f) the project or work description and dates and locations covered by the access.

The first set of clarifying questions should confirm: who exactly must be named as Additional Insured (the full legal names of the owner, property manager, lender, and their respective affiliates, subsidiaries, partners, members, managers, officers, directors, employees, and agents as listed in the agreement); whether the contract requires completed operations coverage; whether there is any requirement for specific ISO endorsement forms; whether the work involves heightened risks (hot work, roofing, structural modification, environmental sampling, confined space) that may implicate exclusions; and whether access is contingent on proof of insurance \

the client.\n\nIf any required document is missing—endorsements are required but not provided, an umbrella is required but no umbrella COI is provided, or policy numbers are omitted—the LLM must pause and request the missing inputs before issuing a final compliance determination. The LLM should prompt the user: \

If the user insists on proceeding, the LLM may produce a preliminary risk memo that clearly labels every conclusion as conditional and identifies what cannot be verified.

## 4. Step-by-Step Process

### Step 1: Parse and Normalize the Access Agreement Insurance Requirements into a Verification Matrix

Start by extracting the insurance clause(s) from the Access Agreement and turning them into a normalized set of requirements that can be tested against the COI and endorsements. Insurance provisions often contain nested conditions—limits, form requirements, Additional Insured status, primary wording, notice obligations, deductible constraints, carrier rating constraints, and special coverages—that cannot be reliably checked if you treat the clause as prose. Translate the clause into objective verification questions.

Execute this step by reading the agreement for: required lines of coverage (CGL, auto, workers' compensation/employers' liability, umbrella/excess, professional, pollution, cyber, etc.); required minimum limits (per occurrence, aggregate, products/completed operations aggregate, personal and advertising injury, fire damage, medical payments, combined single limit for auto); how limits must apply (e.g., \
or \

aggregate versus policy-level aggregate); Additional Insured scope and the exact entities that must be covered; primary and non-contributory language; waiver of subrogation; cancellation and non-renewal notice; required insurer rating (often \

from AM Best); and any requirement that coverage be written on an occurrence form and include contractual liability.\n\nWhere the clause references specific endorsement forms or ISO numbers, treat those as mandatory unless the clause allows \
If the clause uses ambiguous phrases like \
flag them as discretionary and recommend attorney or client confirmation of the standard. A normalized requirement statement, for illustrative purposes, might read: \
\n\nCommon mistakes to avoid include missing that the contract requires completed operations AI (many COIs only show \
generally), ignoring aggregate requirements, assuming umbrella \

without proof, and failing to capture that certain parties such as a lender or property manager must be specifically named. After a claim, the Additional Insured carrier will ask whether the endorsement's AI grant matches the contract's requirement (\
) and whether the named AI matches the claimant entity. If you do not normalize entity names and roles up front, you risk a mismatch—for example, the certificate lists \
but the contract requires \

and its parent.

### Step 2: Review the ACORD 25 Form for Internal Consistency and Baseline Sufficiency

Conduct a disciplined read of each ACORD 25. The purpose is twofold: identify obvious non-compliance quickly (missing coverage line, wrong limits, expired policy) and detect red flags suggesting the COI is unreliable or the broker is not tracking the contract requirements. Importantly, never treat the COI as proof of coverage; it is an informational snapshot only.

Start with the header and policyholder/producer fields. Confirm the \

matches the Recipient entity in the agreement (exact legal name and entity suffix). A common error in CRE practice is for a contractor to provide a COI in the name of a parent company or a related LLC that is not the actual signatory to the Agreement; this creates a privity gap that carriers exploit to deny coverage. Confirm the producer/broker contact information is present and usable. Then check the policy effective and expiration dates. Coverage must be in force for the entire access period; if access is ongoing, require renewal certificates in advance and build a calendar reminder. If the agreement requires that coverage be \

(often for completed operations), note that a COI cannot prove future maintenance; you can only confirm current coverage and impose a contractual obligation and tracking mechanism.\n\nThen review each relevant coverage box. For Commercial General Liability, verify the occurrence limits and aggregates match the contract and that the CGL is listed as \
rather than \

if the contract requires occurrence form. CRE access should almost never be on a claims-made basis, as this requires the policy to remain in effect long after the work is done to cover a later-filed claim. Confirm that \
and \
are shown and meet required amounts. Check the \
field: if the Agreement requires \
or \
aggregates, the COI must reflect this. If it is checked at the \

level, the Recipient's aggregate limits could be exhausted by claims at completely different properties, leaving your client unprotected. For umbrella/excess, confirm it exists, confirm limits, and check whether it is \
or \
If the contract requires it to be \
or to apply to AI coverage, the COI alone will not prove it; request the umbrella declarations and endorsement showing AI status. For auto, confirm \

or the required coverage symbols, and check the combined single limit. For workers' compensation/employers' liability, confirm statutory WC and EL limits (typically at least $500,000 to $1,000,000 each for EL Each Accident, EL Disease-EA Employee, and EL Disease-Policy Limit). If the Recipient is a small firm, check if any proprietors, partners, or executive officers are excluded; if the person actually performing the work is an excluded officer, the client has a significant exposure gap. If the Recipient claims exemption from workers' compensation, treat that as non-compliant unless the contract allows it and the client accepts the risk; request proof of exemption and consider requiring an alternate risk transfer.\n\nCommon mistakes include treating \
as equivalent to \
(it is not—simply being a certificate holder does not grant insured status), relying on the \

box as definitive proof of AI status, ignoring policy dates, and overlooking that the COI may list limits that do not match the policy.

### Step 3: Confirm Additional Insured Status with Endorsement-Level Evidence

The central substantive task is verifying that the client and any other required parties are actually Additional Insureds under the Recipient's CGL policy and, if required, under the umbrella/excess policy. A COI commonly checks an \

box or includes narrative text in the Description of Operations, but that rarely proves the policy has a compliant endorsement or that the endorsement grants the required scope of coverage.\n\nBegin by identifying exactly who must be Additional Insured. If the agreement requires multiple entities, confirm the exact legal names, including entity suffixes, and whether the agreement extends AI to \
If the Recipient's policy uses a blanket Additional Insured endorsement (\

), then compliance depends on there being a written contract in place, the contract requiring AI, and the person or entity seeking AI coverage falling within the endorsement's definition. Request a copy of the blanket endorsement form and read its grant language. If the endorsement is scheduled (specific names listed), insist that the schedule include the correct entities.\n\nThen match the endorsement scope to the Access Agreement's scope. Many agreements require AI for both ongoing operations and completed operations. In standard ISO practice, ISO Form CG 20 10 addresses Additional Insured status for ongoing operations, while ISO Form CG 20 37 addresses completed operations. If the policy provides only ongoing operations AI, it may fail to cover post-completion claims such as property damage discovered after work is finished. If the agreement requires completed operations, request the endorsement that clearly extends AI status to completed operations, and confirm that the products-completed operations aggregate is present at required limits. Also check whether the AI coverage is limited to vicarious liability or extends to losses \

by the named insured's acts or omissions; the scope varies by endorsement edition. Quote the endorsement's operative language in your review and flag any narrowing that could conflict with the agreement's intended risk transfer.\n\nIllustrative deficiency notice language (adapt as needed): \

Common mistakes include accepting AI status without endorsements, failing to check completed operations, ignoring entity-name mismatches, and overlooking that AI endorsements may be limited to certain locations or operations that do not include the premises or the described work.

### Step 4: Verify \
Status\n\nIf the Access Agreement requires coverage to be \

treat this as a separate requirement from AI status. This language ensures that if a claim arises, the Recipient's insurance pays first, and the client's own insurance does not have to contribute until the Recipient's limits are exhausted. Even when the client is an Additional Insured, the policy may still apply on an excess basis absent an endorsement or clear policy wording, particularly where \
clauses conflict.\n\nExecute this step by first locating the contractual requirement and then checking whether the COI's narrative includes explicit \

wording. Do not stop there. Because COI wording is not binding, request the actual endorsement or policy provision that establishes primary and non-contributory status for Additional Insureds. Many carriers offer a standalone primary and non-contributory endorsement; some blanket AI endorsements include primary language when required by contract. Your task is to confirm, with documentary support, that the policy will respond first for claims arising from the Recipient's work.\n\nWhen reviewing the endorsement, focus on whether the primary status is conditioned on there being a written contract requiring it, whether it applies only to ongoing operations, whether it is limited to \
used by the named insured, and whether it is overridden by any \

clause in the umbrella. Without a primary and non-contributory endorsement, the client's insurer may be forced to contribute or defend, leading to deductible spend and premium impacts.\n\nIllustrative internal analysis language: \

Common mistakes include assuming AI status automatically means primary, ignoring that the umbrella may not be primary even if the CGL is, and not advising the client that primary and non-contributory status is most important when the client has a claim history and wants to avoid erosion of its loss runs.

### Step 5: Confirm Waiver of Subrogation, Limits Structure, Umbrella Alignment, and Ancillary Requirements

Beyond AI and PNC, the next frequent failure modes involve waiver of subrogation, limits that look adequate on paper but do not satisfy the contract's structure, and ancillary requirements such as carrier rating and cancellation notice.

Waiver of subrogation prevents the Recipient's insurance company from suing your client to recover the money it paid on a claim. If the agreement requires it, verify via endorsement on all relevant lines (CGL, WC, auto, property). COIs sometimes indicate \

in a column check or narrative, but do not attach endorsements. Require the actual endorsements, especially for workers' compensation where a waiver often requires a specific form.

For limits, confirm the per-occurrence limit, general aggregate, and products-completed operations aggregate. If the agreement requires higher limits via umbrella, verify that the umbrella limit combined with underlying limits equals or exceeds the contractual requirement. If the agreement requires that the umbrella apply to CGL, auto, and employer's liability, request proof of the underlying schedule and confirm the umbrella is not limited to fewer lines. If the umbrella does not recognize AI status, the client may only have AI coverage up to the CGL limit, which is a structural gap your review must identify before access is granted.

For insurer qualifications, if the agreement requires a minimum AM Best rating (e.g., A- VII), the COI may list insurer NAIC numbers but not the rating. Request evidence of rating such as a broker attestation or AM Best confirmation, and note that ratings can change; consider a process for re-verification on renewal.

For cancellation and notice, many agreements require the Recipient to provide advance notice of cancellation or material change. The ACORD 25 includes standard disclaimer language that it \
and that notice is not guaranteed. Most modern ACORD forms have deleted the \

language. Treat any contract requirement that the insurer provide notice directly to the client as difficult to enforce via COI alone; require the Recipient to covenant to provide notice and to request the insurer or broker add a notice endorsement where available. Flag this as a risk if the client is relying on notice for access control.

For deductibles and self-insured retentions, if the agreement caps them, a COI usually will not show them reliably. Request declarations or a broker letter stating the deductible and SIR amounts. If there is a large SIR, advise the client about credit risk: the Recipient may effectively be self-insuring the first layer, and the AI may face delayed defense or indemnity while the Recipient funds the retention.

Common mistakes include ignoring the products-completed ops aggregate, failing to confirm the umbrella attaches over AI coverage, overlooking waiver of subrogation as optional when it is a bargained-for term, and neglecting to check the \
box for suspicious language like \

or geographic exclusions that could invalidate coverage for the specific project.

### Step 6: Produce a Clear Written Compliance Determination, Deficiency Notice, and Escalation Recommendation

Your output should be a concise, professional memo or email-ready report that states whether the submission is compliant, non-compliant, or conditionally compliant pending documentation; lists each requirement and the corresponding evidence; and provides broker-ready corrective instructions. The review itself is part of the client's risk control record: it shows diligence, supports denying access if necessary, and creates a paper trail that the Recipient was notified of deficiencies.

Structure the output so that a non-lawyer operations team can act on it. Use plain language but be precise about what needs to be provided—for example, \
rather than \
Where the issue is a name mismatch, write the exact name to use. Where the issue is missing limits, state the required limit and the currently evidenced limit.\n\nIllustrative \
language (adapt as needed): \

Include an escalation recommendation when the Recipient cannot produce endorsements, when endorsement language appears materially narrower than the contract requirement, when the carrier rating is below the contractual minimum, when the work presents heightened risk, or when the agreement's insurance terms are internally inconsistent or unusually aggressive. Escalation can be to in-house counsel, outside coverage counsel, or the client's risk manager depending on the organization.

Adversarial awareness for the written record: your review may be discoverable in later litigation. Avoid speculative statements about coverage or fault. Stick to contract requirements and documentary evidence. If you must explain risk, frame it as \
rather than \

## 5. Critical Legal Standards and Compliance

Competence and diligence require that the reviewer understand the limits of certificates and avoid overstatements. Under Model Rule 1.1 (Competence), the lawyer—and by extension an LLM operating under attorney supervision—must perform a reasonable review proportional to the risk. In this context, competence includes understanding that a COI is not a policy and that specific endorsements are required to bind a carrier. Under Model Rule 1.3 (Diligence), the reviewer must not treat a COI as conclusive proof where the contract requires endorsements or where material terms cannot be verified. Under Model Rule 1.4 (Communication), the lawyer must explain constraints and risks to the client in a way that permits informed decisions, particularly when the business team wants to grant access despite deficiencies. Never instruct a client that they are \

based solely on a COI; always qualify the analysis by stating that coverage is subject to the actual terms and conditions of the underlying insurance policies.

When communicating with third parties such as the Recipient's broker, Model Rule 4.1 requires truthfulness. When a submission is deficient, the deficiency notice should describe the gap and request specific documents rather than asserting that the Recipient is uninsured.

Confidentiality and privilege require treating the Access Agreement, insurance materials, and internal review notes as client confidential under Model Rule 1.6. If the review is conducted at counsel's direction for legal advice, communications may be privileged; but sharing the analysis broadly—for example, forwarding to third-party property managers not within the scope of privilege—can waive privilege. The skill should instruct the LLM to ask who the client is, who will receive the output, and whether the output should be labeled \

(while recognizing that labeling alone is not determinative; confirm privilege posture with supervising attorney).\n\nMalpractice risk concentrates in three areas: false positives (approving non-compliant insurance), name or entity mismatches that defeat AI coverage, and failure to request endorsements when the COI cannot establish compliance. Mitigation includes requiring documentary proof, using conditional language when proof is absent, and escalating uncertainties. In high-risk jurisdictions where property owners face strict liability exposure—such as New York's Labor Law Sections 240 and 241 (the \
) for gravity-related construction injuries—failing to verify the absence of exclusions such as \
or \

exclusions on the Recipient's policy can expose the client to multi-million dollar uninsured losses. These high-stakes reviews must be escalated to experienced coverage counsel.\n\nAnti-indemnity statutes in multiple states can limit the enforceability of Additional Insured provisions in construction-related contexts. For example, Texas Insurance Code Chapter 151 restricts indemnification in construction contracts for certain types of negligence, and California Civil Code Section 2782 limits risk-shifting for a property owner's \

in construction settings. When the access activity resembles construction or improvements to real property, flag the potential impact of these statutes for attorney review, as the insurance carrier may refuse to honor Additional Insured status that violates state law.

## 6. Quality Control and Review

A high-quality output must accurately restate the Access Agreement's insurance requirements, accurately describe what the COI and endorsements show, and clearly distinguish between \
and \

Review the analysis by re-checking each factual statement against the document, including names, policy numbers, dates, and limits.\n\nBefore finalizing, run the output through these substantive checks. Does the name of the Additional Insured exactly match the name in the Agreement, including entity suffix? Has the LLM checked for the presence of actual endorsement documents, and if only the COI is provided, has the LLM included a disclaimer that the COI is for informational purposes only and does not amend the policy? Do the combined GL and Umbrella limits meet the total limit required by the contract? Does the COI or Agreement address cancellation notice, and has the LLM flagged the ACORD 25's standard limitation on notice? Does the \

box contain any suspicious exclusionary language that could invalidate coverage?

Evaluate whether the output would withstand scrutiny from an experienced risk manager or opposing counsel after a claim. If the client tenders a claim, will the tender package include the endorsements demanded during this review? If the reviewer approved without endorsements, can the decision be justified under the client's standards? If an entity name differs by punctuation or suffix, was it addressed?

Citations and authority: this skill references Model Rules as generally adopted. If the output will be used in a jurisdiction with variations, flag that and require attorney confirmation. Do not provide case citations about certificate legal effect unless verified by web search at the time of execution; if the user requests such citations, the LLM must either perform web verification and provide URLs, or clearly mark the citation as requiring attorney verification.

Every deliverable must include an explicit attorney-review requirement: this output is a draft risk-control assessment that requires review by a licensed attorney or qualified risk professional before being relied upon. It does not constitute a legal opinion on the sufficiency of coverage, and all insurance determinations should be confirmed with the client's insurance broker or risk management department.

## 7. Jurisdiction-Specific Adaptations

This skill is intentionally contract-driven and usable across U.S. jurisdictions because it compares submitted insurance evidence to negotiated requirements. The points that most commonly require jurisdiction-specific adaptation are the enforceability and scope of additional insured and indemnity requirements in construction-related contexts, the legal effect of certificates of insurance and potential liability of brokers for misstatements, and statutory notice-of-cancellation requirements and whether an insurer can be obligated to give notice to third parties.

When the matter is high-risk (large limits, hazardous work, public projects, or known claim history), the skill should adapt by requiring endorsement-level proof as a hard rule and by flagging state-law constraints for attorney verification. Key jurisdiction-specific considerations include:

In New York, pay extreme attention to the Description of Operations and the endorsement language. New York's Labor Law Sections 240 and 241 create strict liability for property owners for gravity-related injuries on construction sites. Look for any exclusion regarding \
or \

in the policy materials; these exclusions are common and devastating to property owners. Reference: NY Insurance Law § 3426 addresses cancellation and non-renewal requirements that may also apply.\n\nIn Texas, the Anti-Indemnity Act (Texas Insurance Code Chapter 151) applies to most construction-related contracts and may limit the enforceability of Additional Insured requirements that attempt to shift liability for the indemnitee's own negligence. Verify whether the Access Agreement involves \
triggering this statute.\n\nIn California, Civil Code Section 2782 limits risk-shifting for a property owner's \

in construction contexts. Confirm that the agreement's indemnity and AI requirements are consistent with these limitations.

In Florida, Fla. Stat. § 627.4137 provides certain rights for claimants to receive information from insurers; if a potential claim is identified, ensure the client is aware of the right to request a certified copy of the relevant policy.

If the user identifies the governing law state in the Access Agreement, the LLM should incorporate that into the analysis, propose a short list of jurisdiction-specific verification questions (such as whether the state restricts AI for sole negligence or limits contractual indemnity scope), and explicitly flag any state-law statements for attorney verification unless the LLM has performed contemporaneous web research and can provide URLs for the authority.

For all jurisdictions, do not assert universal rules about the legal effect of certificates, enforceability of primary and non-contributory clauses, or scope of anti-indemnity statutes. Instead, treat the agreement's requirement as the commercial benchmark, flag statutory or common-law limitations as issues requiring local confirmation, and direct the supervising attorney to verify enforceability before finalizing any compliance determination that turns on state-specific law.

name: California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) Policy
summary: Drafts a comprehensive California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) compliance policy for businesses operating in California. Details categories of personal information collected, usage purposes, consumer rights, and aligns with CCPA and CPRA requirements. Use this skill to create transparent privacy policies ensuring regulatory compliance and consumer disclosure.
content:
# California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) Policy Drafting Workflow

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) compliance policy for a business operating in California. This document must serve as both a regulatory compliance instrument and a transparent disclosure to California residents regarding their privacy rights. The policy should reflect current CCPA and California Privacy Rights Act (CPRA) requirements, incorporate business-specific data practices, and provide clear, actionable information to consumers.

## Document Structure and Requirements

### Introduction Section

Begin by establishing the policy's foundational purpose and legal framework. Explain why this policy exists, emphasizing the business's commitment to protecting California residents' privacy rights under the CCPA. Clearly state the effective date of the policy and define its scope, specifying that it applies to California residents whose personal information the business collects. Address the threshold requirements that make CCPA applicable to this particular business, such as annual gross revenue, volume of consumer data processed, or revenue derived from selling personal information. Ensure all terminology aligns with official definitions from the California Privacy Protection Agency (CPPA) and the California Attorney General's office. The introduction should set a professional yet accessible tone that demonstrates the business's good-faith commitment to privacy compliance.

### Personal Information We Collect Section

Provide a detailed enumeration of the categories of personal information the business collects from California residents. Organize this information according to the statutory categories defined in California Civil Code Section 1798.140, including but not limited to identifiers (names, addresses, email addresses, IP addresses), commercial information (purchase history, consumer preferences), internet activity (browsing history, search history), geolocation data, professional information, and inferences drawn from collected data. For each category, specify the sources from which this information is obtained, whether directly from consumers, automatically through website interactions, from third-party data providers, or from public records. Include concrete, business-specific examples that illustrate what types of data fall within each category in the context of your operations. Review internal business documents, data flow maps, privacy impact assessments, and system inventories to ensure accuracy and completeness. Cross-reference each category with the precise statutory definitions to ensure legal accuracy and avoid ambiguity that could undermine compliance.

### How We Use Your Personal Information Section

Articulate the specific business and commercial purposes for which the collected personal information is processed and utilized. Move beyond generic statements to provide meaningful disclosure about how data supports business operations, such as fulfilling transactions, providing customer service, processing payments, detecting and preventing fraud, debugging and repairing functionality, conducting internal research, improving services, marketing and advertising, and complying with legal obligations. Each stated purpose should align with the permissible business purposes enumerated in CCPA regulations. Explain the relationship between the categories of personal information collected and the purposes for which they are used, creating clear connections that demonstrate necessity and proportionality. Consider industry-specific best practices from organizations such as the International Association of Privacy Professionals (IAPP) and ensure the disclosure meets the CCPA's requirement for reasonably accessible and meaningful information. Avoid overly broad or vague purpose statements that could be interpreted as failing to provide adequate notice.

### Sharing Your Personal Information Section

Disclose all categories of third parties with whom the business shares personal information, distinguishing clearly between sharing for business purposes and selling or sharing for cross-context behavioral advertising purposes. Identify specific types of third-party recipients such as service providers, contractors, vendors, affiliates, advertising networks, data analytics providers, social media platforms, and government entities. For each category of recipient, specify which categories of personal information are disclosed and the purpose of such disclosure. If the business sells personal information or shares it for cross-context behavioral advertising, explicitly state this fact and provide clear instructions for exercising the right to opt-out, including the conspicuous \

link required by statute. Address whether the business has actual knowledge of selling or sharing personal information of consumers under 16 years of age. Ensure this section reflects current data sharing practices by reviewing vendor contracts, data processing agreements, and business associate agreements to capture all relevant third-party relationships.

### Your Rights Under the CCPA Section

Comprehensively outline all privacy rights afforded to California residents under the CCPA and CPRA. Explain the right to know what personal information has been collected, including the specific pieces and categories of information, the categories of sources, the business purposes for collection, and the categories of third parties with whom information is shared. Describe the right to delete personal information held by the business, subject to certain exceptions for legal compliance, fraud prevention, and other specified purposes. Detail the right to opt-out of the sale or sharing of personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising, and the right to limit the use and disclosure of sensitive personal information if applicable. Include the right to correct inaccurate personal information and the right to non-discrimination for exercising CCPA rights, emphasizing that the business will not deny goods or services, charge different prices, provide different quality of service, or suggest such differential treatment solely because a consumer exercised their privacy rights. Reference the specific statutory provisions (California Civil Code Sections 1798.100-1798.150) that establish these rights to provide legal grounding and demonstrate compliance rigor.

### How to Exercise Your Rights Section

Provide clear, step-by-step instructions for California residents to submit requests to exercise their CCPA rights. Specify all available methods for submitting requests, which must include at minimum two designated methods such as a toll-free telephone number and a website address, and may also include email, postal mail, or an online portal. Explain the verification process the business employs to confirm the identity of requestors, including what information consumers must provide and how the business matches this information against existing records. Detail the timelines for responding to requests, noting that the business will acknowledge receipt within 10 days and provide a substantive response within 45 days, with the possibility of a 45-day extension when reasonably necessary. Address how authorized agents may submit requests on behalf of consumers, including the documentation required to verify the agent's authority such as a power of attorney or signed permission. Clarify any limitations on request frequency and explain the business's process for handling requests that fall within statutory exceptions. Ensure this section complies with the detailed procedural requirements in CCPA regulations regarding request intake, verification, and response.

### Children's Privacy Section

Address the business's practices regarding personal information of minors under 16 years of age. If the business has actual knowledge that it collects personal information from children under 16, explain the opt-in consent requirements that apply: affirmative authorization from the consumer for those aged 13 to 15, and affirmative authorization from a parent or guardian for children under 13. Describe the mechanisms implemented to obtain such consent and verify parental authority where applicable. If the business does not knowingly collect information from children under 16, state this explicitly and explain the measures taken to avoid such collection. If the business sells or shares personal information of minors under 16, detail the enhanced protections and consent mechanisms required by statute. Consider age-appropriate privacy practices and additional protections that demonstrate a commitment to children's privacy beyond minimum statutory requirements.

### Changes to This Privacy Policy Section

Explain the business's approach to updating and modifying this privacy policy over time. Describe the circumstances that may necessitate policy changes, such as modifications to business practices, changes in applicable law, or the introduction of new services or technologies. Specify how the business will provide notice of material changes to consumers, whether through email notification, prominent website posting, in-app notifications, or other reasonable means designed to ensure consumers receive actual notice. State the effective date of any changes and clarify whether continued use of services after changes take effect constitutes acceptance of the modified policy, or whether affirmative consent will be sought for material changes. Commit to maintaining prior versions of the policy for reference and establish a reasonable retention period for superseded policies to demonstrate compliance history.

### Contact Information Section

Provide complete and accurate contact information for privacy-related inquiries and CCPA rights requests. Include the business's legal name, physical mailing address, and designated email address for privacy matters. If the business has appointed a Data Protection Officer or Chief Privacy Officer, provide their title and contact information. Ensure the contact methods listed here align with those specified in the \

section to avoid consumer confusion. Include any toll-free telephone number designated for CCPA requests and the URL for any online request portal. Verify that all contact information is monitored regularly and that the business has established internal procedures to route privacy inquiries to appropriate personnel for timely response. This section must satisfy the CCPA's requirement that businesses provide a reasonably accessible means for consumers to submit requests and inquiries.

## Drafting Standards and Compliance Considerations

Throughout the policy, maintain plain language that is reasonably accessible to the average consumer while preserving legal precision. Avoid unnecessary legal jargon, but retain statutory terms of art where they provide clarity and legal accuracy. Ensure consistency in terminology throughout the document, using the same terms to refer to the same concepts. Structure the policy with clear headings, logical flow, and sufficient white space to enhance readability. Consider the policy's presentation format, ensuring it will be conspicuous and accessible on the business's website and available in alternative formats for consumers with disabilities.

Verify that all substantive provisions align with current CCPA and CPRA requirements as codified in California Civil Code Sections 1798.100 et seq. and the implementing regulations adopted by the California Privacy Protection Agency. Cross-reference industry guidance from the California Attorney General's office, CPPA rulemaking materials, and authoritative privacy law resources. Ensure the policy reflects the business's actual data practices rather than aspirational or generic statements, as material discrepancies between the policy and actual practices may constitute deceptive business practices under California law.

Consider the policy's role in the broader privacy compliance program, ensuring it coordinates with other privacy documentation such as cookie policies, employee privacy notices, vendor data processing agreements, and internal privacy procedures. The policy should serve as both an external-facing disclosure document and an internal compliance reference that guides business practices and decision-making regarding personal information handling.

Upon completion, the policy should be reviewed by qualified legal counsel familiar with California privacy law to ensure full compliance and appropriateness for the specific business context. The final document should be formatted professionally, approved by appropriate stakeholders, published conspicuously on the business's website, and incorporated into the organization's privacy governance framework with regular review cycles to maintain ongoing compliance as laws and business practices evolve.

name: California Discovery Verification Builder
summary: This skill generates California-compliant discovery verification forms for interrogatory responses (CCP § 2030.250) and document production responses (CCP § 2031.250). It guides the practitioner through selecting the correct statutory formulation for individuals versus entities, properly deploying personal-knowledge versus information-and-belief language, avoiding the attorney verification trap, and including an execution-ready perjury declaration under CCP § 2015.5 with date, location, and signature block. The skill embeds adversarial awareness, ethical guardrails, and privilege-protection guidance, and requires attorney review before any output is used or served.

# California Discovery Verification Builder (CCP §§ 2030.250, 2031.250)

## 1. Opening Context

In California civil litigation, a discovery response without a properly signed verification is, as a matter of law, no response at all. Under the rule established in *Appleton v. Superior Court* (1988) 206 Cal.App.3d 632, responses served without a verification are treated as a failure to respond, which can result in the waiver of all objections—including attorney-client privilege and work product protection—and expose the party to mandatory monetary sanctions. This skill produces California state-court discovery verifications that comply with Code of Civil Procedure sections 2030.250 (interrogatories) and 2031.250 (requests for production/inspection). Verifications are not mere formalities: they are sworn statements under penalty of perjury that authenticate the discovery responses and can become pivotal evidence for impeachment, sanctions motions, and summary judgment.

Good execution means the verification precisely matches the discovery device, accurately states the capacity of the signer (individual party, corporate representative, agent), correctly uses \
versus \

language in the statutorily authorized way, and includes a legally sufficient perjury declaration under CCP § 2015.5 that is usable in California proceedings. Poorly drafted verifications risk being struck as noncompliant, forcing costly redo work, undermining credibility with the court, and creating avoidable exposure for the client and counsel if the verification overstates personal knowledge or fails to properly invoke \

where permitted. This skill is governed primarily by CCP §§ 2030.250 and 2031.250, and secondarily by California's general perjury declaration statute, CCP § 2015.5, plus applicable ethical duties of competence, confidentiality, and candor under the California Rules of Professional Conduct.

## 2. Understanding the Context and Purpose

California written discovery is structured so that objections are made by counsel, but factual responses must be verified by the responding party or an authorized representative. The verification serves several strategic functions throughout the lifecycle of a case. First, it creates an evidentiary anchor: a verified response can be used against the party as an admission or for impeachment in deposition or at trial, and it shapes the motion practice landscape around further responses and sanctions. Second, it enforces accountability: a verification signals that the party has participated meaningfully in the investigation and review process, which matters when opposing counsel challenges the adequacy of the search, completeness of production, or the factual basis for responses.

The immediate audience for the verification is the opposing party and counsel, who will scrutinize whether the verification is properly executed and enforceable (e.g., through a motion to compel). The court may become an indirect audience if verification defects surface in discovery motion practice. The internal audience is also important: supervising attorneys, in-house counsel, and clients expect verifications that are accurate, minimally risky, and operationally easy to execute with clear signature blocks, correct captioning, and correct \
language.\n\nStrategically, a verification can either help or harm the client depending on how it is framed. Overbroad \
statements can box the client into testimony that is difficult to explain later—creating a trap at deposition where opposing counsel asks, \
Conversely, overuse of \

can invite suspicion and discovery motion practice if it appears evasive, especially where the responding party reasonably should have personal knowledge. The objective is to comply with the statute and align the sworn statement with the actual process the client used to prepare the responses.\n\nFrom a defensive standpoint, practitioners must also be wary of what might be called the \

While CCP § 446 allows an attorney to verify a pleading if the client is absent from the county, an attorney-verified discovery response generally does not satisfy the Discovery Act's requirements for trial or summary judgment purposes and risks making the attorney a witness in the case. This practice is strongly discouraged and carries significant malpractice exposure.

Scope boundary: This skill builds the verification forms and signature blocks for (a) interrogatory responses and (b) responses to requests for production/inspection. It does not draft the substantive responses, objections, privilege logs, or produce documents. It also does not address verifications for requests for admission (CCP § 2033.240), deposition errata, or other sworn filings.

## 3. Prerequisites and Information Gathering

Before drafting any verification, the LLM must identify which discovery device is being verified and who is legally and practically able to sign. The exact statutory wording differs between interrogatory verifications and production/inspection verifications, and it differs again when the responding party is an entity rather than a natural person.

At minimum, collect the following inputs before proceeding. First, you need the operative discovery requests and the draft responses that will be served, including the title page and caption of the response set. The verification must match the document it verifies—for example, \
versus \
versus \

Second, you need the identity of the responding party as it appears in the pleadings, and whether the responding party is an individual, a corporation, an LLC, a partnership, a public entity, or another organization. Third, you need the court name and case number to ensure the caption matches the lead document.\n\nYou must also collect signature logistics: the signer's full legal name, title or role (e.g., \

), the city and state where the signer will physically sign (required by CCP § 2015.5), and the anticipated date of execution. If execution will be done remotely, gather whether the firm's practice is to use wet signature, scanned signature, or an e-signature platform, and confirm that the executed verification will satisfy the requirements of CCP § 2015.5.\n\nFinally, you must understand the factual basis for the responses: which portions are within the signer's personal knowledge, which are based on a reasonable inquiry of the organization's books and records, and which are based on information obtained from employees, agents, counsel, or documents. For entity verifications, determine what steps the organization took to gather information (custodian interviews, document collection, internal database searches). This supports accurate \

language.\n\nIf any required item is missing—especially the discovery type, party type, signer identity, or signing location—the LLM must stop and ask targeted follow-up questions before generating the verification. Do not guess the party type, the signer's authority, or the caption. Insert prominent placeholders like \

when specific information is unavailable and flag such gaps in the output notes.

## 4. Step-by-Step Process

### Step 1: Classify the Discovery Device and Select the Governing Statute

Start by determining whether the verification is for interrogatory responses (CCP § 2030.250) or for responses to inspection demands/requests for production (CCP § 2031.250). This distinction matters because the statutory language differs in its specifics. Treat this as a binary classification and explicitly label the output—for example, \
or \

—in your internal draft notes.\n\nInterrogatories in California include Form Interrogatories, Special Interrogatories, and other authorized interrogatory formats; the verification requirements attach to the responding party's answers, not the objections. Requests for production are typically styled as \
or \

and involve a statement of compliance, inability to comply, or objections.\n\nQuality execution requires you to mirror the exact title of the response document. A common defect is drafting a verification that generically says \
while the served document is titled \
Opposing counsel will argue the verification is not tethered to the served responses, and a court may require a corrected verification. Example titling language that ties properly: \
or \

Adversarial awareness: Opposing counsel will look for technical deficiencies to gain leverage in meet-and-confer correspondence and motions to compel. If you misidentify the device or omit the set number, you create avoidable motion fodder and risk a court order requiring re-service.

### Step 2: Determine Who Must Sign and in What Capacity

Next, identify whether the responding party is a natural person or an entity. CCP §§ 2030.250 and 2031.250 expressly contemplate verifications \

and allow an entity to verify through an officer, agent, or employee. The critical judgment is to align the signer's stated capacity with both the statutory allowance and the real-world basis for the signer's knowledge.\n\nFor an individual party, the signer is ordinarily the party themselves. Avoid having counsel sign an individual's discovery verification; that is a red flag and may be improper because counsel generally lacks personal knowledge and is not the \

For an entity party, choose someone who can honestly state that they are authorized and who has either personal knowledge or has overseen an adequate inquiry into records and personnel. In practice, for a corporate defendant, the signer is often a corporate officer (CEO, CFO, General Counsel) or another authorized employee with oversight of the response process. For a public entity, an authorized official or custodian may sign. For an LLC, a managing member or authorized manager may sign. Do not invent the title: confirm it with the user.\n\nExample capacity lines (illustrative): For an individual: \
For a corporation: \

\n\nCommon mistake: Using an employee-signatory for an entity without stating authorization, or naming the entity in the signature block but having an individual sign without clarifying their title or authority. Another common mistake is having a low-level employee sign without specifying they are an \

which creates an opening for the opposing side to challenge the verification's validity.

Adversarial awareness: If discovery becomes contentious, the other side may challenge whether the signer was truly authorized or sufficiently knowledgeable, especially if later deposition testimony suggests the signer rubber-stamped counsel's work without conducting a genuine inquiry. Draft the verification to be truthful and defensible: it should reflect a reasonable inquiry process, not a fiction of omniscience.

### Step 3: Choose the Correct \
vs. \

Structure

The core statutory nuance in CCP §§ 2030.250 and 2031.250 is that verifications can be made on personal knowledge, or—when permitted—partly on information and belief. The task is to produce a verification that matches the actual epistemic basis for the responses.

For entity responses, it is rarely true that any one person has personal knowledge of all responsive facts across the organization. California statutes accordingly allow verifications stating that the answers are true of the declarant's own knowledge except as to matters stated on information and belief, and that as to those matters the declarant believes them to be true. Use this \
formulation when the responses necessarily incorporate information from records, other employees, or counsel's synthesis of data. For entity parties, the \

clause should be considered the default unless the signer can genuinely attest to personal knowledge of every fact.\n\nFor individual parties, the same split formulation can be appropriate when some responses depend on documents, third-party records, or recollection refreshed by materials the party did not personally create. However, do not overuse \

to avoid accountability for plainly personal facts. If the response concerns the party's own date of birth, that is personal knowledge. If it asks the party to identify all communications between their employer and a third party, it may be partly based on documents and may warrant information-and-belief language.\n\nIllustrative clause that tracks the statutory model: \
\n\nYou must not state \
if that is not accurate. That creates perjury risk for the client and impeachment exposure at deposition or trial. Conversely, do not use a blanket \

clause for all responses when the signer plainly has personal knowledge of the core facts, as this can invite suspicion and meet-and-confer disputes.\n\nAdversarial awareness: Opposing counsel may argue that an entity's information-and-belief verification is too vague if it does not indicate a reasonable inquiry. You can draft a truthful sentence that signals process without creating new obligations—for example, for an entity signer: \

Keep it accurate and modest. Do not describe the role of counsel in preparing responses, as this can implicate privilege waiver.

### Step 4: Draft the Perjury Declaration and Execution Block Under CCP § 2015.5

California verifications must be made under penalty of perjury in compliance with CCP § 2015.5. This statute prescribes specific language and requires the date and place of execution. Strict adherence to its wording is mandatory; any deviation—such as omitting \
—can render the verification void, particularly if signed outside the state.\n\nThe required declaration language is: \

This language should be used regardless of whether the signer is located within or outside California at the time of execution, as it satisfies CCP § 2015.5 in both scenarios.\n\nThe execution block must include the date and the city and state where the document is signed. Example perjury block (California execution, illustrative): \
Example perjury block (out-of-state execution, illustrative): \

Do not include a notary acknowledgment unless specifically required by the client or court order. Verifications under CCP § 2015.5 generally do not require notarization, and adding unnecessary notary language can cause execution delays and create confusion about whether an acknowledgment is now required. Do not abbreviate or paraphrase the CCP § 2015.5 language.

Common mistake: Omitting the place of execution or using an ambiguous location line such as \

without specifying the city and state. Opposing counsel can challenge the sufficiency, and your filing and recordkeeping become unreliable. Another common mistake is dating the verification before the responses were finalized; the date should be contemporaneous with or after the finalization of the responses.

Adversarial awareness: If there is later a perjury or credibility dispute, the execution details become important. Make the execution information explicit and accurate, and preserve the signed original in a defensible manner.

### Step 5: Build the Caption, Case-Identifying Information, and Signature Blocks

Even though CCP §§ 2030.250 and 2031.250 focus on the verification language itself, in practice the document must look like a California pleading attachment and be easy to associate with the served discovery responses. Use the same caption block as the responses, with the same court, parties, case number, and title. If the responses are formatted as California pleadings with attorney service address blocks and line numbering, mirror that format for the verification page(s).

The verification title should exactly match the response title. If the response document is \
then the verification should be titled \
This prevents the \

problem where an opposing party argues the signature page was attached to a different version of the responses.\n\nFor the signature block, include the signer's typed name and capacity. For an entity, the signature line should make clear the person signs on behalf of the entity and state their title. Example signature block (individual, illustrative): A signature line followed by \
Example signature block (entity, illustrative): The entity name on the first line, then \
followed by a signature line, then \
and \
If the entity is \
ensure the verification also says \
—not \

A mismatch between the entity name in the responses and in the verification can render the responses effectively unverified.

Common mistake: Putting only the individual name without the entity name and title, which creates ambiguity about whether the entity itself has verified.

### Step 6: Handle Hybrid Responses (Factual Assertions vs. Objections)

Under CCP § 2030.250(a) and § 2031.250(a), the party verifies the factual responses, but the attorney is responsible for the objections. The verification should not explicitly state that the party is verifying the legal objections, as that could inadvertently suggest the client has \
of the attorney's legal strategy and potentially waive work product protection. The verification language—\

—implicitly applies to the factual portion. The attorney should sign the main response document separately to cover the objections. This division of responsibility should be reflected in the drafting.\n\n### Step 7: Tailor \

Verifications When the Party Cannot Sign

Sometimes a party cannot sign due to unavailability, incapacity, or another legitimate reason. CCP provisions contemplate verification by an agent in some settings, but this is an area where sloppy drafting creates disproportionate risk. If someone other than the party or a regular entity officer signs, the verification must clearly explain the basis of the signer's authority and knowledge.

In practice, an \

verification might be used for an entity (where the agent is effectively an officer or employee) or for an individual under limited circumstances (e.g., conservator, attorney-in-fact). If you are asked to draft an agent verification, do not proceed without collecting the legal basis for the agency (power of attorney, corporate authorization, court appointment), the scope of the agent's authority, and how the agent acquired information about the facts in the responses.\n\nIllustrative language (authorized corporate representative/agent): \
\n\nDo not claim authority (\
) unless it is true and can be supported. If authority is uncertain, flag it for attorney verification. Do not use an \

verification as a convenience when the actual party could sign with minor scheduling effort; that invites meet-and-confer disputes and undermines the credibility of the responses.

Adversarial awareness: An opponent may seek deposition testimony about who verified, what the signer reviewed, and whether the signer conducted any inquiry. Draft with the assumption that the signer could later be questioned about the verification process.

### Step 8: Produce a Clean, Execution-Ready Final Verification Packet

The final output should be an execution-ready verification page or pages that can be appended to the discovery responses and served. Ensure the verification is not inadvertently attached to a draft that changes later; if the substantive responses are still evolving, clearly label the verification \

until the responses are final.

When producing the final packet, include both a standalone verification and, if requested, a version combined at the end of the response document. In California practice, verifications are often attached as the final pages of the response document. If the client will sign electronically, confirm that the firm's practices comply with California rules regarding electronic signatures on sworn statements.

Common mistake: Letting a client sign a verification before counsel has finalized objections and substantive answers, creating a mismatch between what was verified and what was served. Another common mistake is failing to maintain version control between the served responses and the executed verification.

Adversarial awareness: If there is a later motion to compel, the opponent may argue the responses were unverified at the time of service or that the verification does not correspond to the served version. Preserve metadata and maintain a clear chain between the served responses and the executed verification.

## 5. Critical Legal Standards and Compliance

The central statutory requirements are CCP § 2030.250 for interrogatory verifications, CCP § 2031.250 for inspection demand verifications, and CCP § 2015.5 for the perjury declaration form. Under *Appleton v. Superior Court* (1988) 206 Cal.App.3d 632, unverified responses are treated as no response at all, potentially waiving all objections and triggering sanctions.

Professional responsibility constraints are directly engaged because you are preparing a document for signature under penalty of perjury. Under California Rule of Professional Conduct 1.1 (Competence), counsel must ensure the verification is legally correct and tailored to the client's actual knowledge basis. Under Rule 1.4 (Communication), counsel should explain to the client that a verification has the same legal weight as testifying under oath in a courtroom, and that falsifying a verification is a felony under California Penal Code § 118. Under Rule 3.3 (Candor Toward the Tribunal), an attorney cannot allow a client to sign a verification the attorney knows to be false; if the responses contain known inaccuracies, the attorney has a duty to correct them before the client signs.

Confidentiality and privilege warrant special attention. The verification should not unnecessarily disclose privileged communications or attorney work product. Do not describe counsel's advice as the basis for truth unless you intend to waive privilege. If you add process language, describe sources as \
rather than \

unless attorney review concludes otherwise. Be extremely cautious with any attorney-signed verification: under CCP § 446, an attorney verification can sometimes be used as a basis to seek discovery of the attorney's files related to the verified document.\n\nMalpractice risk clusters include defective verifications that render responses effectively unverified and trigger motions, waivers, and sanctions exposure; perjury exposure for the client due to inaccurate \

language; and privilege waiver by including unnecessary narrative about how responses were prepared. Mitigate these by matching the verification to the discovery device and title, accurately selecting the signer and authority, using information-and-belief language where appropriate, and requiring attorney review before sending to the client.

If the verification process reveals that the client's intended sworn statements conflict with counsel's understanding or create exposure—for example, if the client insists on verifying facts counsel believes are false—escalate immediately for attorney intervention. Do not attempt to smooth over inconsistencies in the verification language.

## 6. Quality Control and Review

Before finalizing, test the verification against four substantive questions that mirror how opposing counsel and the court will evaluate it.

First, does the verification accurately reflect the governing statute and discovery device type? Confirm that the verification cites the correct statute—CCP § 2030.250 for interrogatories, CCP § 2031.250 for inspection demands—and that the language is consistent with the statutory requirements. If you include CCP § 2015.5 language, confirm it substantially matches the statutory form and includes date and place of execution.

Second, does the signer have the capacity stated, and is that capacity accurately described? Cross-check the signer's name and title against client-provided information. If the party is \
ensure the signer is an officer or agent of \
—do not have a parent company officer sign for a subsidiary unless they are also an officer of the subsidiary. Flag any uncertainty as requiring attorney verification.\n\nThird, is the \

structure truthful and defensible? Reconcile the verification wording with how the responses were actually compiled. If the responses rely on records and interviews, an information-and-belief clause is generally appropriate. If the responses concern purely personal facts, a stricter personal-knowledge statement may be acceptable. Any mismatch between the verification's knowledge representation and the actual basis for the responses is a red flag.

Fourth, does the document match the served responses in caption, party name, case number, and exact response title? This is a mechanical point with substantive consequences. A mismatch can render the responses effectively unverified and invite a motion to compel.

Additional mechanical checks: Does the CCP § 2015.5 formula contain the exact phrase \

without abbreviation or paraphrase? Are the date and location fields clearly marked for the client, or filled in if known? Are all blank fields that require client input prominently marked?

Citations and authority verification: The LLM must verify any cited statute or case via web search or the official California Legislature website before including it in a verification. If the LLM cannot verify a citation, it must flag it for attorney review. All outputs from this skill require attorney review before being sent to a client for signature or served on opposing counsel. The generated verification is not legal advice and should not be used without supervision by a licensed California attorney responsible for the matter.

## 7. Jurisdiction-Specific Adaptations

This skill is designed exclusively for California Superior Court practice under the Civil Discovery Act. Adaptations are required when the forum or context changes.

If the matter is in federal court in California, interrogatory and production responses are governed by FRCP 33 and 34, and the verification practice differs significantly. Under FRCP 33(b)(3), interrogatory answers must be verified by the responding party under oath, but the form of declaration is governed by 28 U.S.C. § 1746 rather than CCP § 2015.5. Responses to requests for production under FRCP 34 are signed by the attorney and typically do not require a separate party verification. Do not use CCP verification forms in federal court unless a stipulation, local rule, or judge-specific order specifically requires it. While similar in principle, California's CCP § 2015.5 has stricter \

requirements for out-of-state signatures than the federal counterpart.

If the matter is in another state, do not reuse the CCP statutory language. Many states have different perjury declaration statutes and different requirements for who signs and under what knowledge standard.

Within California, remain alert to local custom and judge preferences about formatting. Some local California Superior Courts have specific formatting rules for signature pages or pleading paper (e.g., Los Angeles Superior Court local rules regarding formatting). Always advise the user to check the local rules of the specific county. If the responding party is a governmental entity, verify whether internal policies require a specific official to sign and adapt the signer capacity line accordingly while keeping the statutory perjury framework intact.

## Execution Output Requirements

When executing this skill, produce publication-ready verification documents in California pleading style. Generate an \
compliant with CCP § 2030.250 and/or an \

compliant with CCP § 2031.250, each in both an individual-party version and an entity-party version as applicable. Each version must include a caption-ready title line that can be matched to the discovery response title, the statutory \

structure when appropriate, a CCP § 2015.5-compliant perjury declaration with date and place lines, and a signature block with name and capacity.\n\nIf the user specifies only one discovery device or only one party type, produce only the relevant versions and clearly label what was omitted. If the user does not specify signer authority for an entity, flag that as required input before finalizing. All outputs must include a notation that attorney review is required before the verification is circulated to a client for signature or served on opposing counsel.

name: California Privilege Log Generator
summary: This skill guides an advanced LLM to generate a California-compliant privilege log for withheld or redacted discovery materials under CCP § 2031.240. It walks through metadata normalization, the drafting of sufficiently specific descriptions to satisfy the Hernandez standard, and the proper application of California Evidence Code sections 952 and 954 (attorney-client privilege) and CCP section 2018.030 (work product doctrine). The workflow emphasizes defensible descriptions that enable assessment without revealing privileged substance, flags waiver risks including third-party disclosure and mixed business/legal communications, and includes mandatory anti-hallucination and attorney-review guardrails.
content:
# California Privilege Log Generator

## 1. Opening Context

This skill produces a California-compliant privilege log for documents withheld or redacted in discovery on the basis of attorney-client privilege, work product protection, and closely related California confidentiality doctrines. In California civil practice, the privilege log is not a clerical afterthought; it is a strategic and compliance-critical work product that frequently determines whether privileged material remains protected or is ordered produced. A poorly prepared log—one characterized by boilerplate descriptions, missing metadata, or incomplete participant identification—can trigger waiver arguments, motions to compel, in camera review, cost-shifting sanctions, or court-ordered disclosure of sensitive attorney communications and attorney mental impressions.

Good execution requires a delicate balance: providing sufficient factual information to allow the requesting party and the court to evaluate the privilege claim, while simultaneously avoiding the disclosure of the very confidential information the privilege is intended to protect. The log must align with California's statutory privilege framework (not federal common law), reflect the applicable discovery statutes governing motions to compel and protective orders, and anticipate the adversarial use of the log by opposing counsel. This skill guides an advanced LLM through that workflow with the level of care expected of competent California litigation counsel, subject to mandatory attorney supervision and verification.

## 2. Understanding the Context and Purpose

A privilege log exists because California's discovery regime generally requires parties to respond meaningfully to inspection demands and other discovery requests while preserving legitimate protections. Under Code of Civil Procedure section 2031.240(c)(1), if a party objects to a demand for inspection based on privilege, it must provide sufficient factual information for the other party to evaluate the merits of the claim. The log is therefore both a compliance artifact and a litigation positioning document: it signals the reasonableness of your privilege assertions, frames the dispute for the meet-and-confer record, and often becomes an exhibit to discovery motions.

In California state court, privilege claims are governed primarily by the Evidence Code (attorney-client privilege, Cal. Evid. Code § 950 et seq.) and the Code of Civil Procedure (work product doctrine, CCP § 2018.010 et seq.). Attorney-client privilege is codified at Evidence Code section 954, with key definitional provisions including section 952's definition of \

Work product protection is codified at Code of Civil Procedure section 2018.030, which distinguishes between absolute protection for writings reflecting an attorney's impressions, conclusions, opinions, or legal research and theories, and qualified protection for other attorney work product that may be overcome only upon a showing of denial that would unfairly prejudice the party or result in injustice.

The primary audiences for a privilege log are opposing counsel evaluating whether to accept or challenge your privilege claims, the court if a discovery dispute is presented, and your own client and trial team because the log becomes part of the record of what exists and what is being protected. Opposing counsel's expectations are practical: entries should be consistent, non-evasive, and sufficiently specific to assess privilege. Judges' expectations are similarly pragmatic: they want clarity, internal consistency, and a log that can be used efficiently for sampling or in camera review when justified.

The California standard for log sufficiency, as clarified in Hernandez v. Superior Court (2003) 112 Cal.App.4th 285, requires identification of the document type, date, author, recipients, and the specific ground for withholding. If the log fails to provide this foundation, the court may find the objecting party has failed to meet its burden of proof, potentially leading to in camera review or an order to produce. The party asserting the privilege bears the initial burden of proving that the communication was made in the course of an attorney-client relationship (Wellpoint Health Networks, Inc. v. Superior Court (1997) 59 Cal.App.4th 110).

Strategically, the log should accomplish three things simultaneously. First, it should preserve the privilege by avoiding over-description that discloses substance. Second, it should deter challenges by clearly tying the document's participants and purpose to the statutory elements. Third, it should create a defensible record showing diligence and good faith in response—important because California discovery disputes turn heavily on meet-and-confer efforts and proportional remedies.

Scope boundary: this skill focuses on generating the privilege log itself, including California-tailored privilege descriptions and metadata handling. It does not draft the underlying discovery responses, meet-and-confer letters, motions to compel or protective orders, or declarations supporting privilege claims, although it will flag when those may be needed.

## 3. Prerequisites and Information Gathering

Before generating entries, the LLM must have enough information to accurately describe each withheld or redacted document without revealing privileged substance, and to connect the claim to California's statutory elements. At minimum, the LLM should obtain the following inputs.

The discovery requests at issue are essential context, including the RFP set number, request text, and any applicable definitions and instructions, because the log often references which request prompted withholding. The party's responses and any agreed-upon ESI protocol or logging format should be reviewed because they may dictate specific column headings, metadata fields, or categorical logging approaches.

The population of withheld and redacted documents must be provided, either as a full set or a representative sample if the court or parties agreed to categorical logging. This should include Bates ranges if applicable. For each document, the LLM needs available metadata: date, author, recipients including CC and BCC, subject line or file name, document type, attachment status, custodians, and where it was found.

A party and counsel roles list is indispensable. This should identify key individuals and their roles—for example, \
