You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Certificate of Interested Persons, a critical litigation document required in appellate proceedings to identify potential conflicts of interest and ensure judicial impartiality. This certificate must comply with Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 26.1 and any applicable local court rules, ensuring complete disclosure of all parties and entities with a financial or legal interest in the case outcome.

## Initial Information Gathering and Document Review

Begin by conducting a thorough review of all available case materials to identify every person and entity that must be disclosed. Search through the user's uploaded documents to extract essential information including the complete case caption, all party names as they appear in lower court proceedings, corporate affiliations and ownership structures, law firm representations, and any prior disclosure statements filed in the trial court. Pay particular attention to corporate disclosure statements, complaints, answers, and settlement agreements that may reveal non-obvious interested parties. Extract specific details such as parent corporations, subsidiaries, publicly held companies with ownership interests of 10% or more, insurers providing coverage for the claims, and any third-party litigation funders or indemnitors.

When reviewing corporate parties, trace ownership structures carefully to identify all entities in the corporate family tree. Look for merger and acquisition documents, annual reports referenced in pleadings, and any corporate organizational charts that may have been filed. If the case involves complex corporate structures or special purpose entities, ensure that beneficial ownership is fully disclosed, not merely the immediate corporate parent.

## Document Structure and Jurisdictional Compliance

Construct the certificate with a proper case caption that reflects the specific formatting requirements of the destination appellate court. The caption should include the full name of the appellate court (such as \
), the appellate case number, the complete names of all appellants and appellees exactly as they appear in the notice of appeal, and the document title as specified by local rules (which may be \
or \

depending on the circuit).

Research the specific requirements of the relevant appellate court, as circuits vary significantly in their disclosure requirements. Some circuits require alphabetical listing of all interested persons, while others require categorical organization by party affiliation. Certain jurisdictions mandate disclosure of amici curiae who have filed or indicated intent to file briefs, while others limit disclosure to parties and their corporate affiliates. Verify whether the court requires a negative statement if no interested persons exist beyond the named parties, and confirm any page limitations or formatting specifications unique to that jurisdiction.

## Comprehensive Enumeration of Interested Persons

Draft the substantive disclosure section with meticulous attention to completeness and accuracy. Begin with all named parties to the litigation, including any parties who were dismissed, settled, or otherwise exited the case before appeal, as their interests may still be relevant to potential conflicts. List each party's complete legal name without abbreviations, followed by all law firms representing that party with full firm names, office locations, and the names of individual attorneys of record.

For each corporate party, provide a complete disclosure of the corporate structure. Identify all parent corporations by their full legal names, noting that some corporations may have multiple layers of parent entities that must all be disclosed. List all subsidiaries that could be affected by the litigation outcome, and identify any publicly held company owning 10% or more of the party's stock, including the exact percentage of ownership if known. If a party is a wholly-owned subsidiary, state this explicitly and identify the ultimate parent corporation.

Expand the disclosure to include non-party interested persons who may not be immediately obvious from the case caption. Identify any insurance companies providing coverage for the claims at issue, as insurers often have direct financial interests in appellate outcomes. Disclose any litigation funding entities or third-party financiers who have provided capital in exchange for a share of any recovery. Include any indemnitors or guarantors who may be obligated to satisfy a judgment. If the case involves bankruptcy proceedings, identify the trustee, debtor-in-possession, or any creditors' committee with standing.

Address potential amicus participation by identifying any trade associations, industry groups, advocacy organizations, or other entities that have filed amicus briefs in the trial court or have indicated intent to participate in the appeal. Some circuits require disclosure of amici even before briefs are filed if participation is anticipated.

## Certification Language and Ongoing Obligations

Draft a certification statement that formally attests to the completeness and accuracy of the disclosure. The certification should explicitly reference the governing rule (Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 26.1 or the specific local rule of the circuit), state that the disclosure includes all persons and entities required to be listed to the best of the filer's knowledge and belief after reasonable inquiry, and acknowledge the continuing duty to supplement the certificate if additional interested persons are discovered during the pendency of the appeal.

Include language that reflects the serious nature of this disclosure obligation, noting that the certificate is made under penalty of perjury or subject to the certifications required by Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 32(g). The certification should make clear that counsel has conducted a diligent investigation to identify all interested persons and has consulted with the client to verify corporate affiliations and financial interests.

## Execution, Formatting, and Quality Control

Conclude the certificate with a proper signature block that includes the printed name and signature of the attorney or party filing the certificate, the attorney's bar number and jurisdiction of admission, the complete law firm name and contact information including street address, telephone number, fax number if applicable, and email address, and the date of execution. Ensure the signature complies with any electronic filing requirements of the court, including acceptable formats for digital signatures.

Format the entire document according to professional appellate standards with appropriate margins (typically one-inch on all sides), acceptable typeface (usually 14-point for proportionally spaced fonts or Courier 12-point for monospaced fonts), proper line spacing (typically double-spaced for the certification language, though the list of interested persons may be single-spaced in some circuits), and clear section headings that guide the reader through the disclosure.

Perform a final quality control review to verify that all names are spelled correctly with proper capitalization, all entities are identified by their complete legal names rather than trade names or abbreviations, all required categories of interested persons have been addressed even if only to state that none exist in a particular category, the document complies with any page limitations imposed by local rules, and the certificate is dated and signed appropriately. Cross-reference the certificate against any prior disclosure statements filed in the trial court to ensure consistency and to identify any changes in corporate structure or party representation that occurred during the litigation.

The completed Certificate of Interested Persons should be a polished, accurate, and comprehensive document that fully satisfies the court's disclosure requirements and enables judges to identify any potential conflicts of interest before considering the merits of the appeal. This document serves not merely as a procedural formality but as an essential safeguard of judicial impartiality and public confidence in the appellate process.

name: Certificate of Trust
summary: Drafts a Certificate of Trust, a condensed summary of a trust agreement that verifies trustee authority for transactions without disclosing full trust details. Use this skill in estate planning for real estate, banking, or business dealings requiring privacy protection under state-specific statutes like the Uniform Trust Code. Ensures accuracy to avoid trustee liability for misrepresentations.
content:
# Certificate of Trust Drafting Workflow

You are tasked with drafting a Certificate of Trust, a critical transactional document that serves as an abstract or summary of a trust agreement. This document allows trustees to conduct business on behalf of the trust without disclosing the complete trust instrument, thereby protecting the privacy of beneficiaries and detailed trust provisions while providing third parties with sufficient information to verify the trustee's authority.

## Document Purpose and Legal Context

A Certificate of Trust (also known as a Memorandum of Trust or Abstract of Trust) is a condensed version of a trust agreement used in real estate transactions, banking relationships, and other business dealings. The document must balance two competing interests: providing sufficient information to establish the trustee's authority while maintaining the confidentiality of sensitive trust provisions. This document is governed by state-specific statutes, with many jurisdictions having adopted variations of the Uniform Trust Code provisions regarding certificates of trust. The certificate must be accurate and complete, as trustees may face liability for material misrepresentations or omissions.

## Section 1: Document Header and Jurisdictional Framework

Begin the certificate with a clear, centered title \
or \

as appropriate for the governing jurisdiction. Immediately below the title, include the full legal name of the trust exactly as it appears in the original trust instrument. State the jurisdiction whose laws govern the trust and the date of execution of this certificate (not the trust creation date, which will be referenced separately). Consider including a reference number or file number if the trust has been recorded or if one is maintained for administrative purposes. The header should establish the formal nature of this document and its legal significance as a sworn statement regarding the trust's existence and terms.

## Section 2: Trust Identification and Formation Details

Provide comprehensive identification of the trust by stating its complete legal name, the exact date the trust was created or executed, and the full legal name(s) of the settlor(s) (also known as grantor(s) or trustor(s)) who established the trust. Clearly indicate whether the trust is revocable or irrevocable, as this designation has significant legal and tax implications. If the trust was originally revocable but has become irrevocable due to the settlor's death or incapacity, state both the original status and the current status with the date of change. Include any amendments to the trust by date and briefly note their effect on the trust's revocability status. This section establishes the foundational facts about the trust's legal existence and current status.

## Section 3: Trustee Authority and Powers

Identify all current trustees by full legal name and, if applicable, their official capacity (such as \
or \

). If there are multiple trustees, specify whether they must act jointly or may act independently, as this directly affects the validity of transactions. Clearly state the scope of powers granted to the trustee(s), including but not limited to:

- The authority to buy, sell, mortgage, lease, or otherwise deal with real and personal property
- The power to borrow money, pledge trust assets, and enter into contracts on behalf of the trust
- The ability to manage investments, operate businesses, and make distributions
- Any specific limitations on trustee powers that third parties should be aware of
- The authority of successor trustees to act and the conditions triggering succession

Name any designated successor trustees and describe the mechanism by which they assume authority. This section must provide third parties with confidence that the acting trustee has the legal authority to bind the trust in the contemplated transaction.

## Section 4: Summary of Material Trust Provisions

Provide a concise summary of the trust's key provisions without disclosing information about specific beneficiaries, distribution schedules, or detailed asset inventories. Describe the general purpose of the trust (such as estate planning, asset protection, or charitable purposes) in broad terms. Address any provisions that might affect the trustee's ability to engage in specific transactions, such as restrictions on real property sales, requirements for beneficiary consent, or limitations on borrowing. If the trust contains spendthrift provisions, restraints on alienation, or other protective clauses that might affect creditor claims, these should be noted in general terms. The goal is to provide sufficient information for third parties to understand the trust's legitimacy and the context of the trustee's authority without compromising the privacy that makes a certificate of trust valuable.

## Section 5: Governing Law, Revocability, and Amendment Status

Explicitly state the jurisdiction whose laws govern the interpretation and administration of the trust, including both the state and, if relevant, the specific county where the trust was executed or is being administered. Reaffirm the trust's current revocability status and identify who holds the power to revoke, if applicable. Disclose whether the trust has been amended or restated, providing the dates of any amendments and confirming that the certificate reflects the trust as currently in effect. If the trust contains provisions regarding its own amendment, describe who has the power to amend and whether any limitations apply. Address any choice of law provisions that might affect how the trust is interpreted in different jurisdictions, particularly if the trust holds property in multiple states.

## Section 6: Trustee Certification and Sworn Statement

Include a formal certification statement in which the trustee(s) affirm under penalty of perjury that: the trust identified in this certificate is in full force and effect; the trustee(s) named herein are duly qualified and acting; the trust has not been revoked, modified, or amended except as specifically disclosed; the powers described are accurate and complete for purposes of the contemplated transaction; and no provisions of the trust instrument limit the trustee's authority in ways not disclosed in this certificate. The certification should explicitly state that third parties may rely on the representations made in this certificate and that the trustee accepts personal liability for any material misrepresentations. This sworn statement transforms the certificate from a mere summary into a legally binding representation upon which third parties may rely.

## Section 7: Execution, Acknowledgment, and Notarization

Provide clearly designated signature lines for all acting trustees, with space for each to print their name and title beneath their signature. Include a date line for each signature. Below the trustee signatures, include a notarial certificate appropriate for the governing jurisdiction, with space for the notary public to affix their seal and signature. The notarial acknowledgment should confirm that the trustee(s) personally appeared before the notary, were identified, and acknowledged executing the certificate as their free act and deed. Ensure the notarial language complies with the specific requirements of the state where the certificate will be executed, as notarial forms vary by jurisdiction. Some states may require specific language regarding the trustee's capacity or the document's purpose. If the certificate will be recorded or used in multiple jurisdictions, consider whether additional acknowledgments or certifications may be necessary.

## Drafting Standards and Professional Considerations

Throughout the certificate, maintain formal legal language while ensuring clarity and precision. Every factual statement must be verifiable against the original trust instrument. Avoid legal conclusions or interpretations; state facts directly from the trust document. Be mindful that this certificate may be relied upon by title companies, financial institutions, and other third parties who will not see the complete trust agreement. Any ambiguity or omission could delay transactions or expose the trustee to liability. Consider the specific purpose for which the certificate is being prepared and ensure it addresses the particular concerns of the intended recipient. If the certificate will be recorded in land records, verify compliance with local recording requirements regarding format, paper size, margins, and font size. Remember that a Certificate of Trust is a powerful legal instrument that carries the same weight as the trust agreement itself for purposes of establishing trustee authority, and it must be prepared with corresponding care and accuracy.

name: Certificate of Withdrawal (Foreign Corp)
summary: Drafts a comprehensive Certificate of Withdrawal for a foreign corporation ceasing business operations in a specific US jurisdiction. Incorporates state-specific statutory requirements, corporate entity details, and necessary research on filing guidelines. Use when formally terminating a foreign corporation's authority to transact business in a state.
content:
# Certificate of Withdrawal for Foreign Corporation - Enhanced Workflow

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Certificate of Withdrawal for a foreign corporation ceasing business operations in a specific jurisdiction. This is a formal corporate document that must comply with state-specific filing requirements and serve as the official record of the corporation's withdrawal from doing business in the jurisdiction.

## Document Purpose and Legal Context

Begin by understanding that a Certificate of Withdrawal is a statutory filing required when a foreign corporation (one incorporated in another state or country) wishes to formally cease conducting business in a jurisdiction where it was previously authorized. This document has significant legal implications: it terminates the corporation's authority to transact business, releases the registered agent from further obligations, and establishes the effective date for tax and regulatory purposes. The withdrawal does not absolve the corporation of existing liabilities or obligations incurred while doing business in the state.

## Research and Information Gathering

Start by searching the user's uploaded documents for essential corporate information including the exact legal name of the foreign corporation, its state or country of incorporation, the date it was originally authorized to transact business in the withdrawal jurisdiction, current registered agent details, principal office address, and any relevant corporate resolutions authorizing the withdrawal. Extract specific facts such as entity identification numbers, dates of authorization, and officer names with their titles.

Conduct thorough research on the specific state's requirements for certificates of withdrawal by examining official Secretary of State websites, administrative codes, and filing guidelines. Each jurisdiction has unique requirements regarding format, required statements, filing fees, tax clearances, and supporting documentation. Identify whether the state requires specific statutory language, particular attestations about ceased business activities, tax clearance certificates, certificates of good standing from the home jurisdiction, or final tax returns. Verify current filing fees and processing procedures.

## Document Structure and Required Elements

**Header and Jurisdictional Information**: Draft a formal header identifying the document as a \

and clearly stating both the jurisdiction where the withdrawal is being filed and the corporation's home jurisdiction of incorporation. Include the complete legal name of the foreign corporation exactly as it appears in the original certificate of authority, along with any alternate names or DBAs under which it conducted business.

**Corporate Identity and Authorization Details**: Present comprehensive entity information including the corporation's complete legal name, jurisdiction of incorporation, date of incorporation if relevant to state requirements, the date the corporation was granted authority to transact business in the withdrawal state (with reference to the certificate of authority number if applicable), the corporation's principal office address in its home jurisdiction, and complete registered agent information including name and address in the withdrawal state.

**Withdrawal Declaration and Compliance Statements**: Draft clear, unambiguous statements declaring the corporation's intent to withdraw from conducting business in the jurisdiction and surrender its certificate of authority. Include affirmative representations that the corporation has ceased transacting business in the state, that all taxes and fees owed to the state have been paid or adequately provided for, that all known debts and obligations in the state have been satisfied or adequate provision has been made for their payment, and that the corporation consents to service of process in any proceeding arising from business conducted in the state while authorized. If the state requires specific statutory language regarding post-withdrawal service of process, include the exact required text and designate the appropriate agent or official for such service.

**Effective Date and Supporting Documentation**: Specify the requested effective date of withdrawal, noting whether it is upon filing or a future date if permitted by state law. Reference all required attachments including tax clearance certificates from the state department of revenue, certificates of good standing or compliance from the home jurisdiction if required, evidence of publication if the state mandates newspaper notice of withdrawal, and any final tax returns or reports. Ensure each attachment is properly labeled and corresponds to state-specific requirements.

**Execution and Certification**: Conclude with proper execution blocks for authorized corporate officers, typically requiring the signature of the president, vice president, or other authorized officer as specified by state law and the corporation's governing documents. Include typed names and titles beneath signature lines. If the state requires notarization, provide a complete notary acknowledgment block with appropriate language for the jurisdiction. Some states may require corporate seal attestation or secretary certification—include these elements if mandated.

## Quality Assurance and Finalization

Before finalizing the document, verify that all state-specific requirements have been addressed, including any unique statutory language, required attachments, proper execution formalities, and filing fee information. Ensure consistency between the corporate name as used throughout the document and as it appears in official records. Confirm that all dates are accurate and that the effective date complies with state timing requirements. Cross-reference the withdrawal certificate against the original certificate of authority to ensure all required information is addressed.

Create the final Certificate of Withdrawal as a formal legal document with professional formatting, appropriate spacing and margins for filing, clear section headings, and proper legal citation format for any referenced statutes or regulations. The document should be immediately suitable for execution and filing with the appropriate state authority.

name: Certified Claim under Contracts Disputes Act
summary: Drafts a comprehensive Certified Claim under the Contract Disputes Act (CDA), 41 U.S.C. §§ 7101-7109, for government contractors disputing federal contract issues. Ensures strict compliance with FAR Part 33 requirements, including proper header, contract background, factual support, damages calculation, and certification to preserve appeal rights. Use when submitting formal claims to contracting officers before litigation or appeal.
content:
# Enhanced Prompt: Certified Claim under the Contract Disputes Act

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Certified Claim under the Contract Disputes Act (CDA), 41 U.S.C. §§ 7101-7109. This is a formal legal document that must comply with strict regulatory requirements set forth in the Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) Part 33 and established case law interpreting the CDA. The claim must be precise, well-supported, and properly certified to preserve the claimant's rights to appeal and judicial review.

## Initial Document Review and Information Gathering

Begin by conducting a thorough review of all available contract documents, correspondence, and supporting materials. Search through uploaded documents to identify and extract critical information including the complete contract number with all modification numbers, the exact contract award date, the full legal names and addresses of all parties, the contracting officer's name and official title, and the total contract value. Extract specific contract language from relevant clauses including the disputes clause, changes clause, differing site conditions clause, and any other provisions that form the basis of the claim. Identify and catalog all correspondence between the parties that relates to the dispute, noting specific dates, sender and recipient names and titles, and the substance of each communication. Gather all contemporaneous documentation including daily reports, progress logs, meeting minutes, photographs, and financial records that support the factual narrative and damages calculation.

## Document Header and Foundational Elements

Construct a complete header section that establishes all foundational elements required for proper claim submission. Present the full legal name and complete address of the claimant contractor exactly as it appears in the contract documents. Identify the contracting officer by full name, official title, agency, and office address. State the complete contract number including all modification numbers, the contract award date, and the date of claim submission. Verify that all identifying information matches precisely with the official contract documents, as any discrepancies may create jurisdictional issues or delay processing. Include a clear subject line that identifies the document as a \

and briefly describes the nature of the dispute.

## Contract Background and Contextual Framework

Provide a comprehensive yet concise summary of the underlying contract that gives rise to this claim. Describe the contract's purpose and objectives, the detailed scope of work or services to be performed, the period of performance including any option periods, and the total contract value broken down by base period and options if applicable. Present the contract type such as firm-fixed-price, cost-plus-fixed-fee, or time-and-materials, as this affects the legal standards applicable to certain claim theories. Quote verbatim the specific contract clauses that are central to the dispute, ensuring that clause numbers, titles, and dates match the actual incorporated provisions. Reference the contract by its official designation and cite specific sections, paragraphs, exhibits, or attachments that are relevant to the claim. Describe any unique or unusual contract requirements, site conditions, or performance constraints that provide necessary context for understanding the dispute. This section should enable the contracting officer to immediately grasp the contractual framework without needing to retrieve and review the entire contract file.

## Precise Statement of the Claim

Articulate with absolute clarity and specificity the exact nature of the dispute and the precise relief being sought. State unambiguously whether this is a claim for additional monetary compensation, contract time extension, both, or other equitable adjustment to the contract terms. Identify with particularity the specific government action, inaction, directive, or breach that gives rise to the claim. Frame the claim in terms that align with recognized CDA claim categories such as formal or constructive changes to contract requirements, differing site conditions, government-caused delays, defective or ambiguous specifications, superior knowledge, breach of the duty to cooperate, or other established bases for contractor recovery. Specify the exact amount of monetary compensation sought, stated as a definite sum rather than an estimate or range. If seeking a time extension, specify the exact number of calendar days or work days requested and identify the specific contract milestones or completion dates that should be adjusted. The statement must be sufficiently definite to allow the contracting officer to understand exactly what is being claimed and to conduct a meaningful investigation and evaluation of the merits.

## Detailed Factual Foundation and Chronological Narrative

Present a meticulously detailed chronological narrative of all facts supporting the claim. Begin with relevant background circumstances that existed at the time of contract award, including the contractor's understanding of the work requirements, site conditions, or other material aspects of performance. Proceed systematically through each significant event, communication, directive, discovery, or occurrence that contributed to the dispute. For each factual assertion, provide the specific date or time period, identify all individuals involved by full name and official title, describe exactly what occurred or what was communicated, and reference the specific supporting documentation by exhibit number. Search through all available documents to locate and quote relevant passages from correspondence, meeting minutes, daily reports, or other contemporaneous records that corroborate each factual assertion.

Describe in detail what was required and expected under the original contract terms versus what actually occurred or was encountered during performance, highlighting the material discrepancies that caused injury to the contractor. If claiming a change, describe the original contract requirement with specificity, then describe the altered requirement or directive, explaining how the government's action or inaction effectively changed the contractor's obligations. If claiming differing site conditions, describe the site conditions indicated in the contract documents or reasonably inferable from them, then describe the actual conditions encountered, explaining how they differed materially and were not reasonably foreseeable. If claiming delay, establish the critical path of performance, identify the specific government actions or failures that impacted critical path activities, and demonstrate the resulting extension of the performance period.

Include comprehensive details about the contractor's response to the circumstances giving rise to the claim, including any contemporaneous written notices provided to the government, requests for clarification or direction, protests or objections to government directives, and efforts to mitigate damages. Describe the resulting impacts on labor productivity, equipment utilization, material costs, schedule performance, or other measurable aspects of contract performance. Maintain an objective, factual tone throughout this section, presenting facts clearly and completely while avoiding argumentative or inflammatory language. Ensure that the causal connection between government action and contractor injury is unmistakably clear from the factual narrative.

## Legal and Regulatory Basis for Entitlement

Establish the comprehensive legal foundation for the claim by identifying and explaining all applicable statutes, regulations, contract provisions, and legal precedents that support the contractor's entitlement to relief. Begin by citing the Contract Disputes Act, 41 U.S.C. §§ 7101-7109, as the jurisdictional basis for the claim and the authority under which the contracting officer must issue a final decision. Identify and quote the specific FAR provisions that govern the type of claim being asserted. For changes claims, cite FAR 52.243-1 (Changes—Fixed-Price), FAR 52.243-2 (Changes—Cost-Reimbursement), or the applicable changes clause incorporated into the contract, and explain how the facts satisfy the elements of a compensable change. For differing site conditions claims, cite FAR 52.236-2 and explain how the encountered conditions meet the definition of either a Type I or Type II differing site condition. For delay claims, cite the contract's suspension of work clause or other relevant provisions and explain the government's duty not to hinder or delay the contractor's performance.

Research and cite relevant case law from the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals, the Civilian Board of Contract Appeals, the Court of Federal Claims, and the Federal Circuit that supports the legal theories advanced in the claim. For each cited case, provide the full case name, citation, and a brief explanation of the legal principle established and how it applies to the facts of this claim. Explain how the facts of this case satisfy each element required for recovery under the legal theories asserted. Address any potential affirmative defenses or counterarguments the government might raise, such as lack of timely notice, failure to comply with contract procedures, or contractor assumption of risk, and explain with supporting legal authority why these defenses do not defeat the claim. If multiple legal theories support the claim, explain each theory separately while noting that they may be asserted in the alternative.

## Comprehensive Quantum of Damages and Calculation Methodology

Provide an exhaustive breakdown of the monetary amount claimed, organized systematically by cost category and supported by detailed calculations traceable to source documents. Search through all available financial records, accounting ledgers, payroll records, invoices, and job cost reports to extract specific cost data supporting each element of damages. Present the damages calculation using recognized methodologies appropriate to the type of claim being asserted.

For direct costs, itemize all additional labor hours incurred as a result of the compensable event, broken down by labor classification such as project manager, superintendent, foreman, journeyman, and laborer. For each classification, specify the number of additional hours, the applicable hourly rate, and the total cost, with supporting references to payroll records and timesheets. Itemize all additional materials and supplies purchased, identifying each item by description, quantity, unit cost, and total cost, with supporting references to purchase orders and invoices. Itemize all additional equipment costs including rental equipment, owned equipment calculated at appropriate rates, and equipment purchases, with supporting documentation. Identify all additional subcontractor costs with references to subcontract agreements, change orders, and subcontractor invoices.

For indirect costs, calculate overhead, general and administrative expenses, fringe benefits, and other indirect costs using the rates established in the contract, disclosed in the contractor's accounting system, or calculated using methods accepted by the Defense Contract Audit Agency. Explain the methodology used to calculate each indirect cost rate and demonstrate that the rates are reasonable and properly allocable to the contract. If the contract establishes specific indirect cost rates, apply those rates. If not, explain the basis for the rates used and provide supporting documentation from the contractor's accounting records.

For delay-related costs, specify the exact period of delay measured in calendar days or work days, identify the specific contract activities that were delayed, and demonstrate through critical path method analysis or other accepted scheduling methodology that the delayed activities were on the critical path and caused an extension of the overall contract performance period. Calculate extended field office overhead costs by identifying all personnel and expenses that were required to remain on site during the delay period, including project management, supervision, field office rent, utilities, and equipment. If claiming home office overhead costs, apply an accepted methodology such as the Eichleay formula, explaining each step of the calculation and providing supporting data for total contract billings, total company overhead, contract performance period, and delay period.

For loss of efficiency or productivity impacts, employ recognized methodologies such as the measured mile analysis, industry studies, or other methods accepted by the boards and courts. Provide detailed supporting data demonstrating the baseline productivity rate achieved during unimpacted periods, the actual productivity rate achieved during impacted periods, the quantified difference, and the causal link between the government action and the decreased productivity. Present any expert analysis or reports supporting the productivity loss calculation.

Calculate and include interest on the claimed amount from the date each cost was incurred or the date the claim accrued, whichever is appropriate, through the date of the contracting officer's final decision, as provided under 41 U.S.C. § 7109. Use the interest rates established by the Secretary of the Treasury pursuant to the CDA. Present the total claim amount clearly and unambiguously as a definite sum, with a summary table showing all major cost categories and the total amount demanded.

## Mandatory Certification Requirement and Signatory Authority

For all claims exceeding $100,000, include the mandatory certification statement required by 41 U.S.C. § 7103(b)(1). The certification must contain the precise statutory language without modification or paraphrasing. Present the certification as follows, formatted as a separate section with appropriate spacing and emphasis:

\

This certification must be signed by a senior company official with actual authority to bind the contractor, such as a corporate officer including the president, vice president, chief financial officer, or other authorized representative. The signatory must not be an attorney or consultant representing the contractor, as the certification must come from a company official with personal knowledge of the claim's preparation and the authority to commit the company. Include below the certification statement a signature line with the signatory's printed name, official title, company name, and date of signature. Verify that the signatory has appropriate authority under the company's corporate governance documents to execute such certifications. Note that for claims of $100,000 or less, the statutory certification is not required, but the claim must still be submitted in writing to the contracting officer and must request a final decision.

## Supporting Documentation, Exhibits, and Evidentiary Foundation

Compile and organize all documentary evidence supporting the claim into a comprehensive exhibit package. Create a detailed exhibit index that lists each attachment with an exhibit number, document title or description, date of the document, and a brief explanation of its relevance to the claim. Organize exhibits in a logical sequence that corresponds to the chronological narrative and the structure of the claim document.

Essential supporting documents that should be included as exhibits are the original contract and all modifications, amendments, or supplemental agreements; all correspondence between the parties relevant to the dispute including letters, emails, meeting minutes, and memoranda; all contemporaneous project documentation including daily reports, progress schedules, superintendent's logs, and inspection records; photographs, drawings, or other demonstrative evidence showing site conditions, work progress, or other relevant physical facts; all financial records supporting the damages calculation including invoices, purchase orders, payroll records, accounting ledgers, and job cost reports; any expert reports, analyses, or opinions supporting technical or damages aspects of the claim; and any other documents referenced in the claim narrative.

Search through all available documents to ensure that every factual assertion made in the claim narrative is supported by referenced exhibit evidence. For each significant fact stated in the claim, include a parenthetical citation to the specific exhibit and page number that supports that fact. Ensure that all cost elements included in the damages calculation are traceable to specific source documents included in the exhibits. If voluminous documentation exists, consider providing representative samples in the exhibits while noting that complete documentation is available for the contracting officer's review upon request.

## Professional Formatting, Submission Requirements, and Procedural Compliance

Present the claim in a professional format that facilitates review and evaluation by the contracting officer. Use clear section headings that correspond to the major elements of the claim. Number all paragraphs consecutively throughout the document to enable easy reference in subsequent correspondence or the contracting officer's final decision. Use consistent citation format for all legal authorities, following Bluebook or other standard legal citation format. Include a table of contents if the claim exceeds twenty pages. Use appropriate font size and spacing to ensure readability.

Conclude the claim with a clear and unambiguous demand for relief. State specifically that the contractor demands a final decision from the contracting officer on this claim as required by the Contract Disputes Act and FAR 33.211. Note that for claims exceeding $100,000, the contracting officer must issue a final decision within sixty days or notify the contractor of the time within which a decision will be issued. Expressly preserve all rights to appeal an adverse final decision to the appropriate board of contract appeals or to the United States Court of Federal Claims, as provided by 41 U.S.C. § 7104.

Ensure that the claim is submitted to the proper contracting officer, meaning the individual with authority to enter into, administer, or terminate the contract and make related determinations and findings. Verify the contracting officer's current contact information and preferred method of submission. Submit the claim with proof of delivery such as certified mail return receipt, courier tracking confirmation, or email delivery receipt, as the date of receipt by the contracting officer triggers important procedural timelines under the CDA. Retain complete copies of the claim and all exhibits for the contractor's records. Consider whether to submit the claim in both hard copy and electronic format to facilitate the contracting officer's review.

name: Change in Control Agreement
summary: Drafts a comprehensive Change in Control Agreement for executive-level employees to provide protections during corporate ownership transitions. Balances executive security and retention incentives with company flexibility, tax compliance, and governance considerations. Use in transactional employment matters for mergers, acquisitions, or control changes.
content:
# Change in Control Agreement - Professional Drafting Workflow

## Your Role and Objective

You are an experienced corporate attorney specializing in executive compensation and transactional employment matters. Your task is to draft a comprehensive, legally enforceable Change in Control Agreement that protects executive-level employees during corporate ownership transitions while safeguarding the company's legitimate business interests. This agreement must balance the executive's need for security and retention incentives against the company's desire for flexibility and cost management, all while navigating complex tax regulations and corporate governance considerations.

## Initial Information Gathering and Document Review

Before beginning the drafting process, conduct a thorough review of any existing employment agreements, equity award documents, or prior change in control arrangements that may be relevant to this executive. Search through uploaded documents to identify the executive's current compensation structure, including base salary, target bonus percentages, outstanding equity awards, and any existing severance or retention arrangements. Extract specific details about the company's corporate structure, including its state of incorporation, legal entity type, and any parent-subsidiary relationships that might affect how change in control events are defined. If the company has previously entered into similar agreements with other executives, review those documents to ensure consistency in approach, definitions, and benefit levels unless there are legitimate business reasons for differentiation based on the executive's role or seniority.

Identify any relevant company policies, including those governing severance, equity administration, or executive compensation, as these may need to be referenced or superseded by the agreement. Pay particular attention to any existing equity incentive plan documents, as these often contain provisions regarding acceleration upon change in control that must be coordinated with the agreement you are drafting. If the company is publicly traded, review recent proxy statements to understand the compensation committee's philosophy regarding change in control protections and whether there are any shareholder-approved guidelines or limitations that must be observed.

## Drafting the Introductory Provisions and Recitals

Begin the agreement with a clear, professional caption that identifies it as a \

and includes the date of execution. In the opening paragraph, identify both parties with complete legal precision: the company should be identified by its full legal name, state of incorporation or organization, and entity type (corporation, limited liability company, etc.), while the executive should be identified by full legal name and current title. Consider including brief recitals that establish the context and purpose of the agreement, explaining that the company recognizes the executive's valuable contributions, that the possibility of a change in control may create uncertainty and distraction, and that the company desires to encourage the executive's continued attention and dedication by providing certain protections and benefits.

The recitals should establish that the agreement is intended to align the executive's interests with those of shareholders by removing concerns about personal financial security that might otherwise influence the executive's judgment regarding potential transactions. Acknowledge that the executive's continued employment and willingness to serve the company's best interests during any potential change in control period is valuable consideration for the company's commitments under the agreement. These recitals serve not only to provide context but also to establish the mutual consideration and business purpose that support the agreement's enforceability.

## Constructing Comprehensive and Enforceable Definitions

The definitions section forms the foundation upon which the entire agreement operates, and each definition must be crafted with precision to avoid ambiguity while remaining practical to administer. The definition of \

requires particular attention, as it determines when the agreement's protections become operative. Structure this definition to capture genuine changes in corporate ownership or control while avoiding false triggers from routine transactions or market fluctuations.

The first prong of the Change in Control definition should address direct acquisition of voting securities, typically triggered when any person or group acquires beneficial ownership of more than fifty percent of the combined voting power of the company's then-outstanding securities entitled to vote generally in the election of directors. Include appropriate references to Sections 13(d) and 14(d) of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 for determining beneficial ownership and group formation, and consider whether to exclude from this definition any acquisitions directly from the company, acquisitions by the company or its subsidiaries, acquisitions by employee benefit plans maintained by the company, or acquisitions by any person who owned more than fifty percent immediately prior to the transaction.

The second prong should address merger, consolidation, reorganization, or similar business combination transactions, typically triggered when such a transaction results in the company's shareholders immediately before the transaction owning less than fifty percent of the combined voting power of the surviving or resulting entity's outstanding securities. This formulation captures transactions where the company is acquired even if it remains the surviving legal entity. Consider whether to measure ownership by reference to voting power, equity value, or both, and whether to include exceptions for transactions among commonly controlled entities or transactions undertaken solely to change the company's state of incorporation.

The third prong should capture asset sales, typically triggered by the sale, transfer, lease, or other disposition of all or substantially all of the company's assets in a single transaction or series of related transactions. Define \

with sufficient clarity, either by reference to a specific percentage of asset value or by incorporating the Delaware case law standard that has developed around this concept. Consider whether to exclude asset sales in the ordinary course of business, sales to affiliates, or sales followed by distribution of proceeds to shareholders in liquidation.

Consider whether to include a fourth prong addressing significant board composition changes, such as a situation where individuals who constituted the board at the beginning of a specified period cease to constitute at least a majority of the board, unless their successors were approved by at least a majority of the incumbent directors. This provision can capture hostile takeovers accomplished through proxy contests, but it requires careful drafting to avoid triggering the agreement when the board voluntarily refreshes its composition as part of normal governance practices.

The definition of \

must protect the company's ability to terminate for serious misconduct while providing the executive with clear standards and procedural protections. Begin with conviction of, or plea of guilty or no contest to, a felony or any crime involving fraud, dishonesty, or moral turpitude, as such conduct fundamentally undermines the employment relationship and typically cannot be cured. Include willful and continued failure to substantially perform assigned duties after receiving written notice specifying the deficiencies and a reasonable opportunity to cure, typically thirty days. This formulation requires that the failure be both willful (not mere disagreement about strategy or good faith errors in judgment) and continued (not isolated incidents), and it provides procedural protection through notice and cure rights.

Address willful engagement in conduct that is demonstrably and materially injurious to the company, whether financially or reputationally, without requiring that such conduct be undertaken in bad faith. Include material breach of fiduciary duties owed to the company, gross negligence or willful misconduct in the performance of duties, and material violation of written company policies after notice and opportunity to cure. For each ground, consider whether to require that the company provide written notice specifying the conduct alleged to constitute Cause and whether to provide the executive with an opportunity to cure or contest the determination before a neutral decision-maker.

The definition of \

provides the executive with protection against constructive termination and must be drafted to capture material adverse changes in the employment relationship while avoiding hair-trigger provisions that could be invoked for minor or temporary changes. Include material diminution in the executive's authority, duties, or responsibilities, recognizing that what constitutes \

will depend on the executive's level and role. For a chief executive officer, this might include removal from the board of directors, assignment of duties inconsistent with the CEO position, or requirement to report to anyone other than the board. For other executives, consider whether to define materiality by reference to specific responsibilities or to leave it to reasonable interpretation.

Include material reduction in base salary or target annual bonus opportunity, typically defined as any reduction not applicable to similarly situated executives generally or not consented to in writing by the executive. Some agreements specify a threshold percentage reduction (such as ten percent) to avoid triggering Good Reason for de minimis adjustments, while others treat any unconsented reduction as material. Address whether reductions in actual bonus payments due to company or individual performance should constitute Good Reason, or whether the protection extends only to target opportunity.

Include relocation of the executive's principal place of employment by more than a specified distance without the executive's consent, typically thirty-five to fifty miles from the current location. This protects the executive from being constructively terminated through forced relocation while allowing reasonable office moves within the same metropolitan area. Consider whether to measure distance from the executive's current office or from the executive's residence, and whether to include exceptions for temporary relocations or for executives whose roles inherently involve travel or multiple work locations.

Critically, the Good Reason definition must include procedural requirements that prevent the executive from claiming Good Reason based on stale or cured conditions. Require that the executive provide written notice to the company of the existence of the condition claimed to constitute Good Reason within a specified period after the executive first becomes aware of such condition, typically sixty to ninety days. Provide the company with a cure period following such notice, typically thirty days, during which the company may remedy the condition. Require that if the company does not cure the condition, the executive must terminate employment within a specified period thereafter, typically thirty to sixty days, or the right to claim Good Reason with respect to that condition shall be deemed waived. These procedural requirements ensure that both parties have clarity about whether Good Reason exists and prevent the executive from stockpiling grievances to be asserted at a strategically advantageous time.

Define \

as a termination of the executive's employment either by the company without Cause or by the executive for Good Reason, in either case occurring during the Protection Period. This definition creates the \

structure that is now standard in change in control agreements, ensuring that benefits are paid only when both a change in control occurs and the executive's employment is actually terminated under specified circumstances.\n\nDefine the \

as the period during which a Qualifying Termination will trigger benefits under the agreement. The most common structure is a period beginning on the date of a Change in Control and ending twelve to twenty-four months thereafter, with longer periods for more senior executives. Consider whether to include a pre-change in control protection period, typically three to six months before the Change in Control, to address situations where the executive is terminated in anticipation of or in connection with a transaction that ultimately closes. If including such a provision, require that the termination be at the request of a party to the transaction or otherwise in connection with the transaction to avoid paying benefits for unrelated terminations that happen to occur shortly before a change in control.

## Specifying Severance Benefits with Precision and Tax Compliance

The heart of the agreement lies in the severance benefits that will be provided upon a QualifyingInation, and these must be specified with mathematical precision while addressing all relevant tax and timing considerations. Begin the severance benefits section with a clear statement of the triggering event: \

Specify the cash severance payment as a lump sum equal to a specified multiple of the sum of the executive's base salary and target annual bonus. The multiple typically ranges from one times for mid-level executives to three times for chief executive officers, with one and one-half to two times being common for senior vice presidents and C-suite executives other than the CEO. Define the base salary component as the executive's annual base salary as in effect immediately prior to the Qualifying Termination or, if higher, immediately prior to the Change in Control, ensuring that the executive is protected against salary reductions that might occur during the Protection Period. Define the target bonus component as the executive's target annual bonus opportunity for the year in which the Qualifying Termination occurs, expressed as a percentage of base salary or as a dollar amount.

Address the timing of the cash severance payment with careful attention to Section 409A of the Internal Revenue Code. For executives who are \

of publicly traded companies, Section 409A requires a six-month delay in payment of amounts that constitute deferred compensation and are triggered by separation from service. Include language stating that the cash severance payment shall be made in a single lump sum within a specified period following the Qualifying Termination, typically thirty to sixty days, except that if the executive is a specified employee and the payment would be subject to additional tax under Section 409A if paid within six months of separation from service, payment shall be delayed until the first business day following the six-month anniversary of the separation from service, with any delayed amounts paid with interest at a specified rate.

Consider whether to include a pro-rated annual bonus for the year of termination, calculated based on actual company performance through the termination date and the number of days the executive was employed during the performance period. Some agreements provide for payment of the full target bonus regardless of actual performance or timing of termination, while others exclude any annual bonus payment on the theory that the severance multiple already compensates for lost bonus opportunity. If including a pro-rated or full-year bonus, specify whether it will be paid at the same time as the cash severance or at the time bonuses are paid to continuing executives, and address the Section 409A implications of each approach.

The equity acceleration provisions require detailed attention to ensure that all forms of equity compensation are addressed and that the treatment of performance-based awards is clearly specified. State that upon a Qualifying Termination, one hundred percent of all outstanding and unvested equity awards held by the executive, including stock options, stock appreciation rights, restricted stock, restricted stock units, performance shares, performance units, and any other equity-based compensation, shall immediately accelerate and become fully vested and, in the case of stock options and stock appreciation rights, exercisable. For performance-based awards, specify the level of performance that will be deemed achieved for purposes of determining the number of shares or units that vest, with the most common approaches being target level performance, maximum level performance, or actual performance measured through the date of the Change in Control or the date of termination.

Address the post-termination exercise period for stock options and stock appreciation rights, as the standard ninety-day post-termination exercise period is often inadequate for executives who may face trading restrictions or who may wish to defer the tax consequences of exercise. Provide that stock options and stock appreciation rights that become vested and exercisable in connection with a Qualifying Termination shall remain exercisable for a specified extended period, typically twelve to twenty-four months following termination or, if earlier, through the original expiration date of the award. Include appropriate language confirming that this extended exercise period supersedes any contrary provision in the applicable equity incentive plan or award agreement.

Consider whether the agreement should provide for \

acceleration upon a Change in Control regardless of whether the executive's employment is terminated, or whether acceleration should occur only upon a Qualifying Termination (double trigger). Single trigger acceleration is increasingly disfavored by institutional investors and proxy advisory firms because it can result in significant value transfer to executives even when they remain employed and may create disincentives for potential acquirers. Double trigger acceleration is now the market standard for newly negotiated agreements, though some executives with significant bargaining power may negotiate for single trigger treatment of at least a portion of their equity awards.

The benefits continuation provisions should specify that the company shall provide or pay for the executive's continued participation in the company's group health, dental, and vision insurance plans for a specified period following the Qualifying Termination, typically twelve to twenty-four months, or if earlier, until the executive becomes eligible for substantially similar coverage through a subsequent employer. Structure this benefit as company-paid COBRA continuation coverage, with the executive responsible for making timely COBRA elections and for notifying the company if the executive becomes eligible for comparable coverage with a subsequent employer. Address the tax implications of company-paid COBRA premiums, noting that such payments may be taxable income to the executive under recent IRS guidance, and consider whether to provide a tax gross-up for this purpose or to structure the benefit as a taxable cash payment equal to the COBRA premium amount.

Consider whether to include continuation of other welfare benefits such as life insurance, disability insurance, financial planning services, or executive perquisites, recognizing that each additional benefit increases the cost and complexity of the arrangement. If the company maintains a supplemental executive retirement plan or nonqualified deferred compensation plan, address whether and how the executive's benefits under such plans will be affected by the Qualifying Termination, including whether additional service credit will be granted for the severance period or whether account balances will be immediately distributed.

## Navigating Section 280G and Excise Tax Considerations

The treatment of potential excise taxes under Sections 280G and 4999 of the Internal Revenue Code represents one of the most complex and heavily negotiated aspects of change in control agreements. Section 280G disallows the company's tax deduction for \

while Section 4999 imposes a twenty percent excise tax on the executive who receives such payments, in addition to ordinary income tax. Parachute payments are payments that are contingent on a change in control, and they become excess parachute payments subject to these penalties when they equal or exceed three times the executive's \

which is generally the executive's average annual compensation over the five years preceding the change in control.

Select one of three standard approaches to addressing this issue and articulate it with complete clarity. Under a full gross-up approach, which is now rare in newly negotiated agreements but may still exist in legacy contracts, the company agrees to pay the executive an additional amount sufficient to place the executive in the same after-tax position as if no excise tax had been imposed under Section 4999. This requires calculating not only the excise tax itself but also the additional income and excise taxes that will be imposed on the gross-up payment, resulting in a pyramiding calculation. Specify that the gross-up payment shall be made at the same time as the underlying payments that trigger the excise tax, or if later, promptly after the final determination of the excise tax amount. Include provisions addressing how the gross-up will be calculated if the IRS subsequently challenges the initial determination, requiring either additional gross-up payments or repayment by the executive if the final excise tax is different from the initial calculation.

Under a modified cutback or \

approach, which represents a middle ground, the payments and benefits shall be reduced to the extent necessary to avoid triggering the excise tax under Section 280G, but only if such reduction would result in the executive receiving a greater after-tax amount than the executive would receive if the full payments were made and the excise tax were imposed. This requires a calculation at the time of the change in control comparing two scenarios: the executive's after-tax proceeds if payments are reduced to 2.99 times the base amount (thus avoiding the excise tax entirely), versus the executive's after-tax proceeds if full payments are made and the executive pays the twenty percent excise tax plus ordinary income tax on the full amount. Specify that if the payments are to be reduced, the reduction shall occur in the order that results in the best economic outcome for the executive, typically by first reducing cash payments before equity acceleration, and within each category, by reducing amounts that are subject to Section 409A before reducing amounts that are exempt from or compliant with Section 409A.

Under a no gross-up approach, which is now the market standard for newly negotiated agreements, the executive bears full responsibility for any excise taxes imposed under Section 4999, and the payments and benefits are not reduced to avoid the excise tax. This approach is simplest to administer and is favored by institutional investors and proxy advisory firms as it does not provide executives with a windfall at company expense. If adopting this approach, include a simple statement that the executive shall be solely responsible for any excise taxes imposed under Section 4999 with respect to payments and benefits provided under this agreement, and that no reduction in payments or gross-up shall be provided.

Regardless of which approach is selected, require that all calculations and determinations regarding the application of Section 280G be performed by a nationally recognized accounting firm or tax counsel selected and paid for by the company, and that such firm's determinations shall be final and binding on both parties absent manifest error. Require that the firm provide detailed supporting calculations to both the company and the executive, and address how the costs of any subsequent IRS audit or dispute regarding Section 280G treatment will be allocated between the parties.

## Establishing Conditions Precedent and Release Requirements

The executive's receipt of severance benefits must be expressly conditioned upon satisfaction of certain requirements that protect the company's interests and ensure an orderly transition. The most critical condition is the executive's execution and non-revocation of a general release of claims in a form reasonably satisfactory to the company. Specify that the release must be executed and returned to the company within the time period specified by the company, which shall not exceed sixty days following the Qualifying Termination for executives age forty or older (to comply with the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act) or twenty-one days for younger executives. Require that the release become effective and irrevocable in accordance with its terms, which typically means that any statutory revocation period (seven days under the OWBPA) must expire without the executive revoking the release.

Describe the scope of the release, specifying that it must release all claims arising out of or relating to the executive's employment with the company and the termination of that employment, including but not limited to claims under federal, state, and local employment discrimination laws, wage and hour laws, and common law claims for wrongful termination, breach of contract, and tort. Include appropriate carve-outs for claims that cannot be released as a matter of law, such as claims for workers' compensation benefits, unemployment insurance benefits, and rights to indemnification or coverage under directors and officers liability insurance policies. Confirm that the release does not waive any rights or benefits under this agreement itself, as the release is a condition to receiving those benefits rather than a waiver of them.

Address the timing of severance payments in light of the release requirement and Section 409A compliance. The safest approach is to specify that all severance payments and benefits shall be provided on the sixtieth day following the Qualifying Termination, provided that the release has been executed and has become effective and irrevocable by such date. This ensures that the payment date is objectively determinable and does not depend on when the executive chooses to sign the release, which could create Section 409A issues if the executive has discretion over the taxable year of payment. Include language stating that if the sixty-day period spans two taxable years, payment shall be made in the second taxable year, as required by Section 409A regulations.

Consider whether to include additional conditions such as the executive's return of all company property, compliance with post-employment restrictive covenants, and cooperation with the company in transitioning responsibilities and responding to inquiries about matters handled during the executive's employment. If including a cooperation requirement, specify that the executive shall be reimbursed for reasonable out-of-pocket expenses incurred in providing such cooperation and shall be compensated at a reasonable hourly rate for time spent beyond a de minimis amount, to avoid creating an indefinite and uncompensated obligation.

## Incorporating Essential Legal and Administrative Provisions

The agreement must include a comprehensive set of legal provisions that govern its interpretation, administration, and enforcement. Begin with a section addressing the executive's obligations during employment and following termination, including compliance with any restrictive covenant agreements such as non-competition, non-solicitation, and confidentiality agreements. Specify that the executive's obligations under any such agreements remain in full force and effect and are not modified or superseded by this agreement, except that if this agreement provides for payment of severance benefits, such payment shall constitute the sole consideration for the executive's post-employment restrictive covenants and shall supersede any other severance or consideration provisions in the restrictive covenant agreement.

Include a mutual non-disparagement provision that prohibits both the executive and the company (acting through its officers, directors, and spokespersons) from making any public statements that disparage or criticize the other party. Define appropriate exceptions for truthful statements required by law, made in legal proceedings, or made in the good faith performance of duties to the company. Consider whether to limit the company's non-disparagement obligation to specific individuals or to extend it to all officers and directors, recognizing that broader coverage provides more protection to the executive but may be more difficult for the company to police and enforce.

Address the relationship between this agreement and other agreements or arrangements between the parties. Include a supersession clause stating that this agreement supersedes any prior change in control, severance, or similar agreements between the parties, except that it does not supersede the executive's employment agreement, offer letter, restrictive covenant agreement, or equity award agreements except to the extent those agreements provide for lesser benefits in connection with a change in control or Qualifying Termination. Specify that in the event of any conflict between this agreement and any equity award agreement regarding vesting acceleration or post-termination exercise periods in connection with a change in control, the provisions of this agreement shall control.

Include a section addressing Section 409A compliance in comprehensive detail. State that this agreement is intended to comply with Section 409A of the Internal Revenue Code or to qualify for an exemption therefrom, and that the agreement shall be interpreted, operated, and administered in a manner consistent with this intent. Specify that each payment under this agreement shall be treated as a separate payment for purposes of Section 409A, and that the right to any series of payments hereunder is to be treated as a right to a series of separate payments. Include the standard provision that any reimbursements or in-kind benefits provided under this agreement shall be subject to the following rules: the amount of expenses eligible for reimbursement or in-kind benefits provided during any calendar year shall not affect the amount of expenses eligible for reimbursement or in-kind benefits provided in any other calendar year, the reimbursement of an eligible expense shall be made no later than the end of the calendar year following the calendar year in which the expense was incurred, and the right to reimbursement or in-kind benefits shall not be subject to liquidation or exchange for another benefit.

Specify that any reference in this agreement to the executive's \
or similar phrases shall be construed to require a \

within the meaning of Section 409A, and include the regulatory definition of separation from service for reference. Address the specified employee delay requirement by stating that if the executive is a specified employee at the time of separation from service and any payment hereunder would be subject to additional tax under Section 409A if paid within six months of separation from service, such payment shall be delayed as described in the severance benefits section. Include a savings clause stating that if any provision of this agreement would cause the executive to incur any additional tax or interest under Section 409A, the company and the executive shall cooperate in good faith to amend the provision to avoid such additional tax or interest while preserving the economic benefit to the executive to the maximum extent possible, but clarify that the company makes no representation or warranty regarding the tax treatment of any payments under this agreement and shall have no obligation to indemnify or otherwise protect the executive from any tax consequences, including consequences under Section 409A.

Specify the governing law that will apply to the agreement, typically the law of the state where the company is headquartered or incorporated, without regard to conflicts of law principles. Include a venue or forum selection clause specifying where any disputes must be brought, and consider whether to include an arbitration provision requiring that disputes be resolved through binding arbitration rather than litigation. If including arbitration, specify the arbitration rules that will apply (such as JAMS or AAA employment arbitration rules), the location of the arbitration, how the arbitrator will be selected, and how the costs of arbitration will be allocated. Address whether the arbitrator's decision will be final and binding and whether any judicial review will be available.

Include a provision addressing the executive's obligation to mitigate damages, with the standard approach in change in control agreements being that the executive shall have no duty to seek other employment or to mitigate the amount of any payment or benefit provided under the agreement, and that no payment or benefit shall be reduced by any compensation the executive earns from other employment or by any retirement benefits the executive receives. This distinguishes change in control agreements from standard severance arrangements and reflects the understanding that the benefits are intended as retention incentives and transaction bonuses rather than as temporary income replacement.

Address the company's right to offset amounts owed by the executive to the company against severance payments, typically providing that the company may offset only undisputed amounts owed for legitimate business expenses, loans, or advances, and may not offset disputed amounts or amounts that would reduce the severance payment below the minimum required to avoid excise taxes under Section 280G if a cutback provision applies. Include a provision requiring that the company provide written notice to the executive of any proposed offset at least ten days before the payment date, with an opportunity for the executive to dispute the offset.

Include standard contract provisions addressing notices, amendments, waivers, severability, and assignment. Specify that all notices must be in writing and delivered by hand, overnight courier, or certified mail to specified addresses, with notice deemed given upon receipt. Provide that the agreement may be amended only by a written instrument signed by both parties, and that any waiver of a provision must be in writing and shall not constitute a waiver of any other provision or of the same provision on any other occasion. Include a severability clause stating that if any provision is found to be invalid or unenforceable, the remaining provisions shall continue in full force and effect, and the invalid provision shall be modified to the minimum extent necessary to make it valid and enforceable while preserving its intent.

Address assignment by providing that the agreement shall be binding upon and inure to the benefit of the parties and their respective successors and assigns, but that the executive may not assign any rights or obligations hereunder without the company's prior written consent. Specify that the company may assign the agreement to any successor to all or substantially all of its business or assets, whether by merger, consolidation, sale, or otherwise, and that the company shall require any such successor to expressly assume and agree to perform the company's obligations hereunder.
