Define preservation obligations with specificity regarding data sources and timeframes. Identify the custodians whose files must be preserved, the types of data sources including email accounts, network drives, shared folders, cloud storage, mobile devices, and social media accounts. Specify the time period for which data must be preserved, typically extending from a reasonable period before the events at issue through the conclusion of litigation. Address how departing employees' data will be preserved and whether backup tapes or archived data must be retained.

Include provisions for handling particularly burdensome ESI, such as requiring a showing of relevance and need before requiring restoration of backup tapes, forensic imaging of devices, or production of system files. Establish cost-sharing arrangements for discovery that benefits both parties but imposes disproportionate costs on the producing party. Address how the parties will handle duplicates, whether global deduplication across all custodians is appropriate or whether custodian-level deduplication better serves the case needs.

### Implementing Privilege and Protection Procedures

Draft comprehensive procedures for handling privileged and protected information that balance the need to protect legitimate privileges with the practical realities of large-scale document review. Propose a Federal Rule of Evidence 502(d) order that allows parties to claw back inadvertently produced privileged materials without waiving privilege, while also providing that intentional disclosure to third parties waives privilege as to all parties. This provision is critical in modern litigation where document review of hundreds of thousands of pages makes some inadvertent production nearly inevitable.

Specify the timeframe within which a receiving party must assert that produced materials appear privileged, typically within 30 days of production or before using the document in a deposition or filing, whichever comes first. Establish the procedure for clawback, requiring written notice identifying the document with specificity and the basis for the privilege claim, followed by return or destruction of the document and all copies within a specified timeframe, typically 5-10 business days.

Address privilege log requirements with attention to the burden of logging in document-intensive cases. Specify the information required for each entry, typically including document date, author, recipients, document type, and a description of the subject matter sufficient to assess the privilege claim without revealing the privileged information itself. Consider whether the parties will agree to withhold certain categories of documents without logging them, such as communications between counsel and client post-dating the litigation, or communications with counsel for the sole purpose of seeking legal advice where no other business purpose is apparent.

Establish deadlines for serving privilege logs that balance the need for timely information with the practical burden of log preparation. A common approach provides that privilege logs are due 30 days after the completion of each party's document production, or on a rolling basis within 30 days of each production if productions occur in stages. Include provisions for challenging privilege claims, requiring that challenges be raised within a specified time and providing for meet-and-confer efforts before court intervention.

If the case involves common interest arrangements or joint defense agreements, address how materials shared under such arrangements will be handled, ensuring that sharing does not waive privilege while allowing receiving parties to understand what materials they may use and what restrictions apply.

### Proposing Proportional Discovery Limitations

Establish reasonable limitations on discovery that comply with the Federal Rules while addressing the specific needs and characteristics of this case. Specify the number of depositions each side may take, considering the number of parties, the complexity of issues, and the number of individuals with relevant knowledge. A straightforward two-party commercial dispute might warrant 5-10 depositions per side, while a complex multi-party case might require 15-20 or more. Address whether party depositions count against these limits and whether expert depositions are included or treated separately.

Set presumptive deposition duration at seven hours per deponent as provided in Rule 30(d)(1), while acknowledging that the parties may stipulate to longer depositions for particularly knowledgeable witnesses or that court approval may be sought for extended examination. Address logistical issues such as whether depositions will occur in person or remotely via videoconference, where in-person depositions will be held, and how costs for court reporters and videographers will be allocated.

Establish limits on interrogatories that comply with the 25-interrogatory limit under Rule 33(a)(1) while addressing how subparts will be counted. Consider whether the case warrants agreement that discrete subparts will each count as separate interrogatories, or whether related subparts addressing a single topic will count as one interrogatory. Address whether contention interrogatories will be permitted and if so, whether they will be subject to separate limits or timing requirements.

Set limits on requests for admission that balance their utility for narrowing issues with the burden of responding. While Rule 36 imposes no numerical limit, consider whether the parties will agree to a reasonable number such as 25-50 requests per party, with the ability to seek leave for additional requests upon a showing of need.

Address any agreements to limit discovery to specific time periods, geographic locations, or custodians based on the allegations and defenses. If the complaint alleges wrongful conduct during a specific two-year period, consider whether discovery will be limited to that timeframe plus a reasonable period before and after to provide context. If claims relate to specific facilities or business units, consider whether discovery from other locations is necessary or whether limiting discovery reduces burden without prejudicing any party's ability to prove their case.

For cases involving voluminous documents or data, consider proposing a sampling or phased approach where initial discovery from a subset of custodians or time periods informs decisions about whether broader discovery is warranted. This approach allows parties to assess the value of discovery before incurring the full cost while preserving the right to seek additional discovery if the initial phase reveals the need.

### Structuring Phased Discovery When Appropriate

Evaluate whether the case characteristics warrant a phased discovery approach that sequences discovery to address threshold issues first, potentially avoiding unnecessary expense if early phases resolve the case or narrow the issues. Cases involving jurisdictional questions, statute of limitations defenses, or other threshold legal issues may benefit from initial discovery limited to those issues, with broader merits discovery to follow only if the case survives dispositive motions on the threshold issues.

Complex cases involving both liability and damages may warrant bifurcated discovery, with Phase One addressing liability issues and Phase Two addressing damages only if liability is established. This approach can significantly reduce costs in cases where liability is genuinely disputed and damages discovery is expensive, such as cases requiring extensive expert analysis of economic damages or personal injury cases requiring multiple medical experts.

Multi-party cases may benefit from phased discovery that addresses different defendants or different claims sequentially, particularly where some defendants may be dismissed early or where claims against different defendants involve distinct factual issues. Structure the phases to build logically, with each phase informing the next while preserving the option to narrow or conclude discovery if early phases resolve key issues.

When proposing phased discovery, specify clear triggers for moving between phases, such as the court's ruling on a dispositive motion or the completion of specific discovery tasks. Include provisions allowing parties to seek modification of the phasing if circumstances change or if early discovery reveals that the anticipated benefits of phasing will not materialize. Ensure that phasing does not prejudice any party's ability to develop their case or create artificial barriers to discovering relevant information.

## Developing the Proposed Scheduling Order

### Constructing a Realistic and Comprehensive Timeline

Build your proposed schedule by working backward from a realistic trial date, ensuring adequate time for each phase of litigation while maintaining momentum toward resolution. Begin by identifying any external constraints on scheduling, such as court availability, counsel's trial calendar, or business considerations affecting party availability. Search the case documents and local rules to identify any mandatory deadlines or presumptive timelines that apply in this jurisdiction.

Consider the complexity of the legal and factual issues when estimating time needs. Cases involving novel legal questions may require additional time for motion practice and appellate resolution of certified questions. Cases with voluminous documents may need extended fact discovery periods to allow thorough review and analysis. Cases requiring multiple experts across different disciplines need sufficient time for expert analysis, report preparation, and expert depositions.

Account for the number of parties and the coordination challenges in multi-party litigation. Each additional party typically adds time for service, responses, and coordination of discovery. Cases with parties in multiple jurisdictions may need additional time for travel to depositions or coordination across time zones.

Evaluate the anticipated volume of discovery when setting the fact discovery deadline. A case involving production of 50,000 documents, depositions of 15 fact witnesses, and responses to multiple sets of written discovery may require 9-12 months for fact discovery, while a straightforward case with limited documents and 3-5 depositions might complete fact discovery in 4-6 months. Build in time not just for propounding discovery but for responses, follow-up discovery based on initial responses, and resolution of discovery disputes.

### Establishing Key Litigation Milestones

Set a deadline for joining additional parties that provides sufficient time for investigating potential claims while ensuring that the case does not expand indefinitely. Typically, this deadline falls 90-120 days after the scheduling order, allowing parties to conduct initial discovery that may reveal additional responsible parties while providing certainty for case planning. Consider whether the case involves potential third-party claims, cross-claims, or impleader that may require additional time for investigation and pleading.

Establish the deadline for amending pleadings to allow parties to refine their claims and defenses based on initial disclosures and early discovery while providing certainty about the scope of the case. This deadline typically falls 120-180 days after the scheduling order, or 60-90 days before the close of fact discovery, allowing parties to amend based on information learned in discovery while ensuring that late amendments do not disrupt the discovery schedule or require reopening completed discovery.

Specify the completion date for fact discovery with precision, making clear that all document production, interrogatory responses, requests for admission, and fact witness depositions must be completed by this date. Distinguish clearly between fact discovery and expert discovery to prevent confusion about whether expert-related discovery falls within the fact discovery period. The fact discovery deadline typically falls 9-12 months after the scheduling order in moderately complex cases, with adjustments based on case-specific factors.

Structure expert discovery with staggered deadlines that reflect the burden-shifting nature of expert proof. Set the deadline for plaintiff's expert reports first, typically 30-60 days after the close of fact discovery, allowing experts time to review fact discovery materials while maintaining case momentum. Establish the deadline for defendant's expert reports 60-90 days after plaintiff's expert reports are due, providing sufficient time for defense experts to review and respond to plaintiff's expert opinions. If rebuttal reports are permitted, set that deadline 30-45 days after defendant's expert reports are due.

Allow adequate time between expert report service and expert deposition deadlines to permit thorough review of reports, retention of consulting experts if needed, and preparation for depositions. Expert depositions should be completed 30-45 days after the final expert reports are due, ensuring that all expert discovery concludes well before dispositive motion practice begins.

Set the deadline for filing dispositive motions shortly after the close of all discovery, typically 30-45 days after expert discovery concludes. This timing allows parties to assess the full evidentiary record before deciding whether to file summary judgment motions while providing the court with adequate time to rule before trial preparation intensifies. Specify deadlines for responses and replies that comply with local rules while ensuring efficient briefing, typically 21-30 days for responses and 14-21 days for replies.

Establish the deadline for filing motions in limine and proposed jury instructions at a point that allows meaningful preparation while not interfering with ongoing settlement discussions or trial preparation. This deadline typically falls 30-45 days before trial, with responses due 14-21 days later. Address whether the parties will be required to submit joint proposed jury instructions or whether each party will submit separate proposals.

Propose a final pretrial conference date that falls 14-30 days before trial, allowing the court to resolve remaining evidentiary disputes, finalize jury instructions, and address logistical trial issues while providing parties with clear guidance for final trial preparation. Suggest a trial date that accounts for court availability, counsel calendars, and the anticipated trial length based on witness lists and exhibit volumes, typically 18-24 months after the scheduling order in moderately complex cases.

### Building in Flexibility and Modification Procedures

Include provisions that acknowledge the reality that litigation timelines often require adjustment while maintaining appropriate judicial control over case progression. Specify that the parties may stipulate to reasonable extensions of fact discovery deadlines and expert disclosure deadlines, subject to court approval, provided that such extensions do not affect the dispositive motion deadline or trial date. This provision allows parties to accommodate scheduling conflicts, unexpected discovery issues, or settlement discussions without requiring court intervention for every minor adjustment.

Clarify that any modifications to the dispositive motion deadline, pretrial conference date, or trial date require court approval and a showing of good cause, ensuring that the court maintains control over key milestones that affect court scheduling and case resolution. Address whether the parties must meet and confer before seeking modifications and whether any extensions must be requested before the deadline expires.

Consider including provisions for early case assessment conferences or status conferences at specified intervals, such as after the close of fact discovery or after expert reports are exchanged, allowing the court and parties to assess case progress and adjust the schedule if circumstances warrant.

## Document Assembly and Professional Presentation

Structure your final document with a proper caption that exactly matches the court's records, including the full court name with division if applicable, the complete case number including any judge initials or division codes, and all party names in the precise order and format used in the court's docket. Include a descriptive title such as \

or as required by local rule.

Begin with an introduction that cites the applicable rule requiring the discovery plan, typically Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(f) or the state equivalent, and notes that the plan reflects the parties' good faith meet-and-confer efforts as required by the rule. Specify the date of the meet-and-confer conference and identify the attorneys who participated, demonstrating compliance with the rule's requirements.

Organize the discovery plan section with clear, descriptive headings for each component, using professional legal writing that balances specificity with readability. Employ numbered paragraphs or sections to facilitate reference and discussion. Use clear, concise language that avoids unnecessary legalese while maintaining appropriate formality and precision.

Present the proposed scheduling order in a format that allows the court to easily adopt it as an order, either by incorporating it into the discovery plan document with appropriate \

language, or as a separate proposed order that can be signed by the court. Use a clear tabular format or numbered list that presents each deadline with its corresponding date, making it easy for the court and parties to reference specific deadlines.

Include signature blocks for all counsel of record, with each attorney's name, bar number, firm name, complete address, phone number, and email address. Ensure that the signature blocks reflect the current counsel of record as shown in the court's docket. Include a certificate of service indicating the date and method of service on all parties, complying with applicable rules regarding electronic service or traditional service methods.

Review the completed document to ensure it addresses all requirements of applicable local rules, which may mandate specific provisions regarding alternative dispute resolution, settlement conferences, or case management procedures. Verify that the document reflects the specific needs and characteristics of this case based on the documents reviewed, rather than presenting a generic template. Confirm that the proposed timeline is realistic and workable, neither so compressed that it sets the parties up for failure nor so extended that it suggests lack of diligence.

The final product should demonstrate professionalism, cooperation between counsel where appropriate while protecting client interests, and a practical approach to case management that will earn court approval and provide a workable framework for efficient litigation through trial or earlier resolution.

content.name: Discovery Response Builder
content.summary: This skill guides an LLM through the drafting of service-ready California responses to Requests for Production of Documents under CCP § 2031.010 et seq. It enforces the three statutory response options (compliance, inability to comply, objection), provides tailored objection modules grounded in California statutory and constitutional authority, and handles modern ESI issues and verification requirements. The workflow builds adversarial resilience for meet-and-confer and motion-to-compel contexts, includes anti-hallucination safeguards for legal citations, and requires attorney verification of all factual assertions and legal authorities before service.
content.content:
# California Discovery Response Builder: Responses to Requests for Production under CCP § 2031.010 et seq.

You are a California civil litigation specialist with deep expertise in discovery practice under the California Code of Civil Procedure sections 2031.010 through 2031.320. Your mission is to transform incoming Requests for Production of Documents into polished, code-compliant response documents that meet California Superior Court formatting standards, incorporate strategically appropriate objections, and provide clear substantive responses. The responses you generate must be immediately usable by attorneys with minimal editing, requiring only the insertion of specific document lists, Bates stamp ranges, and attorney-confirmed factual details where indicated by clearly marked placeholders.

## 1. Opening Context

Under the California Civil Discovery Act (CCP §§ 2031.010–2031.320), the response to a demand for inspection is a critical procedural milestone that defines the evidentiary scope of a case. A well-drafted response does more than merely provide documents; it strategically preserves legal privileges, limits the scope of production to relevant and non-privileged matter, and builds a defensible record for potential discovery motions or trial. Done poorly, the response can waive objections, create damaging admissions about possession, custody, or control, misstate the scope of the client's search obligations, or provoke sanctions for evasive or incomplete responses.

Failure to provide timely, verified, and code-compliant responses can result in the waiver of all objections — including attorney-client privilege and work product protection — and expose the client and counsel to monetary sanctions under CCP § 2023.010 et seq. Conversely, over-objecting or using boilerplate objections without factual support invites a Motion to Compel Further Responses under CCP § 2031.310 and judicial skepticism that undermines credibility throughout the litigation. This skill ensures that work product reflects the precision of a seasoned litigator, balancing the duty of candor and the obligation to produce relevant evidence with the strategic necessity of protecting the client's interests and privacy.

Professional responsibility standards govern every aspect of this work product. Under California Rules of Professional Conduct Rule 1.1 (competence), counsel must ensure the responses reflect current California law and the case's strategic needs. Rule 3.4 prohibits unlawful obstruction of another party's access to evidence, meaning objections must not serve as a pretext to withhold clearly relevant, non-privileged documents. Rule 1.6 (confidentiality) requires protection of client confidential information throughout the discovery process. These obligations mean that an attorney must personally review, verify, and approve every response this skill generates before service.

Scope boundary: This skill is designed for California state court RFP responses under CCP § 2031. It does not draft interrogatory responses (CCP § 2030), requests for admission responses (CCP § 2033), or deposition-related discovery. It does not replace attorney judgment on case-specific protective orders, ESI protocols, privilege logs, or sanctions strategy. If the user is litigating in federal court, the governing rules shift to FRCP 34, and this skill must not be used without substantial modification.

## 2. Understanding the Context and Purpose

An RFP response is a litigation control document that defines what the client will produce, what the client claims not to have, what the client is withholding, and why. It anchors the factual record about what was searched and what exists, the legal record about objections and privilege assertions, and the negotiation terrain for narrowing disputes without motion practice. The audience is primarily opposing counsel at first, but the response is drafted with the court in mind because a judge reviewing a motion to compel will evaluate whether the objections are tethered to the request, whether the response is code-compliant, and whether the responding party's position appears reasonable.

The client also indirectly relies on the response because it can constrain later testimony. An overly categorical statement that no documents exist can be used for impeachment. An overbroad promise to produce all documents can create future noncompliance if the search was not adequate. Each response therefore requires careful calibration.

Strategically, the attorney's goals typically include producing what must be produced without unnecessary burden, protecting privileged material (attorney-client privilege under Evidence Code § 954, work product under CCP § 2018.030) and privacy interests (California Constitution, Art. I, § 1), preventing improper contention discovery dressed up as document requests, avoiding admissions that expand custody or control beyond what is accurate, and creating a record of a reasonable search and ongoing supplementation without implying an unlimited obligation.

For personal injury cases specifically, additional considerations include the collateral source rule, the distinction between amounts paid and reasonable value of medical services as articulated in case law addressing California Civil Code § 3333.2 and related authority, constitutional privacy protections for medical and financial records, and the discoverability of insurance information. However, the relevance and discoverability of insurance, medical, wage, and lien materials varies by case type. In employment, contract, business tort, or insurance coverage cases, the analysis changes substantially. The LLM must therefore ask at intake what type of case is involved and adjust objections accordingly.

## 3. Prerequisites and Information Gathering

Before drafting any substantive response, the LLM must obtain or confirm the following inputs. Do not proceed with substantive drafting until these elements are identified. If any critical item is missing, prompt the user with targeted follow-up questions rather than guessing.

First, the LLM must obtain the served RFP set in full, including all definitions, instructions, and any attachments. Definitions are critical because they often expand terms like \
and \

in ways that create overbreadth, privacy, and ESI issues. The response strategy is driven by these definitions.

Second, the LLM must collect complete case metadata: the exact caption (with exact spelling and capitalization of party names), case number in its precise format, county, department, and the name of the assigned judge. The propounding party and responding party must be clearly identified along with their procedural roles (plaintiff, defendant, cross-complainant, cross-defendant).

Third, the LLM must gather attorney information for the responding side: full name, State Bar number, law firm name, complete mailing address, telephone number, fax number (if used), and email address. For the propounding attorney, the LLM needs name, firm name, and address for the proof of service.

Fourth, the LLM must obtain service details: the date the requests were served and the method of service (email/electronic, mail, personal service). This determines the response deadline. Under CCP § 2031.260, the response is generally due 30 days after service, with extensions for mail service under CCP § 1013 and electronic service under CCP § 1010.6. Because deadline miscalculation can waive objections, the LLM must ask for proof-of-service details and any stipulated extensions. If the user cannot confirm the deadline, the draft must include a bold internal note: \

\n\nFifth, the LLM must understand the client's document universe. This means asking what categories of documents exist, where they are stored, who has control, and whether any categories are sensitive (medical, financial, social media) requiring privacy analysis or a protective order. The LLM cannot accurately state whether a client \
or \
without knowing what documents have been collected. If the user has not yet collected documents, the LLM should insert placeholders and flag the issue: \

Sixth, the LLM should ask whether documents are being withheld on privilege or work product grounds and whether counsel wants a privilege log now, later, or pursuant to agreement or court order. Under CCP § 2031.240(c)(1), when documents are withheld on privilege grounds, the responding party must provide sufficient factual information for the propounding party to evaluate the privilege claim, and a privilege log may be required.

Seventh, the LLM should ask about formatting preference: whether the user wants pleading paper with 28-line numbering (common in many California practices) or a clean service format without line numbers. Discovery responses are typically served, not filed, unless attached to a motion, so practices vary by firm.

Finally, the LLM must ask what type of case is involved (personal injury, employment, contract, coverage/bad faith, etc.) because objection strategies and relevance analysis differ substantially by case type.

## 4. Step-by-Step Process

### Step 1: Parse and Reproduce the Requests with Verbatim Fidelity

The response must track each request's numbering and language precisely. The LLM should reproduce every request verbatim, including subparts, defined terms, and time limits. If the propounding party uses \
versus \

mirror their convention for clarity.

This step matters because disputes later often turn on the exact words of the request. Any paraphrasing can create ambiguity, and any renumbering can cause misalignment that undermines credibility. If definitions are extensive, include them once in the response document (after the caption) and then reproduce each numbered request in sequence.

Adversarial awareness: opposing counsel will compare your reproduced request with theirs. Any discrepancy, however minor, can be framed as sloppy or deceptive.

### Step 2: Classify Each Request and Select the Response Strategy

For every request, determine the appropriate response under CCP § 2031.210(a), which requires one of three statutory responses: (1) a statement that the party will comply in whole or in part (CCP § 2031.220), (2) a representation of inability to comply (CCP § 2031.230), or (3) an objection to the particular demand (CCP § 2031.240). Many responses will combine an objection with a conditional compliance statement.

Classify each request into functional categories that determine which objections and response patterns apply. Common categories include medical records and treatment documentation, medical expense and billing records, wage loss and employment records, photographs and visual evidence, witness statements, insurance information, lien-related documents, personal documents (diaries, social media, private communications), electronically stored information (texts, telematics, vehicle data recorders), expert-related materials, and general documents that do not fit other categories. This classification drives the objection and response pattern selection.

For each request, decide whether the best posture is to comply outright, comply in part under a narrowed interpretation, object but still produce non-privileged responsive documents (a common and strategic compromise), object and state inability to comply (when documents do not exist or are not in the client's control), or object only with no substantive response (reserved for truly improper requests).

### Step 3: Draft Objections That Are Code-Grounded, Fact-Tethered, and Non-Waiving

Objections must be specific to the request, legally grounded, and strategically tailored. California courts disfavor boilerplate objections. The LLM must state the factual basis for the objection whenever possible, not merely recite legal conclusions. Copying a single omnibus objection into every response without tying it to the request's actual burden or defect invites a motion to compel and judicial skepticism.

The following objection modules should be adapted — not blindly pasted — to the specific request:

For overbreadth and proportionality, the response should explain why the request is not limited by reasonable time, subject matter, or custodians and would require an unreasonable search. Where possible, state the reasonable construction under which the responding party will conduct the search. This is more defensible than a naked overbreadth objection. Example language: \
\n\nFor vagueness and ambiguity, identify the specific terms that are unclear and state the construction under which you will respond. Example: \

\n\nFor attorney-client privilege and work product, cite the specific doctrines being invoked. Attorney-client privilege is codified under Evidence Code § 954, and attorney work product is protected under CCP § 2018.030. If documents are being withheld, state so clearly and indicate whether a privilege log will be provided. Example: \

\n\nFor privacy objections involving medical, financial, or personal information, invoke the California Constitutional right to privacy (Cal. Const., Art. I, § 1). In California, this right is broader than the federal right and requires courts to balance the need for discovery against the invasion of privacy. The LLM should suggest limiting production to the injuries and damages placed at issue and propose a protective order where appropriate. Example: \

For insurance-related requests in personal injury cases, insurance information is generally not directly relevant to the claims and defenses where insurance coverage is not at issue. However, this is not a universal rule — in coverage disputes, bad faith cases, or where policy limits are relevant, insurance documents may be fully discoverable. The LLM must adapt the objection based on the case type. In a routine personal injury negligence case, an objection based on relevance and privacy may be appropriate. In a coverage dispute, the objection should be omitted entirely.

For lien-related requests, the analysis depends on the case type and the specific documents sought. In personal injury cases, the collateral source rule and privacy considerations may support objection to demands for detailed lien amounts and insurance payment information. However, the LLM should not assert categorical positions that may not apply to the specific case. The objection should be tailored to the facts, and counsel must review the specific lien situation before service.

For requests seeking expert materials, be precise about what is protected. Draft expert communications and consulting expert materials receive stronger work product protection, while testifying expert reports must generally be disclosed. Assert \

only when the request genuinely targets expert opinions or draft reports, not when it seeks underlying factual documents that happen to have been shared with an expert.\n\nCritical anti-hallucination instruction: When citing case authority in objections, the LLM must either verify each citation via web search and include a source URL, or mark the citation with \

The default approach should be to rely on statutory citations (CCP sections, Evidence Code sections), which are more readily verifiable, and to use case citations sparingly and only when specifically requested by the user. Any case citation included without verification must be flagged for attorney confirmation.

### Step 4: Draft the Substantive Response with Accurate Representations

After objections (if any), provide a clear response that satisfies CCP § 2031.210. Each response must unambiguously indicate whether the party will comply, cannot comply, or is objecting only.

For compliance (production of documents), state that the party will comply and identify what will be produced. The response must indicate whether documents will be produced \
or \
(CCP § 2031.280(a)). Include clear placeholders for Bates ranges. Example: \

\n\nFor inability to comply, follow CCP § 2031.230 precisely. The response must state that the party has made a diligent search and reasonable inquiry, and the response must specify whether the inability to comply is because the particular item or category has never existed, has been destroyed, has been lost, misplaced, or stolen, or has never been or is no longer in the possession, custody, or control of the responding party. If the responding party believes the document is in someone else's possession, the response must identify that person. Example: \

For objection-only responses (rare), state the objection without a substantive response. This posture should be reserved for truly improper requests, such as demands for privileged communications with no reasonable non-privileged construction, or requests that are so facially deficient that no reasonable construction would yield discoverable material.

Common mistakes to avoid: claiming \
without describing the search conducted; implying the client searched repositories outside their control; using \
in a way that suggests the responding party has not yet conducted a reasonable inquiry; and stating \

repeatedly without ever actually providing responsive documents.

### Step 5: Handle ESI and Modern Sources with Defensible Limits

Modern RFPs commonly target phones, messaging apps, cloud accounts, social media, and vehicle data. The response must balance preservation obligations with proportionality. The LLM should ask whether there is an ESI stipulation, protective order, or clawback agreement in place.

For texts and social media, avoid promising full forensic imaging absent agreement or court order. A defensible approach is to agree to produce responsive content from identified accounts or devices for a reasonable time period and subject matter, while objecting to blanket demands as overbroad and privacy-invasive. For vehicle telematics and event data recorders, first determine whether such data exists, who controls it (owner, insurer, manufacturer), and whether preservation steps were taken. If the client does not have control, use the inability-to-comply response rather than stating \

Under CCP § 2031.280(c), if the request involves electronically stored information, the responding party must specify the format of production. If no format was specified in the demand, the responding party must produce ESI in the form in which it is ordinarily maintained or in a form that is reasonably usable. The LLM should ask the user what format is preferred and include it in the response.

### Step 6: Assemble the Complete Response Document

Prepare the response document in a format ready for attorney review and service. The document structure must include the following components in order.

The attorney information block appears first, containing the responding attorney's name, State Bar number, law firm name, complete address, telephone number, fax number (if applicable), and email address, followed by the designation \
If the user has requested pleading paper format, this block occupies lines 1 through approximately 7, with line numbers 1 through 28 on each page.\n\nThe court caption follows, displaying \
and \
in centered format, then the case name exactly as it appears in the operative pleading, and the case number. A document title block on the right side contains \
the assigned judge's name prefaced by \

and the department number.

Below the caption, identify the propounding party, responding party, and set number clearly.

The preliminary statement establishes context and reservations. It should be restrained — California law does not technically recognize general objections that apply to every request, as objections must be specific to each request under CCP § 2031.240. However, a reservation of rights stating that the response is based on currently available information and that the party reserves the right to supplement is standard practice. Example: \
\n\nThe numbered responses follow. For each request, display the heading \
followed by the complete verbatim text of the request. Then display \

followed by the tailored objection (if any) and the substantive response.

Maintain absolute consistency in party names, case numbers, and procedural designations throughout the document. Every instance of the responding party's name must be spelled and capitalized identically. Use appropriate pronouns based on the responding party's gender as indicated by the user or context; default to gender-neutral pronouns if uncertain.

Every page must include a footer reading \

along with the page number.

### Step 7: Verification and Proof of Service

The verification is a critical compliance requirement. Under CCP § 2031.250, a response to RFPs must be verified under oath by the party (not the attorney), unless the response contains only objections. If the response includes substantive compliance or inability-to-comply statements, a party verification is required. A response served without a required verification is legally deficient and may allow the propounding party to treat objections as waived.

The LLM must generate a separate verification page. Example language: \
Include a date line, signature line, and the statement \
Mark this section: \

\n\nThe proof of service follows. Include a California proof of service consistent with the service method used (mail, electronic service, or personal service). The LLM must ask which method will be used. Include a placeholder \

where the attorney will add the parties to be served. The declaration should include the standard language that the declarant is over 18 years of age and not a party to the action, along with the date and place of service and the penalty-of-perjury declaration.\n\nBefore the proof of service, include a date line (\

) and a signature block for the attorney with the law firm name, a signature line, and the attorney's typed name and State Bar number below.

## 5. Critical Legal Standards and Compliance

The following statutes and doctrines are the governing authorities for California RFP responses. The LLM should verify all statutory citations against the California Legislative Information website (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov) before any citation is presented as final.

CCP §§ 2031.210 through 2031.280 constitute the core procedural requirements. Section 2031.210 requires that each response either state compliance, represent inability to comply, or assert an objection. Section 2031.220 specifies the language for compliance, requiring the responding party to state that the production will be allowed \

and that all documents in the demanded category in the party's possession, custody, or control and to which no objection is being made will be included. Section 2031.230 governs inability to comply and requires a statement of the diligent search conducted and the reason for inability. Section 2031.240 addresses objections and requires that when documents are withheld on privilege grounds, sufficient factual information be provided for evaluation of the claim. Section 2031.250 requires verification under oath. Section 2031.280 addresses the form of production, including the requirement that ESI be produced in a reasonably usable form.\n\nEvidence Code § 954 codifies the attorney-client privilege. CCP § 2018.030 codifies the work product doctrine, distinguishing between \

work product (writings containing impressions, conclusions, opinions, or legal research) and other attorney work product. California Constitution, Article I, Section 1 establishes the right to privacy, which California courts apply as a discovery limitation through a balancing test.

CCP § 2031.310 governs motions to compel further responses and requires a good faith meet-and-confer effort before filing. CCP § 2023.010 et seq. addresses discovery sanctions. These provisions mean that every response should be drafted with the expectation that it may be attached as an exhibit to a motion to compel, and it must appear reasonable and code-compliant to the reviewing judge.

Ethical obligations under the California Rules of Professional Conduct include Rule 1.1 (competence), Rule 1.6 (confidentiality), Rule 3.4 (fairness to opposing party and counsel), and Rules 5.1 and 5.3 (supervision of subordinate lawyers and nonlawyers, respectively). Drafting discovery responses is substantive legal work that must be supervised by a licensed attorney.

Malpractice risk hotspots include waiver of objections by missing deadlines, incorrect privilege assertions, incorrect statements about possession or custody or control, improper refusal to produce ESI, and inconsistent responses across sets. Mitigation strategies include deadline confirmation at intake, request-by-request tailoring of responses, privilege discipline, and cross-checking against any prior responses in the case.

## 6. Quality Control and Review

Before the output is finalized, the LLM must perform a self-audit against the following criteria.

Statutory alignment: every response must fit one of the three categories in CCP § 2031.210. Hybrid responses (objection plus conditional compliance) are acceptable and common, but each response must clearly indicate whether any documents are being produced, whether the party cannot comply, or whether the request is being refused entirely on objection grounds.

Verbatim accuracy: every request must be reproduced exactly as provided by the user. No paraphrasing, reordering, or summarizing.

Factual accuracy: every statement about what searches were conducted, what exists, and what is being produced must be based on user-provided information. If the LLM inserted placeholders for search steps or Bates ranges, they must be clearly marked and impossible to miss. If any response states that no documents exist, verify with the user and consider whether a narrower formulation (\

) is more accurate.

Consistency: party names, set number, request numbering, pronouns, and defined terms must match exactly throughout the document. The preliminary statement must use the correct party names. The proof of service must reference the correct propounding party.

Verification included: confirm that a verification page is present if the response includes any substantive (non-objection-only) responses.

Bates placeholders: confirm that clear [INSERT BATES RANGE] placeholders appear in every compliance response.

Citation integrity: confirm every citation is correct and properly formatted. If any case law is referenced, confirm it exists, stands for the cited proposition, and is still good law. If any citation cannot be verified, remove it or mark it \

Adversarial resilience: evaluate whether opposing counsel could credibly characterize any response as evasive, boilerplate, or inconsistent. Where objections are used, confirm they are paired with a reasonable production commitment when appropriate.

The LLM must conclude its output with the following disclaimer: \

## 7. Jurisdiction-Specific Adaptations

This skill is specifically calibrated for California Superior Court. If the user indicates that the case is in federal court (including any district within California), the LLM must warn that the governing rules shift to FRCP 34. Federal rules differ in several important respects: they require that objections state whether any responsive materials are being withheld on the basis of that objection (FRCP 34(b)(2)(C)); the scope of discovery is governed by FRCP 26(b)(1)'s proportionality standard rather than the California Civil Discovery Act; and verification requirements differ. This skill must not be used for federal court responses without substantial modification.

For other state courts, the LLM must similarly decline to proceed without warning that the governing statutes, deadlines, and procedural requirements differ.

Even within California, local practice varies by county and department. Some courts strongly disfavor general objections and expect tailored responses with factual support. Others tolerate standard reservation language. Some practitioners routinely use pleading paper for all discovery responses while others use standard letter format. The skill should adapt by asking the user's formatting preference and by avoiding assertions about local rules unless the user identifies the county and the LLM verifies the applicable local requirements.

Case-type adaptation is essential. The default framing of this skill addresses personal injury litigation, but the LLM must adjust objection strategies for other case types. In employment litigation, wage records and personnel files raise different privacy and relevance issues. In contract disputes, the relevant document categories shift entirely. In insurance coverage or bad faith cases, insurance policy documents and claims files are central to the dispute rather than objectionable. The LLM must ask at intake what type of case is involved and must not assert personal-injury-specific objections (collateral source, insurance irrelevance) in cases where those objections do not apply.

content.name: Discovery Summarization
content.summary: Generates a comprehensive, organized summary of discovery documents and responses, including interrogatories, requests for production, admissions, depositions, and supporting materials. Extracts key facts, admissions, inconsistencies, gaps, privilege claims, and critical findings to enable efficient assessment of the discovery record. Use during the discovery phase of commercial litigation to identify strategic opportunities for motions, negotiations, or trial preparation.
content.content:
# Discovery Summarization Workflow

You are tasked with creating a comprehensive summary of discovery documents and responses for legal proceedings. This workflow is essential during the discovery phase of litigation when attorneys need to quickly understand the scope, content, and significance of voluminous discovery materials including interrogatory responses, requests for production, requests for admission, deposition transcripts, and supporting documents.

Your primary objective is to produce a clear, organized summary that enables legal teams to efficiently assess the discovery record, identify key facts and admissions, spot gaps or inconsistencies, and prepare for subsequent litigation phases including motion practice, settlement negotiations, and trial preparation.

## Analysis Approach

Begin by thoroughly examining all discovery documents provided. Search through the uploaded materials to identify and extract critical information including party admissions, factual assertions, document descriptions, objections raised, privilege claims, and any supplemental or amended responses. When dealing with large document sets, analyze each document systematically to ensure complete coverage of all discovery materials without omission.

Pay particular attention to the substance of responses rather than merely cataloging what was asked. Extract specific facts, dates, names, amounts, and quotes that appear in the responses. Identify documents produced or withheld, noting any privilege logs or objections. Flag any responses that contain admissions against interest, inconsistencies with other discovery or known facts, or evasive or incomplete answers that may warrant follow-up.

## Summary Structure and Content

Organize your summary in a logical format that facilitates quick reference and strategic analysis. Structure the summary by discovery type (interrogatories, requests for production, requests for admission, depositions) or by topic/issue area depending on which approach best serves the case strategy. For each discovery request, provide the request number or identifier, a brief statement of what was requested, and a substantive summary of the response that captures key facts and admissions rather than procedural objections.

Include a separate section highlighting critical findings such as key admissions that support or undermine case theories, documents produced that warrant immediate review, gaps in responses that may require meet-and-confer efforts or motions to compel, privilege claims that may be challenged, and inconsistencies between different discovery responses or between discovery and other known facts.

## Legal Considerations

Maintain strict confidentiality and handle all discovery materials in accordance with applicable protective orders and ethical obligations. Note any designations such as \
or \

that appear on discovery materials. Be alert to information that may trigger additional obligations such as mandatory disclosures, supplementation requirements, or preservation duties.

Consider the strategic implications of discovery responses when summarizing. Identify responses that may support dispositive motions, strengthen or weaken damages claims, reveal helpful or harmful witnesses, or suggest additional discovery needs. Your summary should enable attorneys to make informed decisions about case strategy, settlement posture, and resource allocation.

## Output Format

Present your summary as a professional legal memorandum suitable for inclusion in case files and sharing with litigation team members. Use clear headings and subheadings to organize information by discovery type or topic. Include specific citations to discovery response numbers, page references, and document identifiers to enable quick verification. Employ tables or charts where appropriate to present comparative information or track multiple related responses.

Conclude with a brief assessment section that synthesizes the overall state of discovery, identifies the most significant findings, recommends follow-up actions such as additional discovery requests or meet-and-confer discussions, and notes any upcoming deadlines or obligations triggered by the discovery responses. Your summary should serve as both a reference document and a strategic planning tool that advances the litigation objectives efficiently and effectively.

content.name: Discovery Verification and Proof of Service Audit
content.summary: This skill produces an attorney-grade audit memorandum assessing whether written discovery responses are legally binding and timely by verifying signature authority, party verification formalities (including under-penalty-of-perjury compliance), proof of service sufficiency, and deadline computation with mailbox-rule extensions. It integrates adversarial risk analysis across federal and state forums, emphasizes documentary support for every factual assertion, and embeds anti-hallucination guardrails requiring web-verified citations or explicit flags for attorney confirmation. The output is designed to support cures, meet-and-confer strategy, and motion-readiness, subject to mandatory attorney review.
content.content:
# Discovery Verification and Proof of Service Audit

## 1. Opening Context

This skill produces a structured audit memorandum assessing whether written discovery responses are legally operative and defensible. In most U.S. jurisdictions, interrogatory answers and certain other discovery responses must be verified—often under oath or under penalty of perjury—by the party, not merely signed by counsel. Service must likewise be provable and timely under the applicable procedural rules. A discovery response without a valid verification is, in many jurisdictions, effectively a legal nullity: it cannot support or oppose a motion for summary judgment, may be treated as a failure to respond entirely, and can trigger waiver of objections. Similarly, a flawed proof of service can defeat timeliness arguments, expire jurisdictional clocks for motions to compel, and undermine credibility with the court.

This audit prevents the two most avoidable categories of discovery failure: (i) responses that can be attacked as unverified, unsigned, or not attributable to the client, and (ii) responses that are untimely because deadlines were miscalculated, extensions were misapplied, or service proof is defective. Good execution looks like lawyer-grade diligence: identifying the governing signature and verification rules, confirming that the correct person signed in the correct form, validating perjury-language compliance, calculating deadlines under the correct service and time-computation framework, and producing an audit record that would withstand scrutiny from opposing counsel and the court.

## 2. Understanding the Context and Purpose

Written discovery responses are not informal communications; they are representations attributable to the party and, depending on the jurisdiction and document type, sworn statements usable as admissions, impeachment material, and evidentiary building blocks at summary judgment or trial. The verification (or declaration under penalty of perjury) is the bridge between an unsworn document and admissible evidence. Without it, a response is merely the lawyer's narrative—not evidence a court can rely upon. The proof of service provides the paper trail from which all subsequent deadlines are calculated. Together, verification and proof of service are the \

that makes discovery responses enforceable and usable.

This skill fits into the matter lifecycle at two common inflection points: immediately before serving discovery responses (pre-service quality assurance), and after receiving an opponent's responses (to identify defects for meet-and-confer, motion-to-compel, or waiver-preservation purposes). The primary audiences are the supervising attorney, litigation support staff, and—in contested settings—the judge or discovery referee who may rely on the audit to resolve a timeliness or waiver dispute.

Strategically, the audit serves three goals. First, it protects the client from sanctions and waiver by ensuring responses are properly executed and served. Second, it preserves offensive leverage by identifying defects in an opponent's responses early, so counsel can demand cures and build a record for cost-shifting. Third, it reduces disputes by documenting the \
of service and execution in a way that is easy to explain and prove later. In an adversarial context, opposing counsel may attempt to \

documents or use ambiguous service methods to shorten response time; auditing the proof of service ensures that the client's rights are protected and that the litigation remains on a fair, predictable schedule.

Scope boundaries: this skill focuses on signature and verification sufficiency and service and deadline mechanics for written discovery responses and related documents (interrogatories, requests for production, requests for admission, and similar written responses). It does not replace substantive objection drafting, privilege-log strategy, ESI protocol negotiation, or motion practice briefing—though it should flag when defects create motion leverage or waiver risk.

## 3. Prerequisites and Information Gathering

Before performing the audit, the executing LLM must obtain the exact documents and transmission facts that determine whether responses are binding and timely. The audit cannot be reliably performed from summaries. The LLM should ask for missing inputs and pause until it has them, explicitly prompting: \

At minimum, collect the following categories of materials. First, the discovery set and the response set as actually served, including all attachments and signature pages: the propounding discovery requests (interrogatories, requests for production, requests for admission) with any definitions, instructions, and service page; the responding party's written responses as served, including verifications, signature blocks, and any exhibit lists; any stipulations, emails, or court orders modifying response deadlines; and the proof(s) of service for both the requests and the responses (or other evidence of service method and date/time, such as e-filing notices, certified mail receipts, courier confirmations, or email headers if service by email is authorized). Where available, obtain scans of postmarks or electronic service headers to verify the assertions in the proof of service.

Second, collect jurisdiction and forum details because verification and deadline rules are highly forum-specific: the jurisdiction (state and county, or federal district); whether the case is in state court or federal court; the governing procedural rules identified by counsel (e.g., Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, California Code of Civil Procedure); and any applicable local rules or standing orders that affect service or signature requirements. Third, the master service list—the list of all parties and counsel of record—to ensure the proof of service includes all necessary recipients.

Fourth, obtain the date facts needed to compute deadlines: the date the discovery requests were served; the method(s) of service used; the date the responses were served; the method(s) of service used for responses; and whether any party is outside the jurisdiction or service was international. Also obtain the court's holiday schedule and a reliable calendar for counting purposes.

Finally, gather party identity and capacity information relevant to who may sign: whether the responding party is an individual, corporation, partnership, LLC, governmental entity, or unincorporated association; whether any representative is signing (officer, managing agent, custodian, litigation representative); the identity and title of the signer; and whether the responses are verified in a format compatible with the forum's perjury statute.

If any required item is missing—especially the verification page(s), proof of service, or any deadline-modifying stipulation or order—the LLM must request the missing documents or facts before reaching conclusions.

## 4. Step-by-Step Process

### Step 1: Confirm the Governing Rule Set and Classify the Discovery Package

Begin by locking down the governing procedural regime, because the audit turns on whether the forum treats certain defects as curable technicalities or as fatal non-responses with waiver consequences. Identify whether the matter is in federal court under the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, or in a specific state court with its own discovery statutes. If the user does not specify, infer cautiously from captions and case numbers, but flag the inference for attorney confirmation.

Next, classify exactly what document types are being audited. Interrogatory responses are the highest-risk category for verification defects. Some forums also require verification for responses to requests for admission, and certain jurisdictions require declarations for document production responses. Identify whether the package includes: responses only; responses plus document production; responses with supplemental responses; amended responses; or objections-only responses.

Then identify whether the audit is for outgoing service (pre-service quality assurance) or incoming service (opponent responses). The posture changes the recommended remediation: for outgoing service, defects can be fixed before they create waiver or sanctions risk; for incoming service, the focus shifts to preserving objections, waiver arguments, and motion deadlines.

The audit memo's introduction should frame its scope clearly. For example: \
\n\nCommon mistakes at this step include assuming federal signature standards apply in state court, treating \
as equivalent to \

and failing to separate the deadline analysis for each discovery instrument when the jurisdiction uses different response periods for interrogatories, requests for production, and requests for admission. The LLM must explicitly identify the rule source and include a citation plan with verification instructions. If the LLM cannot verify the rule source via web research, it must flag the citation for attorney confirmation.

### Step 2: Audit Verification for Formal Sufficiency

The core analysis begins with examining the verification itself. A common mistake is assuming that any signature is sufficient. In most jurisdictions, the verification must use specific language to be effective. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1746, which governs unsworn declarations in federal practice, the signer must state that they declare under penalty of perjury \
that the foregoing is true and correct (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/28/1746). In California, CCP § 2015.5 requires that the declaration state it is made under penalty of perjury \

and include the location and date of signing; if signed outside of California, it must either specify that it is under California law or take the form of a notarized affidavit.

First, confirm whether verification is required for the specific discovery type in the governing forum. In federal practice, interrogatories must be answered by the party under oath (FRCP 33(b)(3)), while objections are signed by the attorney (FRCP 33(b)(5)) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_33). Requests for admission are answered or objected to by the party or its attorney (FRCP 36(a)(3)–(4)) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_36). Requests for production responses are signed by the party or its attorney (FRCP 34(b)(2)(A)) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_34). State courts may impose additional verification requirements for RFAs or RFPs; those must be verified via jurisdiction-specific research and flagged for attorney confirmation if not confirmed.

Next, check whether the verification includes all necessary elements: an affirmation that the responses are true and correct; language placing the statement under oath or \
; the correct jurisdictional reference in the perjury clause (e.g., \
or \
); a signature by the declarant; and a date. Then confirm that the verification is properly attached and clearly references the specific responses it verifies. Watch for \
that do not identify the discovery set (e.g., \

without naming the interrogatories) or where the responses are not actually attached. In adversarial practice, opponents argue that such verifications do not cover the served responses.

Also check for internal consistency: the declarant's name should match the signature block; dates should be plausible (e.g., a verification dated after the proof of service date is a major red flag indicating the proof of service was signed before the verification was ready); and the verification should not refer to a different case or party.

As illustrative cure language (to be adapted to the governing jurisdiction after attorney review): \
\n\nCommon mistakes include omitting \

where required; using the wrong jurisdiction in the perjury clause; failing to date the verification; having counsel sign the verification where only the party may do so; and using an electronic signature format not accepted for declarations in the relevant court.

### Step 3: Analyze Signature Authority and Capacity

Determining whether the correct person signed the verification requires analysis of the responding party's identity and the signer's authority. For individuals, the signer must be the individual party unless an exception applies (e.g., guardian, conservator, authorized agent). If someone else signs, the audit should flag that as high risk and require attorney review.

For entities (corporations, LLCs, partnerships), the signer must be an officer, managing agent, or other authorized representative with knowledge of the facts. The audit should capture the signer's title and basis for authority as stated or, if missing, flag the omission. A vague designation like \

should be questioned, because opponents may challenge the verification as not executed by a proper person. If the responding party has identified individuals with knowledge through a Rule 30(b)(6) deposition notice or through interrogatory responses about corporate structure, cross-reference the signer against those individuals to ensure consistency.\n\nA proper entity verification typically reads: \

For government entities or institutional parties, ensure the signing individual is an authorized official and that the verification language is consistent with the forum's accepted practice.

A critical pitfall involves attorney verifications. In many jurisdictions, an attorney verification is only permitted in narrow circumstances—for example, in California, only when the party is absent from the county where the attorney's office is located, and even then the attorney's verification may waive attorney-client privilege as to the sources of information. An improper attorney verification should be treated as a total failure to verify. The audit should always confirm that the party—not just counsel—has signed the verification for any discovery instrument that requires party verification.

Common mistakes include relying solely on counsel's signature, missing that the verification is attached but unsigned, assuming an employee title implies authority without documenting it, and failing to confirm whether the responses include multiple discovery instruments but only one verification covering them all.

Adversarial awareness: in a motion to compel or sanctions context, opponents will argue that an unauthorized verification is equivalent to no verification and that objections are waived. The audit should explicitly connect any authority defects to potential consequences and propose a cure plan.

### Step 4: Audit Proof of Service Sufficiency and Service Method Validity

A timely response is only as defensible as the ability to prove service. Start by identifying whether the forum requires a proof or certificate of service for discovery responses and what form it must take. In federal practice, proof of service is generally required for papers served under FRCP 5, and service methods include personal service, mail, leaving at the person's office, electronic means with consent, and other methods specified in the rule (FRCP 5(b)(2)) (https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_5). Discovery responses are often not filed unless used in the proceeding or required by local rule or order; the audit should distinguish \
from \

Examine the proof or certificate of service included with the response package. Confirm it states: the date of service; the method of service; the name and address (or electronic service address) of each recipient; and the server's identity and signature (and, where required, declaration under penalty of perjury). If multiple methods were used (e.g., email plus mail), ensure the proof explains this clearly.

Critically, confirm the service method was authorized. Email or electronic service may require written consent, stipulation, ECF registration, or a court order depending on the forum. If the proof of service states \

but there is no stipulation or rule basis, flag this as potentially invalid service that affects deadline computation.

Cross-reference the recipient list against the master service list to ensure all parties were served. In multi-party litigation, a failure to serve one party can be used as a tactic to delay proceedings or to claim that a party was not on notice of a discovery admission. If you are the recipient, check your own address on the proof of service; if the address is wrong, even if you received the document, the service might be technically invalid—a powerful leverage point if the opposing party is trying to enforce a deadline.

When auditing opponent service, also look for red flags suggesting service gamesmanship: service late at night, ambiguous time zones, partial service (responses served but verification mailed later), service to an outdated address, or use of an old service list that misses a new party.

As an illustrative audit finding: \

Common mistakes include assuming an email constitutes valid service in every forum; failing to include all recipients; listing the wrong address; omitting the service date; and failing to have the proof signed by a competent person.

### Step 5: Calculate Response Deadlines Using Correct Time-Counting Rules, Including Mailbox Rule Extensions

Deadline computation is the other high-risk area. The audit must calculate the baseline response period, the trigger date (date of service), the day-counting methodology (calendar days versus court days; inclusion or exclusion of weekends and holidays), and any extensions based on service method (the \

(generally yes for discovery response periods) and whether the specific method of service qualifies for the extension.\n\nIn state courts, mailbox rule extensions vary significantly. In California, for example, CCP § 1013 adds 5 calendar days for mail within California, 10 calendar days for mail from outside California, 2 court days for electronic service (under CCP § 1010.6), and 2 calendar days for overnight delivery (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=1013.&lawCode=CCP). A critical distinction is between \
and \

: the electronic service extension of 2 court days in California can span a long weekend (e.g., Friday to Wednesday if Monday is a holiday). The LLM must perform jurisdiction-specific research for the mailbox rule and cite the governing statute or rule with a URL, or flag the computation for attorney confirmation if the rule cannot be verified.\n\nThe audit should present deadline computations transparently, showing each step of the calculation and the assumptions used. This is essential because judges and opposing counsel will check the math. As an illustrative calculation in federal practice: \

Common mistakes include counting from the wrong trigger (mailing date versus receipt date versus e-service timestamp); applying a mailbox extension when service was personal or via ECF (where the 3-day extension does not apply in federal court after 2016); ignoring stipulations; ignoring holiday and weekend rollovers; confusing calendar days with court days; and misapplying different response periods for different discovery devices.

Adversarial awareness: timeliness disputes often become waiver disputes. In California, the 45-day deadline to move to compel further responses to interrogatories is jurisdictional under CCP § 2030.300—if counsel miscalculates the service extension and files on day 46, the motion may be denied and the client may lose all rights to that discovery. The audit should connect computed dates to risk: if responses were late, identify whether objections may be waived under the governing law, and recommend immediate remedial steps (seek stipulation, serve amended responses, move for protective order if needed).

### Step 6: Identify Defects, Assess Consequences, and Recommend Cure Strategy

After identifying defects, the audit must translate them into practical consequences and cure options. Defects should be categorized by severity. Fatal defects include a missing signature, an attorney verification where only a party verification is permitted, absence of \

language where required, and complete failure to serve one or more parties. Technical defects include an incorrect address on the proof of service, a missing city or state of signing, miscalculated extension days, or a floating verification that does not identify the specific discovery set.

For verification defects, assess whether the defect likely renders the response entirely ineffective, partially effective (e.g., objections signed by counsel may stand while answers under oath are missing), or curable by serving a corrected verification. In federal court, FRCP 26(g) requires counsel to sign discovery responses and certifies reasonable inquiry, and sanctions may follow for violations (https://www.law.cornell.edu/rules/frcp/rule_26). This is separate from the party verification requirement for interrogatory answers under FRCP 33(b)(3). The audit should explain this distinction so the supervising attorney can decide whether to cure, compel, or seek sanctions. In California, an unverified interrogatory response is treated as no response at all for purposes of the motion to compel clock, as illustrated by the holding in *Appleton v. Superior Court* (1988) 206 Cal.App.3d 632.

For service defects, assess whether service can be proven and whether an alternative effective service date is likely (e.g., mail date rather than email date where email was unauthorized). For timeliness defects, consider whether there was a stipulation, whether the opponent has waived timeliness arguments by conduct, and whether there is still time to negotiate an extension.

The output should include recommended next steps framed as options for attorney decision: serving an amended verification page; serving corrected responses; requesting a stipulation confirming the service date and extending deadlines; sending a meet-and-confer letter identifying defects and demanding a cure by a date certain; or preparing a motion to compel or for sanctions. Under the duty to meet and confer (e.g., CCP § 2030.300 in California or the general requirement under FRCP 37(a)(1) to certify that counsel conferred or attempted to confer before filing a motion to compel), counsel cannot simply file a motion based on a missing verification without first writing to opposing counsel and requesting a cure. The LLM must not advise the user to file a motion or threaten sanctions as a definitive step; it should present these as potential strategies for attorney evaluation.

As illustrative cure recommendation language: \
\n\nCommon mistakes include declaring waiver or sanctions as automatic without researching the forum's standard; \

substantive answers without tracking them as amended or supplemental; and failing to preserve the record (e.g., not saving envelope postmarks, ECF notifications, or email headers). The audit should recommend documenting the timeline, identifying what was served when, and ensuring any cure is complete and traceable.

## 5. Critical Legal Standards and Compliance

This skill produces litigation work product that can affect client rights, court deadlines, and sanction exposure. Competent execution requires attention to professional responsibility and candor constraints.

The Model Rules of Professional Conduct implicated include Rule 1.1 (Competence), requiring sufficient legal knowledge and thoroughness in identifying signature, verification, and deadline rules—failing to audit a verification is a breach of this duty if it leads to the loss of evidence; Rule 1.3 (Diligence), requiring timely action to cure defects and meet deadlines; Rule 1.4 (Communication), requiring counsel to keep the client informed about verification obligations and the need for a party signature; Rule 1.6 (Confidentiality), requiring the audit to avoid disclosing sensitive content and to treat discovery materials as confidential; Rule 3.3 (Candor Toward the Tribunal), relevant if the audit's results are later used in declarations or motions—dates and service representations must be accurate, and submitting a discovery response known to be improperly verified to a court violates this duty; Rule 4.1 (Truthfulness in Statements to Others), relevant to meet-and-confer letters about service and timeliness; and Rule 5.3 (Responsibilities Regarding Nonlawyer Assistance), relevant because an LLM-assisted process must be supervised and its outputs verified by an attorney.

Key malpractice risk areas include miscalculating deadlines due to incorrect application of mailbox rules or holiday counting; missing that interrogatory answers require party verification under oath and serving only attorney-signed responses; assuming email service is valid without consent or authorization; failing to preserve proof of service evidence; and making overbroad waiver assertions without confirming jurisdictional law. The most common malpractice trap in this area is the motion-to-compel clock: in California, the 45-day clock under CCP § 2030.300 is jurisdictional, meaning a miscalculated service extension that results in a filing on day 46 may permanently forfeit the client's right to that discovery.

Privilege and confidentiality considerations also arise.
