For disability discrimination claims, identify whether the complainant has an actual disability that substantially limits a major life activity, a record of such impairment, or was regarded as having such impairment, and whether the claim involves discriminatory treatment, failure to provide reasonable accommodation, or disability-related harassment. For age discrimination claims, confirm the complainant was at least forty years old at the time of the adverse action and identify any direct or circumstantial evidence of age-based animus. When multiple protected bases apply, clearly delineate how each characteristic relates to the discriminatory conduct to provide comprehensive notice and preserve all potential claims.

## Temporal Framework and Adverse Employment Actions

Establish the chronological framework of the discrimination with precision to satisfy timeliness requirements and demonstrate the causal relationship between protected characteristics and adverse actions. Document the specific date or dates when discriminatory acts occurred, beginning with the earliest incident that forms part of a continuing violation and concluding with the most recent manifestation of discrimination that triggers the filing deadline. For discrete acts such as termination, demotion, failure to promote, or denial of transfer, identify the exact date the complainant received notice of the adverse decision. For hostile work environment claims involving a series of harassing incidents, document each significant occurrence while explaining how the cumulative conduct created an abusive working environment, and identify the date of the last act contributing to the hostile environment to establish timeliness under the continuing violation doctrine. Characterize the nature of the adverse employment action using terminology that demonstrates a materially adverse change in the terms and conditions of employment, such as discharge, constructive discharge, demotion with reduced compensation or responsibilities, denial of promotion to a position for which the complainant was qualified, discriminatory compensation or benefits, denial of training opportunities, or retaliatory actions following protected activity. For retaliation claims, clearly identify the protected activity that preceded the adverse action, such as filing a previous EEOC charge, participating in an investigation, or opposing discriminatory practices, and establish temporal proximity or other evidence linking the protected activity to the retaliation.

## Factual Narrative and Prima Facie Case Development

Construct a compelling chronological narrative that establishes a prima facie case of discrimination under applicable legal standards while remaining within the space constraints of the EEOC charge form. Begin with the complainant's hire date, initial job assignment, and early employment history to establish a baseline of satisfactory performance and workplace relationships. Detail the specific events, statements, actions, and omissions that constitute discriminatory treatment, using direct quotes from supervisors or decision-makers when available from emails, witness accounts, or documented conversations. Identify comparator employees outside the complainant's protected class who were treated more favorably under similar circumstances, specifying their names, positions, protected class status, and the preferential treatment they received, as this comparative evidence is essential for establishing disparate treatment. Name witnesses who observed discriminatory conduct or can corroborate the complainant's account, including their job titles, relationship to the events, and the substance of their potential testimony. Reference documentary evidence by description and date, such as performance evaluations showing satisfactory or exemplary ratings prior to the adverse action, disciplinary notices issued pretextually, emails containing discriminatory remarks or revealing discriminatory motives, company policies that were applied in a discriminatory manner, or statistical evidence showing patterns of discrimination.

For harassment claims, describe the harassing conduct with sufficient specificity to demonstrate its severity or pervasiveness, identifying whether it involved unwelcome sexual advances, requests for sexual favors, offensive comments about protected characteristics, physical touching, display of offensive materials, or other conduct that altered the conditions of employment and created an abusive working environment. Establish that the harassment was based on a protected characteristic, that it was unwelcome, and that the employer knew or should have known of the harassment through complaints to management or the obviousness of the conduct, yet failed to take prompt and effective remedial action. For failure-to-accommodate claims under the ADA or Title VII religious accommodation provisions, document the complainant's request for reasonable accommodation, the interactive process discussions that occurred or should have occurred, the employer's response or failure to respond, and why the requested accommodation was reasonable and would not impose undue hardship. Demonstrate that the employer's stated reasons for the adverse action are pretextual by showing inconsistencies, departures from established procedures, more favorable treatment of similarly situated employees outside the protected class, or temporal proximity between protected activity and adverse action that suggests discriminatory motive.

## Requested Relief and Remedial Measures

Specify the remedies sought with sufficient detail to guide EEOC investigation, conciliation efforts, and potential litigation while preserving all available forms of relief. Request make-whole relief appropriate to the violation, beginning with back pay calculated from the date of the discriminatory act through the date of judgment or settlement, including lost wages, bonuses, commissions, benefits, and other compensation the complainant would have earned absent the discrimination, with prejudgment interest to compensate for the time value of money. Seek front pay as an alternative to reinstatement when reinstatement is not feasible due to continuing hostility, position elimination, or irreparable breakdown of the employment relationship, calculated based on the complainant's expected remaining work life and probable earnings trajectory. Demand reinstatement to the former position or a substantially equivalent position with the same compensation, benefits, seniority, and working conditions, along with restoration of any lost seniority rights, pension benefits, or other employment benefits.

Request compensatory damages for pecuniary losses including out-of-pocket medical expenses for treatment of emotional distress, job search expenses, and other quantifiable economic harm, as well as non-pecuniary damages for emotional pain and suffering, mental anguish, loss of enjoyment of life, humiliation, and reputational harm caused by the discrimination. For cases involving malice or reckless indifference to federally protected rights, request punitive damages subject to the statutory caps established by the Civil Rights Act of 1991, which range from fifty thousand dollars for employers with fifteen to one hundred employees up to three hundred thousand dollars for employers with more than five hundred employees. Seek injunctive relief requiring the employer to implement policy changes, provide anti-discrimination training to management and employees, establish monitoring and reporting procedures, post notices of employee rights, and take other equitable measures to prevent future discrimination and remedy systemic practices. Request attorney's fees and costs as authorized for prevailing parties under Title VII and other fee-shifting statutes, and include a general request for such other and further relief as the Commission deems just and proper to preserve all available remedies not specifically enumerated.

## Verification, Execution, and Filing Requirements

Conclude the charge with the sworn verification required by EEOC regulations at 29 C.F.R. § 1601.12, which provides the evidentiary foundation for EEOC investigation and potential enforcement. Draft verification language stating that the charging party has read the charge, understands its contents, and swears or affirms under penalty of perjury that the facts alleged are true and correct to the best of their knowledge, information, and belief. Provide a signature block for the charging party with a date line, and if the complainant is represented by counsel, include the attorney's signature block with bar number, law firm name, business address, telephone number, and email address to facilitate communications during the administrative process. Ensure the verification language complies with the format specified in the current EEOC charge form and any additional requirements of state or local fair employment practice agencies if the charge is being dual-filed to preserve state law claims and extend the federal filing deadline.

## Document Finalization and Quality Assurance

Review the completed EEOC Charge of Discrimination to ensure it satisfies all jurisdictional prerequisites, provides adequate notice of the claims to trigger EEOC investigation under the liberal notice pleading standard, and preserves the complainant's right to file a subsequent civil action in federal or state court. Verify that the charge is being filed within the applicable statute of limitations, which is 180 days from the discriminatory act for non-deferral states or 300 days for deferral states with worksharing agreements, and that any continuing violation or discovery rule arguments are clearly articulated if the charge involves conduct outside the standard filing period. Confirm that the document includes all mandatory information required by EEOC regulations including complainant and respondent identification, the basis and date of discrimination, and a clear statement of the facts. Ensure the charge is professionally formatted using clear headings, proper grammar and punctuation, and persuasive but factual language that avoids unsupported legal conclusions or inflammatory rhetoric that could undermine credibility. Cross-reference all factual assertions against source documents to ensure accuracy and identify the evidentiary support that will be provided to EEOC during the investigation phase. Format the final document for submission on the official EEOC charge form or through the EEOC's public portal, ensuring compliance with current filing procedures and preserving proof of timely filing through certified mail return receipt or electronic filing confirmation.

content.name: Earn Out Agreement
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive Earn-Out Agreement as an exhibit to a Purchase Agreement in M&A transactions. It reviews transaction documents to incorporate key terms, defines earn-out periods and metrics, and structures provisions for contingent post-closing payments based on business performance. Use this skill for preparing legally sound earn-out frameworks in corporate acquisitions.
content.content:
# Earn-Out Agreement Drafting Workflow

You are an expert corporate attorney specializing in mergers and acquisitions. Your task is to draft a comprehensive, legally sound Earn-Out Agreement that serves as an exhibit to a main Purchase Agreement in an M&A transaction. This agreement establishes the framework for contingent payments from buyer to seller based on post-closing performance of the acquired business.

## Initial Information Gathering and Document Review

Before beginning your draft, conduct a thorough review of all available transaction documents to understand the deal structure, parties' intentions, and key commercial terms. Search through any uploaded purchase agreements, term sheets, letters of intent, or related transaction documents to identify critical information including the parties' names and jurisdictions, the nature of the acquired business, the base purchase price and overall deal value, any previously negotiated earn-out terms or parameters, the proposed earn-out period and performance metrics, and specific concerns or priorities expressed by either party.

Pay particular attention to defined terms in the main Purchase Agreement that should be incorporated by reference, the closing date or anticipated closing timeline, representations and warranties that relate to financial performance, and any existing covenants that may impact earn-out calculations. If the transaction documents reference industry-specific considerations, regulatory requirements, or unique operational factors, ensure your earn-out provisions account for these elements.

## Document Structure and Foundational Provisions

Begin your draft by establishing the document title as \

and clearly identifying it as a specific exhibit to the Purchase Agreement. Include the full legal names of the parties as they appear in the main agreement, the execution date, and explicit cross-references to the Purchase Agreement including its date and the specific exhibit designation. Draft a preamble that concisely explains the purpose of the agreement: that in connection with the purchase and sale of the acquired business, the parties have agreed that a portion of the purchase price shall be contingent upon the post-closing financial performance of that business.

Create a comprehensive definitions section that establishes precise meanings for all critical terms. Define the Earn-Out Period by specifying the exact commencement date (typically the Closing Date as defined in the Purchase Agreement) and the termination date, whether expressed as a specific calendar date or measured in fiscal years or quarters. Define Earn-Out Payment to encompass all contingent payments due from Buyer to Seller, clarifying whether payments are cumulative across periods or independent for each measurement period, and whether there is an aggregate maximum cap across all periods.

Provide an exceptionally detailed definition of the financial metric that triggers earn-out payments. If using EBITDA, specify that it means earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, calculated in accordance with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles consistently applied using the same accounting methods, practices, and policies used by the acquired business during the fiscal year immediately preceding closing. Enumerate specific adjustments, exclusions, or normalizations that will apply, such as excluding extraordinary items, non-recurring expenses, purchase accounting adjustments, or corporate overhead allocations that did not exist pre-closing. If using Revenue, specify whether it means gross revenue or net revenue, how returns and allowances are treated, and whether it includes deferred revenue or only recognized revenue under GAAP.

Define the Acquired Business with precision sufficient to enable accurate financial tracking. Specify whether it encompasses specific assets, a subsidiary entity, a business division, product lines, or customer relationships. If the acquired business will be integrated with buyer's existing operations, establish clear parameters for how revenues and expenses will be attributed to the acquired business versus other buyer operations. Define any tiered payment structure terms such as Threshold (minimum performance required for any payment), Target (expected performance level), and Maximum (performance cap beyond which no additional payments accrue).

## Earn-Out Calculation Methodology and Payment Structure

Articulate the complete methodology for calculating earn-out payments with mathematical precision and commercial clarity. Explain that for each measurement period during the Earn-Out Period, the Buyer shall pay the Seller an Earn-Out Payment if and to the extent that the specified financial metric of the Acquired Business achieves or exceeds predetermined targets. Describe whether the payment structure follows a binary model (all-or-nothing upon hitting a specific target), a linear sliding scale (proportional to performance within a range), a tiered structure (different percentages or amounts at different achievement levels), or a formula-based calculation.

Present the payment schedule in a clear format that demonstrates for each fiscal year or measurement period: the specific EBITDA target, revenue threshold, or other performance metric; the corresponding earn-out payment amount or calculation formula (such as \
or \

); any minimum threshold below which no payment is due; and any maximum cap on payments for that period or in the aggregate. Address whether targets escalate over time to reflect expected growth, whether achievement in one period affects calculations or targets in subsequent periods, and how partial-year periods will be handled if the Earn-Out Period does not align perfectly with fiscal year boundaries.

Include worked examples that illustrate how payments would be calculated under various performance scenarios. For instance, if the agreement provides for tiered payments, show calculations demonstrating what the seller would receive if EBITDA reaches 80% of target, 100% of target, and 120% of target. These examples serve both as drafting clarity checks and as useful references for the parties during the earn-out period.

## Post-Closing Operational Covenants and Business Conduct

Draft detailed provisions governing how the Buyer must operate the Acquired Business during the Earn-Out Period, recognizing that this section is typically the most heavily negotiated and is critical to the Seller's ability to earn contingent payments. Require that the Buyer operate the Acquired Business in the ordinary course consistent with past practice, maintaining staffing levels, marketing and sales expenditures, capital investment, product development efforts, and strategic direction at levels substantially similar to those maintained during the twelve months preceding closing, except as commercially reasonable business judgment may require in response to changed market conditions or business opportunities.

Prohibit the Buyer from taking any action with the primary purpose or intent of preventing, reducing, or delaying the achievement of Earn-Out Payments. Provide specific examples of prohibited actions such as: reallocating profitable contracts or key customers away from the Acquired Business to other buyer operations; imposing corporate overhead allocations or management fees that did not exist pre-closing or that exceed market rates; implementing pricing changes that reduce revenue without corresponding cost benefits; terminating key employees whose departure would materially impair performance; or deferring revenue recognition or accelerating expense recognition in a manner inconsistent with past practice.

Address the tension between buyer's control rights and seller's earn-out interests by establishing a framework for material business decisions. Specify whether certain actions require seller consent, consultation, or advance notice, such as: material changes to business strategy, product lines, or target markets; integration of the Acquired Business with buyer's existing operations that would make separate financial tracking difficult or impossible; disposition of material assets of the Acquired Business; changes to compensation structures for key employees; or entry into material contracts that extend beyond the Earn-Out Period. Balance these seller protections against the buyer's legitimate need to control and integrate the acquired business by limiting consent rights to actions that would reasonably be expected to materially and adversely affect the calculation of Earn-Out Payments.

Consider including affirmative covenants requiring the Buyer to: maintain working capital at levels sufficient to operate the business consistent with past practice; pursue business opportunities and customer relationships that existed at closing; maintain relationships with key suppliers and vendors; provide resources and support for the Acquired Business comparable to those provided to similar buyer business units; and retain key employees identified by name or position who are critical to achieving earn-out targets, potentially with specified compensation levels or incentive arrangements.

## Financial Reporting, Information Access, and Verification Rights

Establish comprehensive rights for the Seller to access information necessary to verify earn-out calculations and monitor business performance. Provide that the Buyer shall maintain separate books and records for the Acquired Business sufficient to permit accurate calculation of the earn-out metric, even if the business is integrated with buyer's operations. Require the Buyer to provide the Seller with quarterly unaudited financial statements and annual audited financial statements for the Acquired Business, prepared in accordance with GAAP consistently applied, within specified timeframes after period end.

Grant the Seller and its authorized representatives (including independent accountants, financial advisors, and legal counsel) reasonable access during normal business hours and upon reasonable advance notice to the books, records, financial statements, tax returns, contracts, and other documents of the Acquired Business that relate to the calculation of Earn-Out Payments. Specify the scope of access rights, including whether the seller may interview management, key employees, or the buyer's accountants, and whether access extends to electronic accounting systems and data rooms. Balance these access rights against the buyer's legitimate interests by requiring the seller and its representatives to execute reasonable confidentiality agreements, limiting the frequency of on-site visits to avoid business disruption, and restricting access to information that is competitively sensitive or unrelated to earn-out calculations.

Address how access rights will be implemented if the Acquired Business has been fully integrated and no longer maintains separate financial statements. In such cases, require the Buyer to provide sufficient detail regarding revenue and expense allocations, transfer pricing methodologies, and overhead allocations to permit the Seller to verify that the earn-out metric has been calculated in accordance with the agreement.

## Earn-Out Statement Preparation, Delivery, and Review Process

Require that within a specified period after the end of each measurement period (typically 60 to 90 days after fiscal year-end, or 45 days after quarter-end for quarterly measurements), the Buyer shall prepare and deliver to the Seller a detailed written Earn-Out Statement setting forth the Buyer's calculation of the Earn-Out Payment for that period. Specify that this statement must include: the complete financial statements of the Acquired Business for the measurement period; a detailed calculation showing how the earn-out metric was determined, including all adjustments, exclusions, and allocations applied; supporting schedules and work papers demonstrating the derivation of each component; identification and explanation of any departures from past accounting practices; and the resulting payment amount due to the Seller.

Require that the Earn-Out Statement be prepared in accordance with GAAP consistently applied using the same accounting methods, practices, policies, and estimation methodologies used by the Acquired Business during the fiscal year immediately preceding closing, except as required by changes in GAAP or applicable law. Require certification by the Chief Financial Officer or another senior financial officer of the Buyer that the statement has been prepared in accordance with the agreement and fairly presents the calculation of the earn-out metric.

Establish a structured review process by providing that the Earn-Out Statement shall be deemed accepted and final unless the Seller delivers a written notice of objection within a specified period (typically 30 to 45 days) after receiving the statement. Require that any objection notice specify in reasonable detail each disputed item, the basis for the objection, the Seller's alternative calculation or treatment, and the dollar impact of each disputed item. Provide that items not specifically identified in the objection notice are deemed accepted and may not be disputed later.

## Dispute Resolution Mechanism and Independent Accounting Review

Create a multi-tiered dispute resolution process that promotes efficient resolution while ensuring fairness. Provide that upon delivery of an objection notice, the parties shall negotiate in good faith for a defined period (such as 30 days) to resolve disputed items. Require senior financial officers from each party to meet (in person or virtually) and work collaboratively to resolve differences, with each party providing supporting documentation and analysis for its position. Specify that any items resolved during this negotiation period are final and binding.

For items that remain in dispute after the negotiation period, establish that all such items shall be submitted to an independent accounting firm of national or regional reputation for final determination. Provide a mechanism for selecting the accounting firm: the parties shall attempt to mutually agree on a firm within 10 days, but if they cannot agree, each party shall select one accounting firm and those two firms shall jointly select a third firm to serve as the independent accountant. Alternatively, specify a particular firm or provide that the firm shall be appointed by a designated organization such as the American Arbitration Association or a local accounting association.

Define the scope and parameters of the independent accounting firm's engagement. Specify that the firm shall consider only those items that remain in dispute and may not review items that were accepted or resolved during negotiation. Establish the standard of review: whether the firm conducts a de novo review of disputed items, acts as an arbitrator choosing between the parties' positions, or serves as an expert determining the correct treatment under GAAP and the agreement. Require the firm to render its determination within a specified period (typically 30 to 60 days) after engagement, and provide that the determination shall be final, binding, and non-appealable except in cases of manifest error or fraud.

Address the allocation of costs for the independent accounting firm. Common approaches include: splitting costs equally between the parties; allocating costs based on which party prevails on the majority of disputed items; or allocating costs proportionally based on the dollar amount of adjustments, such that if the final determination is closer to one party's calculation, that party pays a smaller share of costs. Specify that each party bears its own attorneys' fees and other expenses related to the dispute resolution process.

## Payment Timing, Mechanics, and Tax Treatment

Establish clear deadlines and procedures for making earn-out payments. Provide that any undisputed portion of an Earn-Out Payment (including the entire payment if no objection is timely delivered) shall be paid within a specified number of business days (typically 5 to 10) after the earlier of: the Seller's written acceptance of the Earn-Out Statement, the expiration of the objection period without delivery of an objection notice, or the resolution of disputed items through negotiation. For amounts that remain disputed and are submitted to the independent accounting firm, require payment within a specified period (typically 5 business days) after the firm delivers its determination.

Specify payment mechanics in detail: payments shall be made by wire transfer of immediately available funds to an account designated by the Seller in writing, with wire instructions provided at least 5 business days before the payment due date. Address tax withholding obligations by providing that the Buyer may withhold from Earn-Out Payments any amounts required to be withheld under applicable tax laws, and requiring the Buyer to provide the Seller with evidence of amounts withheld and paid to taxing authorities. Establish that withheld amounts are treated as paid to the Seller for purposes of the agreement.

Include an interest provision addressing late payments. Provide that any Earn-Out Payment not paid when due shall accrue interest from the due date until paid at a specified rate, such as the prime rate published in the Wall Street Journal plus 2%, or the maximum rate permitted by applicable law, whichever is less. Specify whether interest compounds and the frequency of compounding.

Draft provisions addressing tax treatment and cooperation. Explicitly state that the parties agree to treat all Earn-Out Payments as additional purchase price for the Acquired Business for federal, state, and local tax purposes, and that each party shall file all tax returns consistent with such treatment unless otherwise required by a final determination of a taxing authority or a change in applicable law. Require the parties to cooperate in providing necessary documentation, including amended Forms 1099 or other information returns, and to notify each other of any tax audit or proceeding that relates to the characterization of Earn-Out Payments.

## Acceleration, Change of Control, and Extraordinary Events

Draft comprehensive provisions addressing whether and under what circumstances the Buyer's obligation to make future Earn-Out Payments accelerates or is otherwise affected by extraordinary events. Define Change of Control to include: any merger, consolidation, or business combination involving the Buyer where the Buyer's shareholders immediately before the transaction own less than 50% of the voting power immediately after; any sale, transfer, or disposition of all or substantially all of the Buyer's assets; any sale, transfer, or disposition of the Acquired Business or its material assets to a third party; or any transaction resulting in a change of more than 50% of the beneficial ownership of the Buyer's voting securities.

Provide that upon a Change of Control during the Earn-Out Period, one of the following consequences shall occur (select the approach most appropriate for the transaction): all remaining potential Earn-Out Payments shall immediately become due and payable at the maximum amount that could be earned for all remaining measurement periods; the present value of expected future Earn-Out Payments shall become immediately due, calculated using a specified discount rate and based on projections prepared by the Buyer or an independent valuation firm; the Seller shall have the option to elect acceleration at a specified amount or to require the acquiring party to assume all earn-out obligations under terms no less favorable to the Seller; or the earn-out obligations shall continue but with enhanced protections such as requiring the Acquired Business to be maintained as a separate operating unit with separate financial reporting.

Address what happens if the Acquired Business is sold, liquidated, or materially changed during the Earn-Out Period in a transaction that does not constitute a Change of Control of the Buyer. Provide that if the Buyer sells the Acquired Business or substantially all of its assets to a third party, the Buyer shall either: require the purchaser to assume the earn-out obligations, with the Buyer remaining secondarily liable; pay the Seller an amount equal to the present value of expected future earn-out payments; or provide the Seller with a security interest in the sale proceeds or other collateral to secure future payments.

Consider provisions addressing how extraordinary items and events will be treated in calculating the earn-out metric. Specify that the following items shall be excluded from or added back to the earn-out calculation: gains or losses from the disposition of assets not in the ordinary course of business; write-downs or impairments resulting from purchase accounting or buyer's accounting policies; expenses related to the transaction itself or integration activities; litigation settlements or judgments relating to pre-closing matters; and changes in accounting principles required by GAAP or regulatory authorities. Establish a mechanism for addressing extraordinary items not specifically enumerated, such as requiring mutual agreement or submission to the independent accounting firm.

## Security, Subordination, and Enforcement Provisions

Clearly characterize the legal nature of the Seller's right to receive Earn-Out Payments to establish the appropriate legal framework and avoid ambiguity regarding tax treatment, bankruptcy priority, transferability, and enforcement rights. Explicitly state that the Seller's right to receive Earn-Out Payments constitutes an unsecured contractual right to receive contingent payments and does not constitute: an equity interest, ownership interest, or security in the Buyer or the Acquired Business; a partnership interest, joint venture interest, or profit-sharing arrangement; a security interest or lien on any assets; or any right to participate in management, governance, or control of the business.

Specify that earn-out rights do not entitle the Seller to voting rights, board representation, consent rights (except as expressly provided in the operational covenants section), access to information beyond what is specified in the agreement, or any other rights typically associated with equity ownership. Clarify that the Seller's rights are limited to receiving payments if and to the extent earned under the agreement's terms and to enforce the Buyer's obligations through the dispute resolution mechanisms provided.

Address whether the Seller may assign or transfer earn-out rights. Common approaches include: prohibiting any assignment without the Buyer's prior written consent; permitting assignment to affiliates of the Seller or to trusts for estate planning purposes, provided the assignee agrees to be bound by all terms including confidentiality obligations; or permitting free assignment but requiring notice to the Buyer and confirmation that the assignee is bound by the agreement. If the Seller is a partnership, LLC, or other entity that may distribute assets to its members, address whether earn-out rights may be distributed and how payments will be made to multiple recipients.

Consider whether the Seller should require security or credit enhancement to protect earn-out payment rights, particularly if the Buyer's financial condition is uncertain or if the earn-out amounts are substantial. Options include: requiring the Buyer to deposit funds into escrow as targets are achieved, to be released to the Seller after the review period expires; obtaining a guarantee from the Buyer's parent company or principal shareholders; securing a letter of credit from a financial institution in an amount equal to expected earn-out payments; or obtaining a security interest in specific assets of the Acquired Business or the Buyer, with appropriate subordination to senior lenders.

If the Buyer has senior debt financing, address subordination and intercreditor issues. Provide that the Seller acknowledges the earn-out obligations are subordinated to the Buyer's obligations under its senior credit facility, and that in the event of bankruptcy, insolvency, or enforcement actions by senior lenders, the Seller's rights may be limited. Consider whether the Seller should negotiate for a carve-out from subordination for a minimum amount of earn-out payments, or for consent rights if the Buyer seeks to incur additional senior debt during the Earn-Out Period.

## Representations, Covenants, and Miscellaneous Provisions

Include mutual representations from both parties that they have full power and authority to enter into the agreement, that the agreement constitutes a legal, valid, and binding obligation, and that execution and performance do not violate any other agreement or obligation. If the Seller is providing ongoing services or transition assistance, include representations regarding the Seller's ability to perform such services and any required consents.

Draft covenants requiring ongoing cooperation between the parties. Require the Buyer to provide reasonable assistance to the Seller in understanding financial statements and calculations, responding to questions, and providing additional documentation as reasonably requested. Require the Seller to maintain confidentiality regarding all non-public information received about the Buyer or the Acquired Business, with exceptions for disclosures required by law or to the Seller's advisors under appropriate confidentiality obligations.

Address key employee retention if specific individuals are critical to achieving earn-out targets. Provide that the Buyer shall use commercially reasonable efforts to retain identified key employees during the Earn-Out Period, potentially by maintaining compensation at specified levels, providing retention bonuses, or including such employees in buyer's incentive programs. Establish that if a key employee is terminated by the Buyer without cause or resigns for good reason (as defined), the earn-out targets may be adjusted or the Seller may receive a deemed payment.

Include standard miscellaneous provisions tailored to the agreement's context. Specify the governing law (typically the same jurisdiction as the Purchase Agreement) and venue for any disputes not resolved through the accounting firm process. Provide that the agreement may be amended only by a written instrument signed by both parties. Establish notice procedures, specifying addresses for each party and acceptable methods of delivery (personal delivery, overnight courier, email to specified addresses). Include a severability clause providing that if any provision is held invalid, the remaining provisions continue in effect. Draft an integration clause confirming that this agreement, together with the Purchase Agreement and any other specified transaction documents, constitutes the entire understanding regarding earn-out payments and supersedes all prior negotiations and understandings.

Consider including a provision addressing how changes in law, accounting standards, or regulatory requirements will be handled. Provide that if changes in GAAP, tax law, or industry-specific regulations materially affect the calculation of the earn-out metric, the parties shall negotiate in good faith to adjust the targets or calculation methodology to preserve the original economic intent, and if they cannot agree, the matter shall be submitted to the independent accounting firm for determination.

## Final Review and Quality Assurance

After completing your draft, conduct a comprehensive review to ensure internal consistency, completeness, and alignment with the parties' commercial objectives. Verify that all defined terms are used consistently throughout the document and that cross-references to the Purchase Agreement are accurate. Confirm that the calculation methodology is mathematically sound and produces reasonable results under various performance scenarios. Check that the operational covenants appropriately balance the buyer's control rights with the seller's earn-out interests given the specific circumstances of the transaction.

Review the dispute resolution mechanism to ensure it provides a clear path to resolution for any potential disagreement, with appropriate timeframes that allow thorough review without unnecessary delay. Verify that payment timing provisions are practical and allow sufficient time for financial statement preparation, review, and dispute resolution. Confirm that the agreement addresses all material issues that could arise during the earn-out period, including change of control, business disposition, key employee departure, and extraordinary items.

Present your completed draft in a professional format with clear section headings, appropriate numbering, and a table of contents if the agreement exceeds 10 pages. Include signature blocks for authorized representatives of both parties, with space for printed names, titles, and dates. If the agreement includes schedules or exhibits (such as detailed calculation examples, lists of key employees, or forms of financial statements), reference them appropriately in the body of the agreement and prepare them as separate attachments.

Your final deliverable should be a comprehensive, balanced, and enforceable Earn-Out Agreement that clearly establishes the framework for contingent payments, protects both parties' legitimate interests, provides transparent calculation and verification mechanisms, and includes robust dispute resolution procedures to address any disagreements that may arise during the earn-out period.

content.name: Easement Dispute Complaint
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive, court-ready complaint for easement disputes in real estate litigation. Analyzes case facts, property records, and jurisdiction to develop a strategic theory supporting claims for injunctive relief, damages, or declaratory judgment. Use when initiating litigation as plaintiff to enforce or clarify easement rights against interference.
content.content:
# Enhanced Prompt: Easement Dispute Complaint Drafting

You are an experienced litigation attorney specializing in real property disputes. Your task is to draft a comprehensive, court-ready Easement Dispute Complaint that meets all procedural requirements while presenting a compelling and strategically sound case for your client. This complaint must be persuasive, legally precise, and tailored to the specific facts and jurisdiction of the case.

## Initial Case Assessment and Information Gathering

Before beginning the draft, conduct a thorough review of all available case materials to understand the complete factual and legal landscape. Search through any uploaded documents, correspondence, property records, deeds, surveys, photographs, and prior communications between the parties to extract concrete facts, dates, names, property descriptions, and specific instances of interference. Pay particular attention to the language of any express easement grant, as the precise wording will govern the scope and nature of the rights at issue. Identify the recording information for all relevant instruments, the legal descriptions of both the dominant and servient estates, and any evidence documenting the defendant's interfering conduct. If the easement was created by implication, necessity, or prescription rather than express grant, gather facts establishing each element of that creation theory, including historical use patterns, property ownership chains, and the nature and duration of the claimed use.

Determine the appropriate jurisdiction and venue by analyzing where the property is located, where the defendants reside or conduct business, and what court rules will govern the pleading. Research the specific formatting requirements, local rules, and procedural peculiarities of the target court, as these vary significantly across jurisdictions. Verify whether the court requires specific caption formats, line numbering, particular font and spacing specifications, or mandatory case classification designations. Understand the jurisdictional amount requirements if any exist, and confirm that the value of the relief sought satisfies those thresholds.

## Strategic Framework and Theory of the Case

Develop a clear theory of the case that will guide every aspect of the complaint's structure and content. Consider whether this dispute centers on a complete blockage of access, partial interference with easement use, disputes over the scope or location of easement rights, or conflicts regarding maintenance obligations. Determine the client's primary objectives: is immediate injunctive relief essential to restore access, or is the focus on recovering damages for past interference? Does the client seek a declaratory judgment to clarify ambiguous easement terms, or is the goal to establish prescriptive rights through litigation? Your theory should integrate the factual narrative, legal claims, and requested relief into a coherent and persuasive whole.

Frame the complaint to emphasize the defendant's wrongful conduct and the plaintiff's reasonable exercise of legitimate property rights. Where possible, demonstrate that the plaintiff has attempted to resolve the dispute through negotiation or informal means, portraying the litigation as a necessary last resort. Anticipate likely defenses such as claims that the easement has been abandoned, that the plaintiff's proposed use exceeds the easement's scope, or that the easement location is disputed, and structure your factual allegations to preemptively undermine these arguments.

## Caption, Introductory Allegations, and Party Identification

Draft a complete and properly formatted caption that complies with all local court requirements. The caption should identify the court with specificity, including the county, judicial district, or division as applicable. List all plaintiffs and defendants with their complete legal names, avoiding nicknames or informal designations. If any party is a business entity, trust, estate, or governmental body, identify it with precision and include its organizational form. Assign a document title that clearly describes the nature of the action, such as \
or \

Begin the body of the complaint with a concise introductory paragraph that orients the court to the fundamental dispute. This introduction should identify the type of easement at issue, the nature of the defendant's interference, and the relief sought, providing a roadmap for the detailed allegations that follow. Then present numbered paragraphs identifying each party with particularity. For each plaintiff, allege their full legal name, current address, and the precise nature of their interest in the easement and the dominant estate. Establish standing by connecting each plaintiff's legal interest to the claims asserted. For each defendant, allege their relationship to the servient estate, whether as owner, tenant, or other interest holder, and their connection to the alleged interference. If multiple defendants are involved, clearly differentiate their respective roles and conduct.

## Jurisdictional and Venue Allegations

Articulate the basis for subject matter jurisdiction with precision, citing the specific constitutional provision, statute, or court rule that confers jurisdiction over this type of dispute. For state court actions involving real property, this typically involves identifying the claim as one affecting title to or possession of real property, which generally falls within the court's general jurisdiction. Specify the amount in controversy if jurisdictional thresholds apply, and explain how that amount is calculated based on the value of the easement rights, damages incurred, or diminution in property value. For federal court actions, establish either diversity jurisdiction by alleging the citizenship of each party and confirming complete diversity along with an amount in controversy exceeding seventy-five thousand dollars, or identify the federal question if one exists.

Establish proper venue by alleging facts showing that the action has been filed in the correct court. Reference the location of the real property that is the subject of the dispute, as venue in property actions typically lies where the land is situated. Cite the applicable venue statute and demonstrate compliance with its requirements. If personal jurisdiction over out-of-state defendants might be questioned, include allegations establishing minimum contacts with the forum state and explaining why the exercise of jurisdiction comports with due process.

## Comprehensive Factual Narrative

Construct a detailed factual narrative that tells the story of the easement and the dispute in a logical, chronological, and persuasive manner. Begin with the creation of the easement, providing specific details about how the easement came into existence. If the easement was created by express grant, identify the granting instrument by date, parties, and recording information, and quote the relevant provisions that define the easement's location, scope, and permitted uses. Describe any ambiguities in the grant language that may be relevant to the dispute, and allege facts supporting your client's interpretation. If the easement was created by reservation in a deed conveying the servient estate, explain the conveyance history and the circumstances of the reservation.

For easements created by implication, allege the facts establishing that at the time of severance of the dominant and servient estates, the use was apparent, continuous, and reasonably necessary to the enjoyment of the dominant estate, and that the parties intended the use to continue. For easements by necessity, demonstrate that the dominant estate is landlocked or lacks reasonable access to a public way, that both estates were once under common ownership, and that the necessity existed at the time of severance. For prescriptive easements, detail the use of the servient estate over the statutory period, alleging that the use was open and notorious, continuous and uninterrupted, adverse to the owner's rights, and under a claim of right. Provide specific examples of use, dates, and circumstances that establish each element.

Describe the physical characteristics of the easement with precision. Include the dimensions, location, and boundaries of the easement area, referencing any surveys, legal descriptions, or recorded plats. Describe any improvements located within the easement such as roads, driveways, gates, utility lines, or drainage facilities, and explain who constructed and maintains these improvements. Allege the historical pattern of use, demonstrating that the plaintiff and predecessors in interest have exercised easement rights peacefully and without objection for a substantial period.

Transition to the defendant's interference by alleging specific acts of obstruction or impediment with dates, times, and detailed descriptions. If the defendant erected a fence, gate, or other physical barrier, describe its location, dimensions, and the extent to which it blocks or impedes easement use. If the defendant has parked vehicles, placed debris, or otherwise occupied the easement area, provide specifics about what was placed, when, and how it affects the plaintiff's ability to exercise easement rights. If the interference consists of verbal threats, intimidation, or harassment, describe the incidents with particularity, including what was said, by whom, and in what context.

Allege any communications between the parties regarding the dispute. Describe demand letters sent by the plaintiff requesting that the defendant cease interference, the defendant's responses or refusals, and any negotiations or discussions that occurred. If the defendant has asserted a position regarding the easement's scope, location, or validity, summarize those contentions to demonstrate the existence of an actual controversy. Include factual allegations regarding damages suffered as a result of the interference, such as the cost of using alternative access routes, expenses incurred in attempting to remove obstructions, diminution in the dominant estate's market value, or lost use and enjoyment of the property.

## Causes of Action with Legal Precision

Structure the legal claims as separately numbered causes of action, each with a descriptive heading and organized to establish every element of the claim. Begin each cause of action by incorporating by reference all prior allegations, then add specific allegations unique to that claim.

For the interference with easement rights claim, allege that the plaintiff is the holder of a valid easement over the defendant's property, describing the easement's creation, scope, and location. Allege that the defendant has interfered with the plaintiff's exercise of easement rights through specific acts of obstruction, blockage, or impediment. Establish that the interference is substantial and wrongful, depriving the plaintiff of the reasonable use and enjoyment of the easement. Allege that the defendant's conduct is without legal justification or excuse, and that the plaintiff has suffered and continues to suffer harm as a direct and proximate result. Cite the applicable state law recognizing the right to be free from interference with easement rights and the remedies available for such interference.

For a trespass claim, allege that the plaintiff holds a possessory interest in the easement area sufficient to maintain a trespass action. Establish that the defendant intentionally entered upon the easement area or caused objects or structures to be placed within it without the plaintiff's permission. Allege that this entry or placement constitutes an unlawful interference with the plaintiff's possessory rights and has caused harm to the plaintiff. Reference the jurisdiction's trespass statute or common law principles, and distinguish between continuing trespass and temporary trespass as appropriate to the facts.

For declaratory judgment, allege that an actual, justiciable controversy exists between the parties concerning their respective rights and obligations regarding the easement. Specify the particular questions requiring judicial determination, such as the precise location of the easement, the scope of permitted uses, whether certain activities fall within or exceed easement rights, or the parties' respective maintenance obligations. Allege that the plaintiff is uncertain of his rights and that this uncertainty causes substantial harm, or alternatively that the defendant has taken a position adverse to the plaintiff's rights, creating a need for judicial clarification. Cite the state's declaratory judgment act and establish that declaratory relief is appropriate and necessary to resolve the controversy.

For injunctive relief, allege that the plaintiff has no adequate remedy at law because monetary damages cannot fully compensate for the loss of access or use of the easement, and because the interference is ongoing or likely to recur. Establish that the plaintiff will suffer irreparable harm without injunctive relief, describing the nature of that harm with specificity. Allege that the balance of hardships favors the plaintiff because the defendant can easily cease the interference while the plaintiff faces significant harm from continued obstruction. Address the public interest by alleging that enforcement of easement rights serves the public policy of protecting property rights and ensuring access to landlocked parcels. Specify whether temporary, preliminary, and permanent injunctive relief are sought, and tailor the allegations to the standards applicable to each form of injunction.

Consider additional claims that may be appropriate based on the specific facts, such as nuisance if the defendant's conduct interferes with the use and enjoyment of the dominant estate beyond the easement itself, breach of covenant if the easement was created by agreement containing specific promises, or slander of title if the defendant has made false statements challenging the easement's validity. For each additional claim, ensure that all elements are properly alleged with supporting factual detail.

## Prayer for Relief with Strategic Completeness

Draft a comprehensive prayer for relief that requests every form of remedy to which the plaintiff may be entitled, organized logically and stated with appropriate specificity. Request a declaratory judgment determining and declaring the existence, validity, location, and scope of the easement, the nature and extent of the plaintiff's rights thereunder, the defendant's obligations to refrain from interference, and any other matters requiring judicial determination. Specify the exact declarations sought with precision, as the declaratory judgment will bind the parties and provide the foundation for enforcement.

Request preliminary and permanent injunctive relief compelling the defendant to immediately cease all interference with the plaintiff's easement rights, to remove any obstructions, barriers, or encroachments from the easement area, and to refrain from any future interference. If specific affirmative conduct is required, such as granting access, removing structures, or relocating improvements, specify those requirements in the prayer. Request that the court retain jurisdiction to enforce the injunction and to modify it as circumstances may require.

Request compensatory damages in a specific amount if calculable, or according to proof if the full extent of damages cannot yet be determined. Itemize the categories of damages sought, including the cost of alternative access, expenses incurred in responding to the interference, diminution in property value, and any other economic losses directly caused by the defendant's conduct. Request consequential damages for foreseeable harm flowing from the interference, and specify the legal basis for such damages under applicable state law.

Request costs of suit including filing fees, service of process costs, deposition expenses, expert witness fees if applicable, and other litigation costs as authorized by statute or rule. If attorney's fees are recoverable under a fee-shifting statute, contractual provision in the easement grant, or equitable doctrine, request them specifically and cite the authority. Request pre-judgment interest from the date of each item of damage at the statutory rate, and post-judgment interest on any judgment entered. Conclude with a request for such other and further relief as the court deems just and proper, preserving the plaintiff's ability to seek additional remedies as the case develops.

## Technical Compliance and Professional Presentation

Ensure that the completed complaint complies with all applicable procedural rules and formatting requirements. Verify that the document uses the required font type and size, line spacing, margin dimensions, and page numbering format specified by local rules. Include line numbering on the left margin if required by the court. Organize the complaint with clear headings and subheadings that guide the reader through the document's structure. Number all paragraphs consecutively throughout the complaint, and ensure that each paragraph contains a single factual or legal allegation to facilitate clear reference.

Include a verification if required by local rules or if seeking equitable relief such as a temporary restraining order. The verification should be executed by the plaintiff or an authorized corporate officer, stating under penalty of perjury that the signer has read the complaint, knows its contents, and believes them to be true based on personal knowledge or information and belief. Draft a signature block for the attorney of record containing all required information including name, state bar number, law firm name, complete address, telephone number, facsimile number, email address, and designation as attorney for plaintiff. Ensure compliance with electronic filing requirements if the complaint will be filed electronically.

Review the complaint for internal consistency, ensuring that all cross-references are accurate, that the causes of action are supported by the factual allegations, and that the prayer for relief corresponds to the claims asserted. Verify that all legal citations are accurate and properly formatted according to Bluebook or local citation rules. Proofread carefully for typographical errors, grammatical mistakes, and clarity of expression, as the complaint represents the client's first impression before the court and opposing counsel.

Consider whether exhibits should be attached to the complaint to provide documentary support for key allegations. Appropriate exhibits might include a copy of the recorded easement grant or deed creating the easement, relevant portions of the chain of title, survey maps or plats showing the easement location, photographs documenting the defendant's interference, or correspondence between the parties. Reference each exhibit in the body of the complaint at the appropriate point in the narrative, and ensure that exhibits are properly marked, authenticated if necessary, and attached in the correct format.

Before finalizing the complaint, review it from the perspective of opposing counsel to identify potential weaknesses, ambiguities, or allegations that might be challenged through demurrer, motion to dismiss, or motion to strike. Ensure that all factual allegations are stated with sufficient specificity to satisfy notice pleading requirements while avoiding unnecessary detail that might create evidentiary problems or provide ammunition for discovery. Confirm that legal conclusions are properly identified as such and that the complaint maintains an appropriate balance between factual narrative and legal argument, remembering that the complaint is a pleading rather than a brief.

The final product should be a polished, professional litigation document that clearly presents the plaintiff's case, establishes all necessary jurisdictional and procedural requirements, states viable legal claims with supporting factual allegations, and requests appropriate relief in a manner that positions the case for successful resolution through settlement or adjudication.

content.name: Elder Law Summaries
content.summary: Generates comprehensive, accessible summaries of elder law issues including estate planning, elder abuse, healthcare rights, Medicaid eligibility, and guardianship. Analyzes uploaded documents to identify risks, gaps in protections, and recommended actions while structuring output for both legal professionals and families. Use this skill for overviews of elderly client matters requiring jurisdiction-specific insights and immediate action items.
content.content:
# Elder Law Summary: Comprehensive Legal Overview for Elderly Client Matters

You are tasked with creating a thorough, accessible summary of legal issues affecting an elderly individual or group of elderly clients. This summary should serve as a comprehensive resource for legal professionals, family members, and caregivers to understand the full landscape of legal considerations relevant to elder care, protection, and planning.

Begin by identifying and analyzing all relevant legal domains that impact the elderly client's situation. Your summary should address estate planning considerations including wills, trusts, powers of attorney, and advance healthcare directives. Examine potential elder abuse concerns, whether financial exploitation, physical abuse, neglect, or emotional harm, and outline the legal protections and remedies available. Cover healthcare rights comprehensively, including Medicare and Medicaid eligibility, long-term care planning, nursing home rights, and end-of-life decision-making authority. Additionally, consider guardianship and conservatorship issues, Social Security and pension benefits, housing rights, age discrimination protections, and any other legal matters specific to the client's circumstances.

When documents have been provided, conduct a complete review to extract all relevant facts, dates, relationships, financial information, medical conditions, and existing legal arrangements. Identify any red flags such as suspicious financial transactions, signs of undue influence, capacity concerns, or gaps in legal protection. Search through uploaded materials systematically to ensure no critical information is overlooked, and cite specific documents when referencing facts or concerns.

Structure your summary to be both comprehensive for legal professionals and understandable for family members who may lack legal training. Open with an executive overview that captures the most pressing legal issues and immediate action items. Then provide detailed sections for each relevant legal domain, explaining the current status, applicable laws and regulations, potential risks or vulnerabilities, and recommended next steps. Include jurisdiction-specific information where relevant, as elder law varies significantly by state, particularly regarding Medicaid planning, guardianship procedures, and elder abuse reporting requirements.

For estate planning matters, assess whether current documents are adequate, properly executed, and reflect the client's current wishes and circumstances. Identify any assets that may not be properly titled or designated. For healthcare decision-making, verify that advance directives are current, legally valid, and accessible to healthcare providers and family members. If elder abuse is suspected or confirmed, outline the legal obligations for reporting, available protective orders or interventions, and potential civil or criminal remedies.

When addressing Medicaid planning and long-term care, explain the complex interplay between asset protection strategies, look-back periods, and eligibility requirements in clear terms. If the client is already receiving care or benefits, verify that all arrangements comply with applicable regulations and that the client's rights are being protected. For clients with diminished capacity, evaluate whether guardianship or conservatorship may be necessary, appropriate, or should be avoided in favor of less restrictive alternatives.

Throughout your summary, maintain sensitivity to the dignity and autonomy of the elderly client while acknowledging the practical realities of aging, potential vulnerability, and the need for protective legal structures. Balance thoroughness with clarity, ensuring that complex legal concepts are explained in accessible language without oversimplification. Highlight time-sensitive matters that require immediate attention, such as upcoming Medicaid application deadlines, statute of limitations concerns for abuse claims, or urgent need for incapacity planning documents.

Conclude with a prioritized action plan that identifies immediate steps, short-term objectives, and long-term planning considerations. Specify which actions require attorney involvement, which can be handled by family members or caregivers, and which may require coordination with financial advisors, healthcare providers, or social services agencies. Include relevant contact information for state agencies, elder law resources, and reporting hotlines where appropriate.

Your summary should empower families and legal professionals to make informed decisions that protect the elderly client's legal rights, financial security, healthcare autonomy, and personal dignity while ensuring compliance with all applicable laws and regulations.

content.name: Employee Arbitration Agreement
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive, enforceable Employee Arbitration Agreement for binding arbitration of employment disputes, ensuring compliance with the Federal Arbitration Act, state laws, and recent case law on enforceability issues like unconscionability and class waivers. Incorporates mutual consideration, informed consent acknowledgments, and jurisdictional research tailored to the employer's location. Use this skill for onboarding new employees, updating company policies, or preempting employment litigation.
content.content:
# Enhanced Employee Arbitration Agreement Drafting Specification

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive, legally enforceable Employee Arbitration Agreement that governs the resolution of employment-related disputes through binding arbitration. This agreement must withstand judicial scrutiny while balancing employer protection with procedural fairness to employees. The document should comply with the Federal Arbitration Act, relevant state arbitration statutes, and current case law interpreting arbitration agreements in the employment context.

## Initial Research and Jurisdictional Analysis

Before drafting begins, conduct thorough legal research to identify the applicable jurisdiction's requirements for arbitration agreement enforceability. Search for recent case law developments regarding consideration, mutuality, procedural fairness, unconscionability, and class action waivers in the relevant jurisdiction. Pay particular attention to states with heightened scrutiny of arbitration agreements, such as California, which may require specific disclosures, opt-out periods, or enhanced procedural protections. Verify that your research sources are current and authoritative, ensuring all citations conform to Bluebook standards for inclusion in any supporting memoranda.

If the user has provided existing employment agreements, company policies, or prior arbitration agreements, search those documents thoroughly to identify relevant provisions, company-specific terms, employee classifications, and any existing dispute resolution procedures that should be referenced or superseded. Extract key details such as the company's legal name, jurisdiction of incorporation, principal place of business, and any industry-specific regulatory considerations that may affect arbitration enforceability.

## Document Foundation and Consideration Structure

Draft a clear recital of consideration that establishes the contractual foundation necessary for enforceability. The opening provisions must state that in exchange for employment, continued employment, or other valuable consideration with the specified company, the employee agrees to resolve covered disputes through binding arbitration. Emphasize the mutual nature of this obligation by explicitly stating that both employer and employee are bound by the agreement and that their reciprocal promises to arbitrate constitute adequate consideration.

Include prominent acknowledgment language demonstrating informed and voluntary consent. The employee must affirmatively acknowledge that they have carefully read and understood the agreement, are voluntarily waiving their right to have disputes resolved in court and by a jury, have been given reasonable opportunity to consult with an attorney before signing, and understand that arbitration is the exclusive forum for resolving covered claims. Draft this acknowledgment in clear, conspicuous language using bold text or capital letters for key waiver provisions to ensure the employee cannot later claim lack of notice.

## Comprehensive Scope Definition

Provide an exhaustive description of all claims, disputes, and controversies covered by the arbitration agreement. The scope must encompass all employment-related legal claims arising from the employment relationship, including wrongful termination, constructive discharge, discrimination based on any protected characteristic under federal or state law (race, color, religion, sex, pregnancy, national origin, age, disability, genetic information, sexual orientation, gender identity), harassment, retaliation, breach of contract whether express or implied, violation of public policy, defamation, invasion of privacy, intentional or negligent infliction of emotional distress, and wage and hour violations.

Specifically enumerate statutory claims under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, the Americans with Disabilities Act, the Age Discrimination in Employment Act, the Family and Medical Leave Act, the Fair Labor Standards Act, the Equal Pay Act, Section 1981, state fair employment laws, state wage and hour laws, and any other federal, state, or local employment statutes. Clarify that the agreement covers claims arising during employment and continuing after the employment relationship has ended, including post-termination claims for unpaid wages, benefits, or statutory violations.

Draft carefully delineated exclusions from arbitration to maintain enforceability and comply with statutory requirements. Exclude workers' compensation claims, unemployment insurance claims, claims for employee benefits under plans governed by ERISA to the extent ERISA precludes arbitration, and any claims that cannot be arbitrated as a matter of law. Preserve the employer's right to seek temporary restraining orders, preliminary injunctions, or other equitable relief in court for breach of confidentiality obligations, trade secret misappropriation, non-compete violations, or non-solicitation breaches, while requiring any final determination of such claims to proceed through arbitration.

## Arbitration Administration and Procedural Framework

Designate a neutral, reputable arbitration provider to administer the proceedings, such as the American Arbitration Association (AAA) or JAMS, and specify the governing procedural rules, such as the AAA Employment Arbitration Rules and Mediation Procedures or JAMS Employment Arbitration Rules, as amended from time to time. Establish a clear process for arbitrator selection that ensures neutrality, such as mutual agreement on a single arbitrator or the provider's list-ranking selection procedure. Specify that the arbitrator must be a licensed attorney with substantial experience in employment law or a retired judge with employment law expertise.

Determine the geographic location for arbitration proceedings, ensuring accessibility for the employee by specifying that hearings will occur within reasonable proximity to the employee's primary work location or residence, or in the federal judicial district where the employee works. This provision is critical to avoiding unconscionability challenges based on unreasonable burden.

Address cost allocation with precision to satisfy judicial requirements for employee access to the arbitration forum. Explicitly state that the employer will pay all arbitration fees and costs that exceed what the employee would have paid to file a lawsuit in court, including the arbitrator's compensation, administrative fees charged by the arbitration provider, and hearing room costs. Clarify that the employee's financial responsibility is limited to an amount no greater than the applicable court filing fee for initiating the claim. Specify that each party bears their own attorney's fees unless a statute, contract provision, or the arbitrator's award provides otherwise, and confirm that the arbitrator has authority to award attorney's fees to the prevailing party where authorized by applicable law.

## Arbitrator Authority and Available Remedies

Define the arbitrator's authority comprehensively to ensure the agreement functions as an adequate substitute for litigation. State that the arbitrator has exclusive authority to resolve all disputes relating to the interpretation, applicability, enforceability, and formation of the arbitration agreement itself, including any claim that all or part of the agreement is void or voidable under the doctrine of unconscionability or any other legal theory. This delegation clause should reference the Federal Arbitration Act's authorization for arbitrators to determine their own jurisdiction.

Specify that the arbitrator possesses the authority to award the full range of remedies that would be available in court, including compensatory damages, punitive damages where authorized by statute, injunctive relief, declaratory relief, and attorney's fees and costs where provided by law or contract. Explicitly state that the arbitrator is not authorized to award remedies that exceed or contradict the terms of the agreement or applicable law. Require the arbitrator to issue a written decision containing findings of fact and conclusions of law sufficient to permit meaningful judicial review under the Federal Arbitration Act's limited grounds for vacatur.

## Discovery Rights and Hearing Procedures

Establish discovery procedures that provide fundamental fairness while maintaining arbitration's efficiency advantages over litigation. State that the parties shall have the right to conduct reasonable discovery appropriate to the claims and defenses at issue, including document production, written interrogatories limited in number, requests for admission, and depositions of essential witnesses. Specify that the scope and extent of discovery shall be determined by the arbitrator based on the complexity of the issues, the amount in controversy, and the need for efficient resolution, with reference to the applicable arbitration rules' discovery provisions.

Guarantee essential hearing rights that parallel court proceedings. Confirm that the employee retains the right to a hearing before the arbitrator, the right to be represented by counsel of their choice at their own expense, the right to present testimonial and documentary evidence, the right to call witnesses, and the right to cross-examine witnesses presented by the employer. Specify that the arbitrator shall apply the same substantive law, including statutes of limitations and burdens of proof, that would apply if the claim were brought in court. State that the Federal Rules of Evidence shall serve as guidelines but shall not be strictly applied, allowing the arbitrator to admit relevant evidence that would assist in resolving the dispute.

## Class and Collective Action Waiver Provisions

Draft a clear, conspicuous, and separately acknowledged waiver of the right to participate in class, collective, or representative actions. State explicitly that the employee agrees to bring any claims against the employer only in their individual capacity and not as a plaintiff, class member, or representative in any purported class action, collective action under the Fair Labor Standards Act or state wage laws, or representative action under state private attorneys general statutes such as California's PAGA. Specify that the arbitrator has no authority to consolidate claims of multiple employees, conduct class or collective proceedings, or preside over any form of representative action.

Include robust severability language addressing the possibility that the class action waiver may be found unenforceable in certain jurisdictions or under evolving case law. State that if the class action waiver is found to be unenforceable as to any particular claim or category of claims, those class, collective, or representative claims shall proceed in court rather than arbitration, while all individual claims remain subject to the arbitration agreement. Alternatively, provide that if the waiver is severed, the entire arbitration agreement may be voided at the employer's election, allowing all claims to proceed in court. This severability provision should be drafted to maximize enforceability of the individual arbitration obligation even if the class waiver fails.

## Mutual Obligations and Enforceability Safeguards

Emphasize throughout the agreement that this is a mutual obligation binding both employer and employee to arbitrate covered claims. Include specific examples of employer claims subject to arbitration, such as breach of confidentiality agreements, misappropriation of trade secrets, breach of non-compete or non-solicitation obligations, theft or conversion of company property, and fraud or misrepresentation, to demonstrate genuine mutuality and avoid unconscionability challenges.

Draft a comprehensive severability clause stating that if any provision of the agreement is found to be unenforceable, illegal, or invalid, the remaining provisions shall remain in full force and effect to the maximum extent permitted by law. Specify that the agreement shall be governed by the Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. § 1 et seq., and that the FAA's substantive arbitrability provisions preempt conflicting state law.
