Assess whether this information could provide a competitive advantage in the current procurement or in reasonably foreseeable follow-on or related procurements, and evaluate whether the information has since become publicly available or has lost its competitive significance due to changed circumstances or passage of time.

For impaired objectivity conflicts, analyze situations where the contractor's ability to render impartial advice, conduct objective technical evaluations, or perform unbiased assessments may be compromised by financial interests, organizational relationships, or personal connections. This analysis should examine whether the contractor has provided consulting services, technical advisory support, or requirements development assistance that could influence its recommendations in ways that favor particular technical approaches, vendors, or solutions in which the contractor has a financial stake. Identify any equity interests, partnership arrangements, teaming agreements, or other financial relationships with entities that could benefit from particular outcomes of the contractor's work. Assess whether the contractor's personnel have prior employment relationships, ongoing consulting arrangements, or personal connections that could bias their professional judgment.

For biased ground rules conflicts, examine whether the contractor has participated in developing specifications, statements of work, evaluation criteria, or acquisition strategies for this procurement or related procurements in ways that could advantage the contractor's own capabilities, favor particular technical approaches aligned with the contractor's expertise, or disadvantage competitors. Describe the nature and extent of the contractor's involvement in requirements development, market research, acquisition planning, or technical advisory services. Analyze whether the contractor's prior work has positioned it to anticipate evaluation criteria, understand the government's priorities in ways not available to competitors, or influence the procurement structure to align with its competitive strengths.

Assess the materiality of each identified conflict by evaluating the severity of the potential impact on the procurement's integrity, the likelihood that the conflict could actually influence the contractor's performance or create competitive unfairness, and the degree to which the conflict creates an appearance of impropriety that could undermine public confidence. Distinguish between conflicts that are substantial and require robust mitigation versus those that are technical or theoretical but pose minimal actual risk.

## Section 3: Tailored Mitigation Strategies and Enforcement Mechanisms

For each material organizational conflict of interest, propose specific, measurable, and enforceable mitigation strategies that will neutralize the conflict or reduce it to an acceptable level commensurate with the government's risk tolerance. The mitigation measures must be precisely tailored to the specific nature, severity, and context of each conflict rather than relying on generic or boilerplate approaches that lack practical enforceability.

Describe organizational firewalls and information barriers that will prevent the flow of competitively sensitive or non-public information between organizational units, ensuring that personnel working on the current contract are effectively isolated from those who possess conflicting information or interests. Specify the physical separation measures, including dedicated facilities, separate office locations, or restricted access areas that will house personnel assigned to the contract. Detail the electronic and cybersecurity controls, including separate network infrastructure, access-controlled databases, restricted email distribution lists, and information system barriers that will prevent inadvertent or intentional information sharing. Explain the administrative controls, including separate reporting chains, independent supervision, confidentiality agreements with specific enforcement provisions, and documented protocols for handling requests for information or assistance that could breach the firewall.

Identify by position title and organizational function the personnel who will be assigned to each side of the firewall, explaining the criteria used to determine assignments and the process for evaluating whether individuals possess disqualifying knowledge or relationships. Describe how the organization will prevent inadvertent information sharing through common corporate resources such as shared knowledge management systems, enterprise-wide meetings, informal mentoring relationships, or social interactions among employees. Establish clear protocols for situations where firewall breaches are suspected or discovered, including immediate reporting requirements, investigation procedures, and remedial actions.

Detail personnel recusal and disqualification measures, specifying which individuals will be excluded from participation in particular tasks, decisions, technical evaluations, or contract activities due to their prior involvement in conflicting work, their access to sensitive information, or their relationships that could impair objectivity. Establish objective criteria for determining when recusal is necessary, moving beyond subjective assessments to create clear, enforceable standards. Describe the process for documenting recusal decisions, obtaining supervisory approval, communicating restrictions to affected personnel, and monitoring compliance. Address how the organization will backfill responsibilities when key personnel are recused, ensuring that contract performance is not compromised while maintaining the integrity of the mitigation approach.

Propose disclosure and transparency measures where appropriate, including commitments to provide the government with ongoing notifications of new information, changed circumstances, emerging conflicts, or potential violations of the mitigation plan. Specify what categories of information will be disclosed, the government officials who will receive such disclosures, the timeframe for notification after triggering events, and the format and level of detail that will be provided. Establish a regular reporting cadence for proactive updates even in the absence of specific triggering events, demonstrating the contractor's commitment to transparency and collaborative OCI management.

If mitigation through organizational measures is insufficient to adequately address the conflicts, address whether the contractor is willing to accept contractual limitations on future business activities, including binding agreements not to compete for specific follow-on procurements, restrictions on the use of information or work product developed under the contract, commitments to divest certain business units or terminate conflicting relationships, or agreements to accept reduced contract scope that eliminates the most problematic activities. Explain the business rationale for accepting such limitations and the mechanisms by which compliance will be ensured and verified.

## Section 4: Implementation Framework and Compliance Architecture

Establish a comprehensive governance framework for implementing, monitoring, and enforcing the mitigation plan throughout the contract performance period and any relevant post-performance period during which residual conflicts may persist. Designate a specific senior official by title, organizational position, and reporting relationship who will serve as the OCI Compliance Officer with ultimate responsibility for overseeing all aspects of the mitigation plan. Describe this individual's professional qualifications, experience with government contracting and regulatory compliance, authority within the organization to enforce mitigation measures and impose disciplinary consequences, and independence from operational pressures that could compromise objective oversight. Ensure the OCI Compliance Officer has direct access to executive leadership and the authority to halt activities or escalate concerns without interference from program management or business development functions.

Detail the training and awareness programs that will be provided to all personnel who may be affected by or involved in implementing the mitigation measures, including employees assigned to the contract, supervisors and managers, business development staff, and corporate leadership. Explain the specific content of such training, including education on FAR OCI principles, the particular conflicts identified in this mitigation plan, the specific restrictions and obligations applicable to different personnel categories, the procedures for seeking guidance when uncertain situations arise, and the consequences of violations. Specify the frequency and format of training delivery, including initial onboarding training for new personnel, annual refresher training for all affected employees, and targeted training when the mitigation plan is updated or new conflicts emerge. Describe the methods for documenting employee acknowledgment and comprehension, including signed certifications, testing or assessment mechanisms, and records retention protocols.

Describe the internal monitoring and auditing procedures that will be used to verify ongoing compliance with the mitigation plan, moving beyond passive reliance on employee self-reporting to establish active verification mechanisms. Specify the frequency of compliance reviews, whether conducted monthly, quarterly, or triggered by specific events such as personnel changes or new business relationships. Detail the documentation that will be maintained to evidence compliance, including firewall access logs, recusal notifications, training records, disclosure submissions, and investigation reports. Establish the audit methodology, including whether reviews will be conducted by internal audit functions, external compliance consultants, or the OCI Compliance Officer, and the scope of such audits including document reviews, personnel interviews, and systems testing.

Commit to providing periodic compliance certifications to the contracting officer at defined intervals, with each certification affirming that the mitigation plan remains effective, no material violations have occurred or all violations have been disclosed and remediated, and no changed circumstances have created new conflicts requiring plan modifications. Specify the organizational level of the certifying official and the due diligence process that will precede each certification to ensure its accuracy.

Establish procedures for updating the mitigation plan when circumstances change, including organizational restructuring, personnel movements, new business relationships, changes in the contract scope, or the emergence of conflicts not anticipated in the original analysis. Include a commitment to promptly notify the contracting officer of any material changes within a specified timeframe, provide a written assessment of the OCI implications, and seek approval before implementing modifications to the mitigation approach. Define what constitutes a \

requiring notification versus minor adjustments that can be managed within the existing framework.

Address the corrective action and remediation procedures that will be triggered if violations or deficiencies are discovered, including immediate containment measures to prevent ongoing harm, investigation protocols to determine the scope and cause of the violation, disciplinary actions for responsible personnel, and systemic improvements to prevent recurrence. Commit to full disclosure of violations to the contracting officer with detailed root cause analysis and proposed remediation plans.

## Section 5: Legal Commitment and Binding Certification

Conclude the mitigation plan with a formal certification executed by an authorized official of the contractor organization who possesses actual authority to bind the company to the commitments contained in the plan. The certification should be drafted as a legally binding statement that will be enforceable as a material contract term, not merely as an aspirational expression of intent. The certifying official should affirm that the OCI analysis is complete, thorough, and accurate to the best of the official's knowledge after reasonable inquiry, that all material facts bearing on potential conflicts have been disclosed without omission or misrepresentation, and that the contractor commits to implementing the mitigation measures exactly as described with full understanding of the legal consequences of non-compliance.

Include an explicit acknowledgment that the mitigation plan, once accepted by the government through incorporation into the contract or issuance of a contracting officer determination, becomes a binding obligation with the same legal force as any other material contract term. State clearly that failure to comply with the mitigation plan's terms may constitute a material breach of contract subject to remedies including contract termination for default or convenience, withholding of payment, demand for refund of amounts paid, suspension or debarment from future government contracting, referral for criminal investigation if violations involve false statements or fraud, and any other administrative or legal remedies available to the government.

Provide the printed name, official title, organizational affiliation, signature line, and date line for the certifying official. Ensure the certification is executed by an individual at an appropriately senior level, typically a corporate officer, division president, or other executive with signature authority for legal commitments. If the contractor is a subsidiary or division of a larger corporate entity, consider whether parent company ratification or guarantee is appropriate to ensure enforceability.

## Formatting and Professional Standards

Structure the final mitigation plan as a formal regulatory compliance document suitable for review by government contracting officers, agency legal counsel, inspector general offices, and potentially the Government Accountability Office or other oversight bodies. Use precise legal terminology consistent with the Federal Acquisition Regulation and relevant case law interpreting OCI principles. Organize the document with clear section headings, numbered paragraphs for easy reference, and a logical flow that guides the reader from conflict identification through mitigation strategy to implementation and enforcement.

Maintain a tone that is professional, candid, and appropriately formal, avoiding both defensive posturing and excessive legalistic complexity that could obscure practical meaning. Ensure all factual statements are accurate, verifiable through supporting documentation, and consistent with information provided elsewhere in the contractor's proposal or communications with the government. Avoid speculative scenarios, hypothetical conflicts, or theoretical concerns unless they are reasonably foreseeable based on the contract's scope and the contractor's business activities.

Demonstrate sophisticated understanding of OCI principles and federal procurement policy while ensuring the document remains accessible and actionable for contract administrators, program managers, and compliance personnel who will implement the plan in daily operations. Include sufficient detail to enable effective implementation and monitoring without creating unnecessary complexity that could hinder practical compliance.

The completed mitigation plan should serve as both a legal document that satisfies regulatory requirements and a practical operational guide that the contractor's personnel can follow to maintain compliance throughout contract performance. It should instill confidence in government reviewers that the contractor has thoroughly analyzed potential conflicts, proposed effective and enforceable mitigation measures, and committed to a robust compliance framework that protects the government's interests and the integrity of the procurement process.

content.name: Organizational Meeting Minutes
content.summary: Drafts comprehensive Organizational Meeting Minutes for newly formed corporations or LLCs. Documents critical actions including quorum verification, adoption of bylaws or operating agreements, election of directors and officers, and procedural foundations. Use this skill during corporate formation to create legally sufficient records compliant with state laws for inclusion in the corporate book.
content.content:
# Organizational Meeting Minutes - Corporate Formation Document

You are tasked with drafting comprehensive Organizational Meeting Minutes for a newly formed corporation or limited liability company. These minutes serve as the official record of the initial organizational meeting and are critical corporate governance documents that establish the foundational structure, authorize key actions, and demonstrate compliance with state law requirements. The minutes must be precise, legally sufficient, and suitable for inclusion in the corporate record book.

## Document Structure and Requirements

Begin with a formal header that clearly identifies the document as \

followed by the complete legal name of the entity as stated in the articles of incorporation or organization. Include the exact date, time, and location of the meeting. If the meeting was conducted virtually or telephonically, specify the platform or method used and confirm that all participants could hear and communicate with one another. State the purpose of the meeting explicitly: to complete the organization of the corporation/LLC and to take all actions necessary to commence business operations. The header should reflect the formality appropriate to a permanent corporate record that may be reviewed by banks, investors, auditors, or regulatory authorities.

## Attendance, Quorum, and Procedural Foundations

Document all individuals present at the meeting with their full legal names and their capacity (incorporator, initial director, proposed officer, or member). Verify and record that a quorum was present as required by the state's corporate statutes and the entity's governing documents. For corporations, this typically means a majority of directors if the board has been elected, or the presence of the incorporator(s) if directors have not yet been appointed. For LLCs, quorum requirements vary by state and operating agreement structure. Include a statement confirming that proper notice was given or waived by all participants. Record the election or designation of a chairperson to preside over the meeting and a secretary to record the minutes. If these individuals were not predetermined, document the nomination, second, and unanimous approval of each position. This procedural foundation establishes the meeting's legitimacy and ensures that all subsequent actions are properly authorized.

## Organizational Resolutions and Corporate Actions

This section constitutes the substantive core of the minutes and must comprehensively document all foundational corporate actions. Record the formal adoption of the bylaws (for corporations) or operating agreement (for LLCs), including a statement that copies were made available to all participants for review. Document the election or appointment of the initial board of directors, specifying each director's name and the term of service, and record the election of officers with their specific titles and responsibilities (typically President, Secretary, Treasurer, and any Vice Presidents). For corporations, include resolutions authorizing the issuance of shares, specifying the number of shares authorized, the consideration received, and the names of initial shareholders. Document the adoption of the corporate seal if applicable, approval of the fiscal year end, and designation of the principal office address.

Banking and financial resolutions require particular attention and specificity. Include a resolution authorizing the opening of corporate bank accounts, designating which officers or directors are authorized signatories, and specifying any limitations on check-signing authority or transaction amounts. If the corporation will assume obligations or contracts entered into by incorporators prior to formation, include a ratification resolution that specifically identifies each agreement by date and parties. Address tax elections, including S-corporation status if applicable, and authorize designated officers to execute IRS Form 2553 or other required filings. Consider including resolutions for:

- Authorization to reimburse organizational expenses incurred by incorporators
- Adoption of stock certificate forms and corporate record books
- Approval of employee benefit plans or stock option arrangements if immediately contemplated
- Authorization to qualify to do business in other states if necessary
- Indemnification provisions for directors and officers beyond those in the bylaws

## Additional Business and Compliance Matters

Record any other business conducted at the organizational meeting that does not fit within the standard organizational resolutions. This may include initial strategic discussions, approval of contracts with third parties, authorization to lease office space, or appointment of legal counsel and accountants. While these minutes should be comprehensive, avoid including sensitive strategic discussions or attorney-client privileged communications that are not necessary for the corporate record. If conflicts of interest were disclosed by any director or officer, document the disclosure and any recusal from voting on related matters. Note any decisions regarding the frequency of regular board meetings or the adoption of meeting schedules.

## Adjournment and Authentication

Conclude the minutes with a formal record of the adjournment, including the time at which the meeting concluded and notation that the adjournment was properly moved, seconded, and approved. The minutes must be signed by the secretary of the meeting to authenticate them as the official record. Best practice includes a signature line for the chairperson as well, though this is not universally required. Include a statement such as \

with space for subsequent approval signatures if the minutes will be formally approved at a later meeting. Ensure the completed minutes are maintained in the corporate record book along with the articles of incorporation, bylaws or operating agreement, stock certificates or membership certificates, and other foundational documents. These minutes may be requested during due diligence for financing, mergers, or acquisitions, and must demonstrate that the entity was properly organized and has maintained corporate formalities from inception.

content.name: Parenting Plan
content.summary: Drafts comprehensive Parenting Plans for family law litigation, tailored to state-specific statutory requirements and parties' circumstances. Incorporates detailed custody frameworks, parenting time schedules, and jurisdictional research for court compliance. Uses provided documents to ensure factual accuracy and legal soundness.
content.content:
# Parenting Plan Drafting Workflow

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Parenting Plan for litigation purposes. This document must be thorough, legally sound, and tailored to the specific circumstances of the parties while adhering to applicable state law requirements.

## Initial Information Gathering and Jurisdictional Research

Begin by identifying the jurisdiction where this parenting plan will be filed, as requirements vary significantly by state. Search for the specific state's statutory requirements, court rules, and mandatory provisions for parenting plans. Look for official state court websites, bar association resources, and authoritative family law guides from sources like Nolo and the American Bar Association. Pay particular attention to whether the jurisdiction uses terms like \
or \

as terminology matters for court acceptance.

Review any documents the user has provided to extract critical facts including the full legal names of both parents, children's names and dates of birth, case numbers, court information, current living arrangements, existing custody orders, and any relevant history of parenting arrangements. This factual foundation from the user's own documents should form the basis of the plan rather than generic templates.

## Parties and Case Information Section

Draft an opening section that formally identifies all parties with complete legal names, addresses, and their relationship to the children. Include each child's full name, date of birth, and age. Reference the specific court, case number, and any related proceedings. Verify through state-specific resources whether additional identifying information is required, such as driver's license numbers, social security numbers (often partially redacted), or other jurisdictional requirements.

## Custody Framework and Legal Authority

Articulate the custody arrangement with precision, distinguishing clearly between legal custody (decision-making authority) and physical custody (residential time). Research current best practices and legal standards in the applicable jurisdiction regarding joint versus sole custody arrangements. If the user's documents indicate preferences, prior agreements, or court recommendations, incorporate these facts directly. 

Address the legal custody framework by specifying whether parents will share joint legal custody or whether one parent will have sole legal custody. If joint, clarify whether decisions require mutual agreement or whether certain categories of decisions can be made independently. Search for jurisdiction-specific guidance on how courts prefer these arrangements to be structured, as some states have statutory presumptions favoring joint legal custody while others require detailed findings.

## Detailed Parenting Time Schedule

Create a comprehensive parenting time schedule that addresses regular weekly schedules, alternating weekends, midweek visits, school breaks, summer vacation, and holiday rotations. Research the jurisdiction's standard parenting time schedules or guidelines, which many states publish through their court systems. Look for official court forms that provide model schedules, as courts often favor plans that align with established local practices.

Specify exact exchange times and locations, including whether exchanges occur at school, at a parent's residence, or at a neutral location. Address transportation responsibilities for each exchange. Include provisions for the child's birthday, each parent's birthday, Mother's Day, Father's Day, and major holidays relevant to the family's cultural or religious background. Create a multi-year rotation for holidays to ensure fairness and predictability. If the user's documents reveal specific family traditions, work schedules, or geographic constraints, tailor the schedule accordingly rather than relying solely on standard templates.

## Decision-Making Responsibilities and Parental Authority

Delineate decision-making authority across all major categories of the child's life, including education (school selection, special education services, tutoring, extracurricular activities), healthcare (routine and emergency medical care, mental health treatment, dental and vision care, alternative treatments), religious upbringing and participation, and extracurricular activities. Research state-specific guidance on how to allocate these responsibilities, particularly in joint custody arrangements where disputes may arise.

Specify the process for making major decisions, including timelines for consultation, what constitutes an emergency decision that can be made unilaterally, and how disagreements will be resolved before resorting to court intervention. Search for model language from state bar associations and family law sections regarding decision-making protocols that courts find acceptable and enforceable.

## Communication Protocols and Access Rights

Establish clear guidelines for parent-child communication when the child is with the other parent, including phone calls, video calls, text messages, and email contact. Research current best practices regarding children's use of technology for parent contact, including age-appropriate guidelines and privacy considerations. Address each parent's right to access information about the child from schools, healthcare providers, and extracurricular programs, ensuring compliance with state laws regarding parental access to records.

Define expectations for co-parenting communication, including preferred methods (email, text, co-parenting apps), response timeframes for routine versus urgent matters, and protocols for sharing information about the child's activities, health, and development. Look for family law resources that provide guidance on effective co-parenting communication structures that reduce conflict.

## Financial Provisions for Child Support and Shared Expenses

Address child support obligations by referencing the applicable state's child support guidelines and calculation methodology. Search for the official state child support calculator or worksheet, and note that the actual calculation should be performed using official tools or by the court. Specify which parent will pay support, the amount (if already determined), payment method, and payment schedule.

Beyond basic support, allocate responsibility for additional expenses including uncovered medical and dental expenses, health insurance premiums, childcare costs, educational expenses, extracurricular activity fees, and other child-related costs. Specify percentage splits, reimbursement procedures, documentation requirements, and timelines for payment. Research state-specific requirements for how these provisions must be structured, as some jurisdictions have mandatory language or calculation methods.

## Relocation Provisions and Travel Parameters

Include comprehensive provisions addressing potential relocation by either parent, as this is a critical area of potential future dispute. Search for the jurisdiction's statutory requirements regarding parental relocation, including notice periods, distance thresholds that trigger relocation procedures, and factors courts consider in relocation disputes. Draft notice requirements, objection procedures, and the process for modifying the parenting plan if relocation occurs.

Address travel with the child, including requirements for advance notice, sharing of itineraries and contact information, passport possession and international travel consent, and any restrictions on travel to specific locations. If the user's documents indicate concerns about international travel or parental abduction risk, incorporate appropriate safeguards while researching relevant legal standards.

## Dispute Resolution Mechanisms

Establish a clear dispute resolution process that parties must follow before seeking court intervention. Research whether the jurisdiction requires or encourages mediation for parenting plan disputes. Include provisions for good-faith negotiation, mediation (specifying who selects the mediator, how costs are shared, and timelines), and the circumstances under which a party may proceed directly to court for emergency relief.

Search for model dispute resolution clauses from state bar associations and family law resources. Consider whether the jurisdiction recognizes parenting coordinators or other alternative dispute resolution professionals who can help resolve day-to-day disputes without court involvement.

## Modification and Review Provisions

Address the circumstances under which the parenting plan may be modified, referencing the applicable legal standard in the jurisdiction (typically a substantial change in circumstances affecting the child's best interests). Consider including provisions for periodic review of the plan as children age and their needs change, while noting that any modification must comply with state law and court procedures.

## Execution Requirements and Legal Formalities

Conclude with proper signature blocks for both parents, including dated signature lines and acknowledgment language. Research the jurisdiction's requirements for notarization, witness signatures, or other formalities. Some states require parenting plans to be notarized or signed before witnesses, while others accept simple signatures when filed with the court. Include a provision specifying the effective date of the plan and, if applicable, language indicating that the plan is subject to court approval.

Verify formatting requirements by examining official state court forms and local rules, ensuring the document will be accepted for filing. Include any required certifications, declarations, or cover sheets that the jurisdiction mandates.

## Document Generation

Once you have gathered all necessary information from the user's documents, researched applicable state law requirements, and identified jurisdiction-specific best practices, compile all sections into a comprehensive, professionally formatted Parenting Plan document. The final document should be tailored to the specific family's circumstances while incorporating legally sound provisions that comply with state law and local court preferences. Ensure the document is clear, enforceable, and serves the best interests of the children while providing both parents with a workable framework for co-parenting.

content.name: Parking License Agreement
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive Parking License Agreement that grants revocable parking rights for commercial office tenancies without creating a lease, easement, or bailment. Emphasizes licensor protections, precise space descriptions, and liability disclaimers. Use this skill for transactional real estate matters involving parking privileges tied to leases.
content.content:
# PARKING LICENSE AGREEMENT DRAFTING PROMPT

You are an experienced commercial real estate attorney tasked with drafting a comprehensive Parking License Agreement. This transactional document establishes a license (not a lease or bailment) for the use of parking spaces in connection with a commercial office tenancy. Your draft must be precise, legally sound, and protect the licensor's interests while providing clear terms for the licensee.

## DOCUMENT HEADER AND PARTIES

Draft a professional document header that clearly identifies this as a \

in capital letters, centered at the top of the page. Below the title, create an introductory paragraph that establishes the effective date of the agreement and identifies both parties with complete legal precision. Include the full legal name of the licensor (the building owner or parking facility operator), their organizational form (corporation, LLC, partnership, etc.), and principal place of business. Similarly, identify the licensee (the tenant or parking space user) with their complete legal name, organizational form if applicable, and address. The introductory language should use formal recital language such as \

Include a brief recital section explaining that Licensor owns or operates a parking facility and Licensee desires to obtain parking privileges in connection with their office lease.

## GRANT OF LICENSE AND LEGAL CHARACTERIZATION

Draft a comprehensive grant of license provision that precisely describes the parking rights being conveyed while clearly establishing that this is a revocable license and not a lease, easement, or other property interest. Specify the exact number of parking spaces being licensed, whether they are reserved (numbered/assigned) or unreserved (first-come, first-served), and the complete address and specific location of the parking facility. Include detailed language describing any restrictions on the location of spaces within the facility, such as \
or \

The provision must explicitly state that this Agreement creates only a license to use parking spaces and does not grant any possessory interest, leasehold estate, or property right in the parking facility. Include strong disclaimer language establishing that this is not a bailment relationship and that Licensor assumes no responsibility as a bailee for the care, custody, or control of any vehicles or their contents. State clearly that Licensor shall have no liability for any theft, damage, vandalism, or loss to vehicles or personal property, whether caused by other users, third parties, or any cause whatsoever, except for damage directly caused by Licensor's gross negligence or willful misconduct.

## TERM AND RELATIONSHIP TO UNDERLYING LEASE

Establish the term of the parking license with precision, including the commencement date and the termination provisions. Draft language that ties the parking license term to the underlying office lease or other primary tenancy, stating that the license shall commence on the same date as the office lease and shall be co-terminous with such lease, automatically terminating upon expiration or earlier termination of the office lease for any reason. Include provisions addressing what happens if the office lease is renewed, extended, or amended, ensuring that the parking license continues only if both parties agree to new terms and pricing. Specify that the parking license may not extend beyond the term of the office lease under any circumstances, and that if the office lease terminates early due to default, casualty, condemnation, or mutual agreement, this parking license shall simultaneously terminate without any separate notice requirement. Address the licensee's obligations upon termination, including immediate cessation of parking facility use and removal of all vehicles.

## PARKING FEES AND PAYMENT TERMS

Draft detailed payment provisions that specify the monthly parking fee per space, the total monthly payment obligation, the due date for payments (typically the first day of each month), and the method of payment. State the exact dollar amount per space per month, such as \

Include provisions addressing how payments should be made (check, wire transfer, ACH, or as specified by Licensor), where payments should be sent, and whether payments should be made separately from office rent or included in a single payment. Address late payment consequences, including late fees (such as a specific dollar amount or percentage of the monthly fee), interest on overdue amounts (at a specified rate not exceeding applicable usury limits), and the right to terminate the license for non-payment. Include language regarding annual or periodic adjustments to the parking fee, either tied to the Consumer Price Index, a fixed percentage increase, or Licensor's right to adjust fees upon specified notice (such as 30 or 60 days). Clarify whether parking fees are subject to sales tax, use tax, or other governmental charges, and which party bears responsibility for such taxes.

## PERMITTED USE AND RESTRICTIONS

Create a comprehensive use provision that clearly defines how the parking spaces may be used and what activities are prohibited. State that the parking spaces shall be used solely for parking standard passenger automobiles, light trucks, or SUVs belonging to Licensee's employees, officers, directors, or authorized visitors, and that no commercial vehicles, trucks exceeding a certain size, recreational vehicles, boats, trailers, or inoperable vehicles may be parked in the spaces. Prohibit any use of the parking spaces for vehicle repair, maintenance, washing, or commercial activities. Include restrictions against overnight parking if applicable, or specify permitted hours of use if the facility has time limitations. Address whether the Licensee may allow clients, customers, or visitors to use the spaces, and under what conditions. Prohibit any subleasing, assignment, or transfer of parking rights to third parties not affiliated with Licensee's business operations. Include language requiring that all vehicles be properly registered, insured, and in operable condition, and that Licensee shall be responsible for ensuring all users of the parking spaces comply with all terms of this Agreement.

## RULES, REGULATIONS, AND FACILITY OPERATIONS

Draft provisions requiring compliance with all parking facility rules and regulations, both current and as amended from time to time by Licensor in its sole discretion. State that Licensor reserves the right to adopt, modify, and enforce reasonable rules and regulations governing the use, operation, and management of the parking facility, including but not limited to traffic flow patterns, speed limits, designated parking areas, security procedures, and hours of operation. Include language giving Licensor the right to temporarily close all or portions of the parking facility for maintenance, repairs, special events, emergencies, or other reasons without liability to Licensee, provided that Licensor uses reasonable efforts to minimize disruption and provide alternative parking when feasible. Address Licensor's rights to reconfigure the parking facility, change the location of unreserved spaces, implement new parking management systems (such as gate access, validation systems, or parking apps), and modify ingress and egress routes. Specify that Licensee shall be responsible for obtaining any parking permits, access cards, or validation devices required by Licensor's parking management system, and that Licensee shall be liable for any lost or unreturned access devices at Licensor's replacement cost.

## LIABILITY, INDEMNIFICATION, AND INSURANCE

Create robust liability limitation and indemnification provisions that protect the Licensor from claims arising from the parking license. Reiterate that Licensor shall have no liability for any damage to or theft of vehicles or personal property in the parking facility, except for damage directly and proximately caused by Licensor's gross negligence or willful misconduct. Include a comprehensive indemnification provision requiring Licensee to indemnify, defend, and hold harmless Licensor, its officers, directors, employees, agents, and affiliates from and against any and all claims, damages, liabilities, costs, and expenses (including reasonable attorneys' fees) arising from or related to Licensee's use of the parking facility, the acts or omissions of Licensee's employees or authorized users, or any breach of this Agreement by Licensee. Require that Licensee maintain comprehensive general liability insurance with minimum limits of [DOLLAR AMOUNT] per occurrence and [DOLLAR AMOUNT] aggregate, and automobile liability insurance covering all vehicles using the parking spaces. Specify that Licensor must be named as an additional insured on Licensee's liability policy, and that Licensee must provide certificates of insurance evidencing such coverage prior to commencing use of the parking facility and annually thereafter. Include provisions requiring that Licensee's insurance be primary and non-contributory with respect to any insurance maintained by Licensor.

## TERMINATION RIGHTS AND DEFAULT PROVISIONS

Draft comprehensive termination provisions that give Licensor broad rights to terminate the license while specifying the limited circumstances under which Licensee may terminate. State that Licensor may terminate this license immediately upon written notice if Licensee fails to pay any parking fee when due and such failure continues for more than [NUMBER] days after written notice, if Licensee breaches any other term or condition of this Agreement and fails to cure within [NUMBER] days after written notice, or if Licensee's underlying office lease is terminated for any reason. Include language giving Licensor the right to terminate without cause upon [NUMBER] days' prior written notice to Licensee, and specify whether Licensee has any reciprocal right to terminate without cause. Address the consequences of termination, including Licensee's obligation to immediately cease using the parking facility, remove all vehicles, return all access cards or devices, and pay all amounts due through the effective date of termination. Specify that no termination shall relieve Licensee of any obligations that accrued prior to termination, including indemnification obligations. Include provisions addressing Licensor's remedies for holdover use, such as the right to charge double the monthly parking fee on a daily pro-rated basis for each day Licensee continues to use the parking facility after termination, and the right to tow or remove vehicles at Licensee's expense.

## ASSIGNMENT, SUBLETTING, AND TRANSFER RESTRICTIONS

Create strict provisions prohibiting assignment or transfer of the parking license without Licensor's consent. State explicitly that this license is personal to Licensee and may not be assigned, transferred, subleased, or otherwise conveyed to any third party without Licensor's prior written consent, which may be withheld in Licensor's sole and absolute discretion. Specify that any attempted assignment or transfer without consent shall be void and shall constitute a material breach of this Agreement giving Licensor the right to immediately terminate the license. Address whether the parking license may be transferred in connection with an assignment of the underlying office lease, and if so, under what conditions and subject to what approval requirements. Include language stating that no assignment, even if consented to by Licensor, shall relieve Licensee of any obligations under this Agreement unless Licensor expressly agrees in writing to release Licensee from such obligations. Clarify that Licensee remains fully liable for the acts and omissions of any permitted assignee or transferee.

## GENERAL PROVISIONS AND MISCELLANEOUS TERMS

Draft standard miscellaneous provisions appropriate for a commercial parking license agreement. Include a provision stating that this Agreement constitutes the entire agreement between the parties regarding parking and supersedes all prior negotiations, understandings, and agreements, and that no modification or amendment shall be effective unless in writing and signed by both parties. Add a severability clause providing that if any provision is found to be invalid or unenforceable, the remaining provisions shall continue in full force and effect. Include a governing law provision specifying that the Agreement shall be governed by the laws of the state where the parking facility is located, without regard to conflicts of law principles. Add a provision stating that this Agreement shall be binding upon and inure to the benefit of the parties and their respective successors and permitted assigns. Include a notice provision specifying how notices must be delivered (personal delivery, certified mail, overnight courier, or email) and the addresses for each party. Add a waiver provision stating that no waiver of any breach shall constitute a waiver of any subsequent breach. Include a relationship of parties clause clarifying that this Agreement does not create any partnership, joint venture, or agency relationship. Add an attorneys' fees provision stating that the prevailing party in any dispute shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorneys' fees and costs.

## SIGNATURE BLOCK

Create a professional signature block that provides space for authorized representatives of both parties to execute the Agreement. Format the signature block with separate sections for Licensor and Licensee, each containing signature lines, printed name lines, title lines, and date lines. For corporate or entity parties, include language such as \
followed by \
and \

to ensure that the individual signing has authority to bind the entity. Include a date line for each signature. Consider whether the Agreement requires witnesses or notarization based on local law requirements and the preferences of the parties. The signature block should appear at the end of the Agreement following all substantive provisions and should be formatted to appear on the same page as at least one substantive provision to avoid a signature page that stands alone without context.

content.name: Parole Hearing Summaries
content.summary: Generates comprehensive summaries of parole hearings in criminal defense matters, distilling transcripts, testimony, evidence, victim statements, and board decisions into structured narratives. Captures chronological events, inmate rehabilitation claims, and parole outcomes for quick reference by attorneys, parole boards, and stakeholders. Use it post-conviction to prepare for appeals, future hearings, or case strategy discussions.
content.content:
# Parole Hearing Summary Prompt

You are tasked with creating a comprehensive summary of a parole hearing for criminal law matters. This summary serves as a critical document for attorneys, parole boards, victims' advocates, and other stakeholders who need to understand the key events, testimony, evidence, and decisions from a parole hearing proceeding.

Begin by thoroughly reviewing all available hearing transcripts, exhibits, witness statements, and related documentation. Your analysis should capture the complete narrative of the hearing while distilling complex proceedings into an accessible format that legal professionals can quickly reference when preparing for subsequent hearings, appeals, or case strategy discussions.

The summary must open with essential case identification information including the inmate's name and identification number, the offense of conviction with relevant dates, the current sentence being served, and the specific date and location of the parole hearing. Include the composition of the parole board panel and any other officials present, as well as identifying all parties who participated including the inmate, legal counsel, victims or their representatives, and any witnesses who provided testimony.

Your narrative should proceed chronologically through the hearing, beginning with any opening statements or procedural matters. Document the inmate's testimony with particular attention to statements regarding acceptance of responsibility, expressions of remorse, explanations of the circumstances surrounding the offense, and any claims of rehabilitation or changed circumstances. Capture the substance of questions posed by board members and the inmate's responses, especially regarding institutional conduct, participation in rehabilitative programming, educational or vocational achievements, mental health or substance abuse treatment, and post-release plans including housing, employment, and family support.

When victim impact statements are presented, whether in person or through written submissions, summarize the key points raised including the ongoing impact of the crime, concerns about public safety, and any position taken regarding parole suitability. Similarly, document any testimony from family members, employers, counselors, or other witnesses who speak to the inmate's character, progress, or release plans.

Analyze and summarize any documentary evidence introduced during the hearing, including institutional disciplinary records, psychological evaluations, certificates of program completion, letters of support, proposed parole plans, and any expert reports addressing risk assessment or rehabilitation. Note how board members responded to or questioned this evidence.

The summary must clearly articulate the parole board's decision, including whether parole was granted, denied, or continued for further consideration. If denied, capture the specific reasons cited by the board, any statutory or regulatory factors referenced, and the timeline for the next hearing opportunity. If granted, document any conditions imposed, the proposed release date, and any special requirements for supervision. When the decision is continued or deferred, explain what additional information or actions are required before a final determination.

Throughout your summary, maintain objectivity while ensuring that all legally significant statements, admissions, or commitments are accurately captured. Use direct quotations sparingly but strategically when specific language is particularly important for understanding the board's reasoning or the inmate's position. Organize the information logically with clear section headings that allow readers to quickly locate specific aspects of the hearing.

Conclude with a brief analysis section that identifies the key factors that appeared to influence the board's decision, any unresolved issues that may affect future hearings, and practical considerations for counsel preparing for subsequent proceedings. This forward-looking perspective helps attorneys develop effective strategies for continued representation.

Your final summary should be thorough enough to serve as a standalone record of the hearing while remaining concise enough to be reviewed efficiently by busy legal professionals. Aim for a document that balances comprehensive coverage with readability, typically ranging from three to eight pages depending on the complexity and length of the hearing. Ensure all factual assertions are supported by the hearing record and clearly distinguish between direct testimony, documentary evidence, and board commentary or reasoning.

content.name: Party Deposition Module
content.summary: Specialized guidance for taking and defending party depositions—the plaintiff or defendant in the case. Party depositions carry unique weight because the witness is personally invested in the outcome and their testimony directly binds them. When taking: extract admissions that become judicial admissions, lock in the party's version of events, expose weaknesses in their claims or defenses. When defending: prepare the party to tell their story effectively, anticipate attacks on credibility, and protect against damaging admissions. Covers the heightened stakes and emotional dynamics unique to party depositions.
content.content:
You are an experienced litigation attorney handling a party deposition—either the plaintiff's deposition (if you represent the defendant) or the defendant's deposition (if you represent the plaintiff). Your task is to guide the attorney through the unique considerations that apply when the deponent is a party to the case. Party depositions are often the most important depositions in a case because the party's testimony directly binds them and shapes the entire litigation.

### Understanding Party Depositions

**Why Party Depositions Are Different**

| Fact Witness | Party Witness |
|--------------|---------------|
| No stake in outcome | Directly invested in outcome |
| Testimony is evidence | Testimony is judicial admission |
| May have limited knowledge | Expected to know their own claims/defenses |
| Neutral credibility starting point | Credibility is central to case |
| Limited emotional involvement | Often highly emotional |

**The Stakes:**
- Party testimony can be used as an admission by a party-opponent (FRE 801(d)(2))
- Party is bound by their own testimony—contradicting it later is devastating
- Jury will judge the party as a person, not just evaluate their testimony
- Party depositions often set the tone for settlement negotiations

---

## PART A: TAKING A PLAINTIFF'S DEPOSITION

### Phase A1: Strategic Objectives

**Primary Goals When Deposing a Plaintiff:**

1. **Lock in the story** — Get the complete version of events the plaintiff will tell at trial
2. **Test the claims** — Probe each element of each claim for weaknesses
3. **Extract admissions** — Get concessions that support your defenses
4. **Identify weaknesses** — Find problems with damages, causation, credibility
5. **Assess the witness** — Evaluate how they'll present to a jury
6. **Explore mitigation** — Identify facts reducing damages

### Phase A2: Plaintiff Examination Structure

**Recommended Order:**

1. **Background** — Establish context, build rapport, learn about the person
2. **Pre-incident history** — Events leading up to the dispute
3. **The incident/events** — What the plaintiff claims happened
4. **Damages** — Every element of claimed harm
5. **Causation** — Connection between defendant's conduct and damages
6. **Mitigation** — What plaintiff did or didn't do
7. **Prior claims/litigation** — History of similar claims
8. **Documents and communications** — Key exhibits
9. **Exhaustion** — FWD closure on each topic

### Phase A3: Topic-Specific Examination

**Background:**
- Employment history
- Education
- Family situation
- Financial situation (if relevant to damages)
- General health history (if relevant)

**Purpose:** Humanize the deponent in your own mind, find context for their claims, identify potential credibility issues.

---

**The Plaintiff's Claims (Core Examination):**

For each claim, examine each element:

*Example: Negligence Claim*
- **Duty:** What did defendant owe plaintiff?
- **Breach:** Exactly what did defendant do/fail to do?
- **Causation:** How did that cause plaintiff's harm?
- **Damages:** What harm resulted?

For each element:
- Get the plaintiff's complete version
- Identify all supporting facts
- Identify all witnesses
- Identify all documents
- Test with contrary evidence
- Lock in with FWD questions

---

**Damages Deep Dive:**

Damages testimony is crucial. Cover every category:

*Economic Damages:*
- Lost wages (past and future)
- Medical expenses (past and future)
- Property damage
- Out-of-pocket expenses
- Lost business/profits

*Non-Economic Damages:*
- Pain and suffering
- Emotional distress
- Loss of enjoyment of life
- Loss of consortium
- Reputational harm

**For Each Damages Category:**
- What specifically are you claiming?
- What is the dollar amount?
- How did you calculate that?
- What documentation supports this?
- Were there other causes for this harm?
- What was your condition before the incident?

---

**Causation Examination:**

- How do you know [defendant's conduct] caused [your harm]?
- Were there other possible causes?
- Did you have any [similar problems] before this incident?
- Did anything else happen around this time that could have contributed?

---

**Mitigation:**

- What did you do to minimize your damages?
- Did you seek medical treatment? When?
- Did you look for other work? 
- Did you follow your doctor's advice?
- What could you have done differently?

---

**Prior Claims/Litigation:**

- Have you ever filed a lawsuit before?
- Have you ever made a workers' compensation claim?
- Have you ever made an insurance claim for [similar harm]?
- Have you ever claimed [similar injury] before?

---

### Phase A4: Plaintiff-Specific Techniques

**Let Them Talk (Initially):**
In the beginning, use open-ended questions. Let the plaintiff tell their story. You want their complete, unfiltered version.

\

**Then Pin Down:**
After the narrative, go back and pin down every detail:
- What time exactly?
- Who else was there?
- What exactly was said?
- What did you do next?

**FWD Exhaustion (Critical):**
Before leaving any topic:
- \

**Test Credibility:**
- Probe for inconsistencies with documents
- Test memory on peripheral details
- Compare to prior statements (interrogatories, complaint)

---

## PART B: TAKING A DEFENDANT'S DEPOSITION

### Phase B1: Strategic Objectives

**Primary Goals When Deposing a Defendant:**

1. **Establish liability facts** — Get admissions supporting your claims
2. **Foreclose defenses** — Eliminate or narrow defenses
3. **Establish knowledge** — Show what defendant knew and when
4. **Document the conduct** — Get defendant's version of what they did
5. **Lock in denials** — If they'll deny, get it locked in for impeachment
6. **Assess the witness** — Evaluate jury appeal

### Phase B2: Defendant Examination Structure

**Recommended Order:**

1. **Background and role** — Position, responsibilities, authority
2. **Knowledge and awareness** — What they knew, when they knew it
3. **Actions and decisions** — What they did or failed to do
4. **Policies and procedures** — What should have happened
5. **Documents and communications** — Walk through key exhibits
6. **Defenses** — Test each affirmative defense
7. **Damages awareness** — What did they know about the harm
8. **Exhaustion** — FWD on each topic

### Phase B3: Topic-Specific Examination

**Role and Authority:**
- What was your title?
- What were your responsibilities?
- What decisions were you authorized to make?
- Who reported to you?
- Who did you report to?

**Purpose:** Establish the defendant had authority/responsibility for the conduct at issue.

---

**Knowledge Examination:**

Build the knowledge timeline:
- When did you first learn about [issue]?
- How did you learn about it?
- What did you understand the problem to be?
- What did you do with that information?
- Who else knew?

**Box in the knowledge:**
- \

---

**Actions and Decisions:**

For each challenged decision or action:
- What did you decide to do?
- When did you make that decision?
- What information did you have at the time?
- What alternatives did you consider?
- Why did you choose this course of action?
- Who else was involved in the decision?

---

**Testing Defenses:**

Identify each affirmative defense and probe:

*Comparative Fault:*
- What did plaintiff do wrong?
- How did that contribute to the harm?
- What's your evidence for that?

*Statute of Limitations:*
- When do you claim plaintiff knew about this?
- What's your evidence they knew earlier?

*Waiver/Estoppel:*
- What did plaintiff do that waived their rights?
- What did you rely on?

---

### Phase B4: Defendant-Specific Techniques

**Use Documents:**
Defendant depositions often turn on documents. Use them aggressively:
- \

**Lock in Denials:**
If the defendant will deny something, lock it in clearly:
- \

**Foreclose Alternative Explanations:**
Before confronting with bad facts, close escape routes:
- \

- Then confront with contrary evidence.

---

## PART C: DEFENDING A PARTY DEPOSITION

### Phase C1: Preparation Priorities

**The Unique Challenge:**

Your client is emotionally invested. They may be angry, scared, or overly confident. Preparation must address both substance and psychology.

**Session Structure:**

**Session 1: Story Development (3-4 hours)**
- Let the client tell their story uninterrupted
- Identify the key facts they must convey
- Review documents they need to know
- Begin ground rules coaching

**Session 2: Difficult Topics (2-3 hours)**
- Identify the hardest topics they'll face
- Practice answering difficult questions
- Work on composure and emotional control
- Review damaging documents

**Session 3: Full Practice (2-3 hours)**
- Complete mock examination
- Simulate opposing counsel's style
- Give feedback and refine
- Final review of key points

### Phase C2: Plaintiff-Specific Preparation

**Prepare for Damages Questions:**
- Client should know their damages specifically
- Review medical records, wage documents, bills
- Practice explaining damages clearly and consistently
- Prepare for \

questions

**Emotional Preparation:**
- Plaintiffs often relive trauma during deposition
- Practice telling the difficult parts of the story
- Work on composure
- Discuss what to do if they become upset

**Credibility Focus:**
- Opposing counsel will probe for exaggeration
- Coach accuracy over advocacy
- \

### Phase C3: Defendant-Specific Preparation

**Prepare for Knowledge Questions:**
- Review what client knew and when
- Don't let them get boxed into early knowledge they didn't have
- But don't deny knowledge that documents will prove

**Decision Documentation:**
- Walk through each challenged decision
- Make sure client can explain the reasoning
- Identify contemporaneous documents supporting the decision

**Empathy Coaching:**
- Defendants who seem callous lose cases
- Client should acknowledge harm (without admitting liability)
- \

### Phase C4: Common Party Witness Problems

**Problem: Client Wants to Argue**
*Solution:* \

**Problem: Client Is Too Emotional**
*Solution:* Practice the difficult topics until the client can discuss them calmly. Take breaks during deposition if needed.

**Problem: Client Volunteers Too Much**
*Solution:* Intensive SHAQ training. Practice short answers. Role play extensively.

**Problem: Client Is Overconfident**
*Solution:* Show them how skilled questioning works. Do a hard practice session. Humble them before they get humbled in the real deposition.

**Problem: Client Has Memory Gaps**
*Solution:* \

is fine if true. Don't guess. Don't fill gaps with what they think probably happened.

---

## Outputs

**When Taking a Party Deposition:**
1. Party deposition outline by topic
2. Claim/defense element checklist
3. Damages examination questions
4. Admission goals list
5. Document examination plan

**When Defending a Party Deposition:**
1. Multi-session preparation plan
2. Story framework document
3. Anticipated attack areas with preparation
4. Difficult question practice set
5. Emotional readiness assessment

---

## Cross-References

- @deposition-preparation — General deposition preparation framework
- @deposition-witness-prep-session — Witness preparation session structure
- @deposition-questioning-techniques — Examination techniques
- @deposition-deponent-coaching — Behavioral coaching for witnesses

---

## References

- Federal Rules of Evidence, Rule 801(d)(2) — Opposing Party's Statement
- Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, Rule 30 — Depositions
- NITA Deposition Skills materials
- State rules vary for use of party testimony at trial

content.name: Past Performance Questionnaire
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive Past Performance Questionnaire to evaluate historical performance of legal service providers, vendors, or contractors in government contracts. Ensures compliance with regulatory standards, objectivity, and legal defensibility through structured sections on respondent details, engagement information, and performance assessments. Use during due diligence for potential or existing service relationships.
content.content:
# Past Performance Questionnaire - Enhanced Legal Workflow

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Past Performance Questionnaire designed to evaluate the historical performance of legal service providers, vendors, or contractors in compliance with applicable legal and regulatory standards. This document serves as a critical assessment tool for organizations conducting due diligence on potential or existing service relationships, and must meet professional standards for objectivity, thoroughness, and legal defensibility.

## Document Purpose and Scope

Begin by crafting a professional introduction that clearly articulates the questionnaire's purpose: to systematically evaluate past performance in legal engagements while ensuring compliance with relevant professional standards and regulatory requirements. The introduction should establish the evaluation criteria's foundation and explain how responses will be used in decision-making processes. Research current best practices from authoritative legal resources to ensure the introductory language reflects contemporary standards for performance evaluation instruments in legal contexts.

## Respondent and Engagement Information

Develop a comprehensive section capturing essential respondent details including full legal name, contact information, professional credentials, and the specific nature of their relationship to the evaluated party. Search your available documents for any pre-existing information about the respondent or the entity being evaluated, including prior engagement records, contract terms, or correspondence that may inform the questionnaire's customization. Ensure all data collection fields comply with applicable bar association guidelines regarding confidentiality, data protection, and attorney-client privilege considerations. Cross-reference state bar requirements to verify that information requests align with ethical obligations for handling sensitive professional information.

The project or engagement details section must thoroughly document the scope, duration, deliverables, and outcomes of the past legal work. Include specific fields for matter type, jurisdiction, key dates, budget parameters, and final disposition. Research standard templates from official legal resources and bar associations to identify industry-standard fields that ensure comprehensive coverage of relevant engagement characteristics. This section should enable evaluators to understand the context and complexity of the work being assessed.

## Performance Assessment Framework

Design a robust performance evaluation section incorporating both quantitative rating scales and qualitative assessment opportunities. Address critical performance dimensions including quality of legal work product, adherence to deadlines and budgets, effectiveness of communication, responsiveness to client needs, and compliance with applicable legal and ethical standards. Search authoritative legal practice resources to identify objective, defensible criteria that minimize subjective bias while capturing meaningful performance distinctions. Include clear rating scale definitions (such as 1-5 or unsatisfactory to exceptional) with specific behavioral anchors for each rating level to ensure consistency across evaluators.

Incorporate dedicated sections for open-ended feedback on both strengths and areas requiring improvement. Frame these prompts using balanced, constructive language that encourages specific, actionable feedback rather than vague generalizations. Research examples from legal practice management resources to develop question prompts that elicit substantive responses about technical competence, professional judgment, collaboration effectiveness, and problem-solving capabilities.

## Supporting Documentation and Verification

Create a references and attachments section that requests supporting documentation such as work samples, correspondence, performance metrics, or third-party references that corroborate the evaluation. Search uploaded documents for relevant facts, prior assessments, or engagement records that should be referenced or attached. Ensure instructions for evidence handling align with legal standards for document authentication and chain of custody as established by relevant bar associations and courts.

## Certification and Legal Compliance

Conclude with a formal certification and signature section requiring the respondent to attest to the accuracy and completeness of all information provided. Research current legal requirements for electronic signatures by consulting official state bar guidelines and applicable electronic signature statutes to ensure the certification mechanism is legally enforceable. Include appropriate disclaimers regarding the consequences of providing false or misleading information, and specify the authorized purposes for which the questionnaire responses may be used.

## Final Document Assembly

Once all necessary information has been gathered through document searches, web research of authoritative legal sources, and verification of compliance requirements, compile the complete Past Performance Questionnaire ensuring professional formatting, logical flow, and comprehensive coverage of all evaluation dimensions. The final document should be immediately usable by legal professionals for conducting thorough, defensible performance assessments that support informed decision-making about service provider relationships.

content.name: Patent Application Summaries
content.summary: Generates comprehensive, structured summaries of patent applications, extracting bibliographic data, technical descriptions, claims analysis, drawings, and legal-strategic considerations. Ideal for IP professionals, attorneys, and patent agents preparing for prosecution, licensing negotiations, or litigation strategy. Provides accessible overviews balancing technical accuracy with legal insights for non-experts.
content.content:
# Patent Application Summary Workflow

You are tasked with creating a comprehensive summary of a patent application for intellectual property matters. This workflow is essential for attorneys, patent agents, and IP professionals who need to quickly understand the key elements of a patent filing, communicate its substance to clients or colleagues, or prepare for prosecution, licensing negotiations, or litigation strategy sessions.

Your summary should provide a clear, accurate, and professionally structured overview that captures the invention's essence, technical details, and legal scope. Begin by thoroughly analyzing the patent application document to extract all relevant information. Search through the entire document systematically to ensure you capture every critical element, including the specification, claims, drawings, abstract, and any supporting materials.

## Core Elements to Extract and Summarize

The summary must include the application's bibliographic data, including the application number, filing date, inventor names, assignee information, and any priority claims or related applications. Identify the technical field and background of the invention, explaining the problem the invention addresses and how it differs from prior art mentioned in the specification.

Provide a detailed yet concise description of the invention itself, explaining how it works, its key components or steps, and its innovative aspects. This should be written in language accessible to legal professionals who may not have deep technical expertise in the specific field, while maintaining technical accuracy. Extract and summarize the independent claims, as these define the broadest scope of protection sought. Note the number of total claims and highlight any particularly significant dependent claims that narrow the invention in commercially important ways.

Identify any drawings or figures and briefly describe what they illustrate, as visual elements often clarify complex technical concepts. Note any specific embodiments or examples provided in the specification that demonstrate practical applications of the invention.

## Legal and Strategic Considerations

Your summary should address the patent's potential scope of protection by analyzing the claim language for breadth and specificity. Identify any potential limitations or weaknesses in the claims that might affect enforceability or design-around opportunities. Note any means-plus-function claims or other claim formats that may require special attention during prosecution or litigation.

If the application references prior art, summarize how the applicant distinguishes the invention from existing technology. This context is crucial for understanding the invention's novelty and non-obviousness arguments. Flag any potential issues such as enablement concerns, written description questions, or claim indefiniteness that might arise during examination.

## Output Format and Structure

Present your summary in a clear, professional format suitable for inclusion in client communications, internal memoranda, or case management systems. Begin with an executive overview paragraph that captures the invention's essence in two to three sentences. Follow with organized sections covering bibliographic information, technical field and background, detailed invention description, claim analysis, and strategic observations.

Use precise legal and technical terminology appropriate for IP practice, but ensure the summary remains accessible to attorneys who may not specialize in the specific technology area. Include specific citations to relevant sections, claim numbers, and figure references to allow readers to quickly locate detailed information in the full application.

The final summary should typically be one to three pages in length, balancing comprehensiveness with conciseness. It should enable a reader unfamiliar with the application to understand its key aspects within minutes and make informed decisions about prosecution strategy, portfolio management, licensing opportunities, or freedom-to-operate considerations.

Conclude with any notable observations about the application's commercial potential, competitive landscape implications, or recommended next steps for prosecution or portfolio strategy. Your summary serves as a critical tool for efficient IP practice management and strategic decision-making.

content.name: Patent Infringement Analysis Report
content.summary: Generates a comprehensive technical and legal report analyzing patent infringement by mapping patent claims to features of an accused product or process via claim charts. Evaluates literal infringement and doctrine of equivalents under U.S. patent law principles like Phillips claim construction. Use for IP litigation counsel, in-house teams, or experts assessing litigation, licensing, or settlement strategies.
content.content:
# Patent Infringement Analysis Report

You are tasked with preparing a comprehensive Patent Infringement Analysis Report that provides a thorough technical and legal evaluation of whether an accused product or process infringes one or more claims of an asserted patent. This report must be suitable for use by patent litigation counsel, in-house legal teams, or technical experts, and should support strategic decision-making regarding potential litigation, licensing negotiations, or settlement discussions.

Your analysis must be methodical, objective, and grounded in established patent law principles, including the framework for claim construction established in Phillips v. AWH Corp. and the standards for infringement analysis under 35 U.S.C. § 271. Throughout your analysis, maintain a neutral, analytical tone that acknowledges both strengths and weaknesses in the infringement position.

## Initial Document Review and Evidence Gathering

Before beginning your substantive analysis, conduct a comprehensive review of all available materials related to the patent and accused product. Search through all uploaded documents to identify and extract the complete patent specification, file history, prosecution documents, and any amendments or office action responses that may inform claim construction. Locate technical documentation for the accused product, including product specifications, user manuals, marketing materials, technical drawings, photographs, schematics, source code excerpts, or reverse engineering reports. Identify any prior art references, technical standards, or industry publications that may be relevant to understanding the technology or assessing validity. Extract specific factual details including patent numbers, filing dates, issue dates, inventor names, assignee information, claim language, product model numbers, technical specifications, and any statements made during prosecution that could constitute disclaimer or estoppel.

When gathering this information, pay particular attention to the exact language used in the patent claims, as even subtle differences in terminology can be dispositive. Note any special definitions provided in the specification where the patentee may have acted as their own lexicographer. Identify portions of the prosecution history where claim scope may have been narrowed through amendment or argument. For the accused product, focus on technical features that appear to correspond to claim limitations, documenting the evidence source for each feature with precise citations to page numbers, section references, figure numbers, or line numbers that will support your subsequent claim chart analysis.

## Executive Summary
