The buyer must diligently complete all loan requirements and conditions, providing any additional documentation or information requested by the lender. The buyer must obtain a homeowner's insurance policy meeting the lender's requirements and provide proof of coverage to the title company before closing. The buyer must conduct the final walk-through inspection to verify that the property's condition has not materially changed and that all agreed-upon repairs have been completed. The buyer must arrange for the wire transfer or delivery of all required closing funds, typically due at the title company by a specified time on the day before closing. The buyer must execute all necessary closing documents including the deed of trust or mortgage, promissory note, and any other lender or title company requirements.

Establish with precision when possession of the property will transfer from seller to buyer. The standard provision is that possession transfers at closing upon recordation of the deed or disbursement of funds, but some transactions require possession to be delayed for a specified period to allow the seller time to vacate. If possession will be delayed, include a post-closing occupancy agreement addressing the daily occupancy fee the seller will pay, the seller's obligations to maintain insurance and utilities, the condition in which the property must be delivered, and the consequences if the seller fails to timely vacate.

Address the allocation of risk of loss between contract acceptance and closing, specifying that the seller bears the risk of loss or damage to the property until closing. If the property is materially damaged by fire, flood, or other casualty before closing, specify the buyer's options including the right to terminate and receive return of all deposits, the right to proceed with the purchase and receive an assignment of the seller's insurance proceeds, or the right to proceed with a reduction in purchase price equal to the deductible or uninsured portion of the loss.

## Default Provisions, Remedies, and Dispute Resolution Mechanisms

Define with clarity what constitutes a default by either party and specify the remedies available to the non-defaulting party, providing certainty and discouraging breach. A buyer default occurs when the buyer fails to obtain financing after the financing contingency has been waived or has expired, fails to close the transaction when all conditions precedent have been satisfied and the buyer has no remaining contingencies, or materially breaches any other term of the agreement including failure to deposit earnest money, failure to conduct inspections timely, or failure to maintain confidentiality of information learned during due diligence.

Upon buyer default, specify the seller's available remedies with clarity about any limitations or elections required. The seller may retain the earnest money deposit as liquidated damages, representing a reasonable pre-estimate of the seller's damages including the costs of taking the property off the market, lost opportunity to sell to other buyers, continuing carrying costs, and remarketing expenses. Alternatively, the seller may elect to pursue specific performance, seeking a court order compelling the buyer to complete the purchase, which remedy is available because real property is unique and monetary damages may be inadequate. The seller may also pursue actual damages including all costs incurred as a result of the buyer's breach, though this option may be limited if liquidated damages are specified.

A seller default occurs when the seller fails to deliver marketable and insurable title by the closing date, fails to complete agreed-upon repairs or deliver the property in the required condition, fails to close the transaction when all conditions precedent have been satisfied, or materially breaches any other term of the agreement including failure to maintain the property, failure to provide required disclosures, or failure to cooperate with the buyer's inspections.

Upon seller default, specify the buyer's available remedies including the right to terminate the agreement and receive immediate return of all earnest money deposits and reimbursement of all out-of-pocket expenses incurred in connection with the transaction. These expenses typically include inspection costs, appraisal fees, loan application fees, attorney fees incurred in reviewing the transaction, and any temporary housing costs if the buyer has already vacated their prior residence. The buyer may elect to pursue specific performance, compelling the seller to convey the property, which is an appropriate remedy given the unique nature of real property. The buyer may also pursue actual damages for any losses caused by the seller's breach.

Include comprehensive dispute resolution provisions that encourage efficient resolution of conflicts while preserving the parties' legal rights. Require the parties to first attempt to resolve any dispute through good faith negotiation, with written notice of the dispute and a specified period for the parties to meet and confer. If negotiation is unsuccessful, require mediation before either party may initiate litigation, specifying that the parties will jointly select a qualified mediator experienced in real estate disputes, or if they cannot agree, that a mediator will be appointed by a specified organization such as the American Arbitration Association or a local bar association.

Address the allocation of mediation costs, typically providing that the parties will share equally the mediator's fees and expenses while each party bears their own attorney fees. Establish a reasonable timeframe for mediation, such as 30 to 60 days from the date the dispute is submitted to mediation. If mediation does not result in resolution, specify that either party may then pursue litigation or arbitration as provided in the agreement.

Establish the jurisdiction and venue for any litigation, typically specifying the state and county where the property is located, and confirm that the parties consent to personal jurisdiction in that location. Include a prevailing party attorney fees provision, specifying that in any litigation or arbitration arising from this agreement, the prevailing party shall be entitled to recover reasonable attorney fees, expert witness fees, and costs of suit from the non-prevailing party. This provision encourages reasonable behavior and settlement while ensuring that a party who must enforce their rights is not penalized by having to bear their own legal expenses.

Consider whether the parties prefer binding arbitration as an alternative to litigation, and if so, include comprehensive arbitration provisions specifying the arbitration organization that will administer the proceeding, the number of arbitrators (typically one or three), the process for selecting arbitrators, the scope of discovery permitted, and whether the arbitrator's award may be appealed or is final and binding.

Address force majeure events that may excuse performance or extend deadlines, including natural disasters such as earthquakes, floods, or fires, government actions such as condemnation proceedings or regulatory changes, public health emergencies, or other events beyond the parties' reasonable control. Specify the process for invoking force majeure, the documentation required, and whether the agreement will be extended or may be terminated if the force majeure event prevents closing for an extended period.

## Professional Execution Standards and Legal Compliance

Prepare this agreement in clear, precise language that is accessible to parties who may not have legal training while maintaining the legal precision and enforceability required for a binding real estate contract. Use defined terms consistently throughout the document, capitalizing them upon first use and providing clear definitions. Number all sections and subsections hierarchically for easy reference and cross-referencing. If the agreement exceeds five pages, include a table of contents at the beginning to facilitate navigation.

Ensure that all monetary amounts appear in both numerical and written form to prevent ambiguity or alteration. Express all dates with specificity, using complete calendar dates rather than relative references where possible. State all deadlines clearly, using specific calendar dates or measurable timeframes such as \
rather than vague terms like \
or \

Include appropriate signature blocks for all parties with space for full legal names to be printed, signature lines, and date lines. If the property is located in a state requiring witnesses to real estate contracts, include appropriate witness signature blocks. If notarization is required or customary in your jurisdiction, include proper acknowledgment sections with space for the notary's seal and signature.

Specify that the agreement becomes effective only when it has been signed by all parties and the last signature has been obtained, and establish how acceptance will be communicated, whether by physical delivery of the signed document, email transmission of a PDF copy, or electronic signature through a designated platform. Include standard contract provisions essential to enforceability, including an entire agreement or integration clause stating that this written agreement supersedes all prior negotiations, representations, and agreements whether oral or written.

Include a modification provision requiring that any amendments or changes to the agreement must be in writing and signed by all parties to be effective. Add a severability clause providing that if any provision is found to be invalid or unenforceable, the remaining provisions will continue in full force and effect. Specify the governing law, identifying which state's laws will govern the interpretation and enforcement of the agreement, typically the state where the property is located.

Address how notices must be delivered between the parties, specifying acceptable methods such as personal delivery, certified mail return receipt requested, overnight courier, or email to the addresses provided in the agreement. Include a time is of the essence provision making clear that all deadlines and timeframes are material terms of the agreement and strict compliance is required. Add a counterparts clause allowing the agreement to be executed in multiple copies, each of which will be deemed an original and all of which together will constitute one agreement.

Before finalizing the document, verify compliance with all applicable state and local laws governing residential real estate transactions. Research any jurisdiction-specific requirements that must be addressed, such as mandatory disclosure forms, required addenda, or specific language required by state statute. If you are uncertain about any jurisdiction-specific requirements, note these issues for attorney review and verification.

Format the final document professionally with consistent fonts, appropriate spacing, and clear visual hierarchy. Ensure the document is completely free of typographical errors, grammatical mistakes, and formatting inconsistencies. Include any required addenda or exhibits, such as the complete legal description if too lengthy for the main document, a detailed list of included and excluded items, seller disclosure forms, or homeowner association documents. Attach these exhibits in the order they are referenced in the agreement and ensure each is properly labeled and incorporated by reference.

Your final work product should be a comprehensive, legally sound Residential Purchase Agreement that protects all parties' interests, addresses all material terms of the transaction, complies with applicable law, and is ready for review by the parties' attorneys and execution by the clients. The agreement should anticipate potential issues and provide clear mechanisms for resolution, while maintaining the flexibility needed to accommodate the unique circumstances of each residential real estate transaction.

content.name: Residential Purchase Agreement Summary for Title & Escrow
content.summary: This skill instructs an LLM to analyze a fully executed residential purchase agreement package—including all addenda, amendments, and counteroffers—and produce a structured, scannable operational summary for title company closers and processors. It extracts all deal-critical terms including parties, property identifiers, price and earnest money, financing, contingencies, title and survey provisions, HOA and assessment details, closing cost allocations, prorations, and possession terms, presenting them in organized tables with source pointers. The skill flags missing information, document conflicts, unusual clauses, and tight or passed deadlines without offering legal advice, and requires human review before reliance.
content.content:
# Residential Purchase Agreement Summary for Title & Escrow (US)

## 1. Opening Context

In the lifecycle of a residential real estate transaction, the title company acts as the neutral clearinghouse and fiduciary for all parties. The Residential Purchase Agreement (RPA) is not merely a contract between a buyer and seller; it is the primary source of instruction for the title company's entire closing workflow. This skill transforms a dense, often messy legal contract into a surgical, scannable roadmap that a title closer or processor can use to open a file, order title, clear requirements, coordinate payoffs, schedule closing, and prepare the settlement statement.

The output is not a legal memo and not a contract interpretation. It is a high-reliability \

derived from the signed residential purchase agreement and its addenda, with explicit flags for missing information, unusual or non-standard provisions, and deadlines that are tight or already passed. Execution requires a high degree of precision because even minor oversights—failing to note a seller credit, missing a tight earnest money deadline, overlooking a controlling amendment that changed the purchase price—can result in delayed closings, financial liability for the title company, or a breach of escrow instructions. A superior summary does not just repeat the contract's words; it organizes the contract's mechanical requirements so that a processor can identify every required action item at a glance, from ordering a payoff to verifying HOA status, without reading the entire agreement.

## 2. Understanding the Context and Purpose

The title company serves as the bridge between the contract's intent and the actual transfer of property. The purpose of this summary is to decode the Purchase Agreement into actionable data points aligned with the title agency's workflow. For a title closer, the contract is a list of conditions precedent to closing. This document functions as the operational equivalent of escrow instructions, dictating how funds are to be held, how costs are to be split, and when the property may legally change hands.

The summary serves three primary internal stakeholders. The Closer and Processor use it to prepare the settlement statement (ALTA or Closing Disclosure), verify that all conditions are met, and identify what must be ordered or cleared next. The Lender relies on the title company to ensure the contract terms match the loan underwrite, particularly regarding seller credits and financing contingencies. The Real Estate Agents depend on the title company to track critical dates and coordinate scheduling. By flagging unusual clauses—such as post-closing occupancy agreements, non-standard credit structures, or trust sellers requiring additional documentation—the title company protects itself from being caught in a dispute between buyer and seller at the closing table.

This summary also plays an important coordination role even in a neutral posture. Buyer and seller (and their agents) may disagree about what the contract requires. The lender may impose requirements not reflected in the agreement. Addenda may alter deadlines or costs in ways that contradict earlier documents. The summary must therefore be rigorously source-grounded: every extracted term should include a pointer to where it appears (page, section, or document label), and paraphrases must not change meaning. When the agreement is ambiguous or internally inconsistent—for example, two different closing dates appearing in different addenda—the skill must not resolve the conflict. It must flag it prominently and require human review.

## 3. Prerequisites and Information Gathering

Before generating the summary, the executing LLM must obtain the complete agreement package and enough context to compute and flag deadlines. A title file cannot be accurately summarized based on an incomplete or draft agreement. At minimum, the LLM must have the fully executed residential purchase agreement, including all pages, exhibits, riders, and signature blocks with signatures from all buyers and all sellers. It must also have all addenda and amendments referenced in the agreement, including but not limited to financing addenda, inspection addenda, appraisal addenda, well and septic addenda, lead-based paint disclosures for pre-1978 housing, FHA or VA addenda if applicable, seller concession addenda, escalation addenda, and any attorney riders. Any counteroffers incorporated by reference must be included. The LLM also needs the effective date (often defined as the date of last signature or acceptance) and any defined \

convention in the contract. Where available, earnest money receipts, MLS sheets, or closing instructions may be provided for cross-checking addresses and names.\n\nIf any of these documents are missing—particularly the legal description, signed amendments referenced in the main body, or execution signatures—the LLM must explicitly flag this for the user immediately rather than proceeding with incomplete data. If the effective date is not explicit, the LLM must ask: \
If the user cannot provide it, the summary should still extract all stated dates, but deadline calculations must be flagged as \

The LLM should also ask what state the property is in and whether the title team wants state-specific headings while still producing a jurisdiction-agnostic baseline summary.

## 4. Step-by-Step Process

### Step 1: Intake, Document Normalization, and Scope Control

The skill begins by confirming its scope: the output is an operational summary for title and escrow processing. It does not opine on enforceability, interpret ambiguous legal language, or advise whether a party is in default. This boundary must be stated at the top of every output.

Next, normalize the document set. Residential transactions often include multiple PDFs, scanned pages, and addenda with overlapping fields. The LLM should identify every distinct instrument in the package—for example, \
—and assign each a short label used later for source references. If the PDF includes page numbers, preserve them; if not, use a stable internal page index (such as \
) and note that numbering is based on the provided file.\n\nQuality execution here means resisting the common mistake of extracting only from the first \

pages while ignoring addenda that supersede terms. Many markets routinely change price, closing date, possession, or seller contributions in later amendments. The LLM must treat amendments as potentially controlling and must flag when a later document modifies a key term previously extracted.\n\nThe LLM must also verify the presence of signatures and initials where the form expects them and flag \

when signature blocks are blank, when an addendum appears unsigned, or when initials are missing on a critical page such as a price-change amendment. An unsigned contract is not a valid instruction for the title company.

### Step 2: Extract Parties, Vesting-Relevant Details, and Contacts

The LLM must look beyond the names on the first page. It must extract the buyer(s) and seller(s) exactly as written, including middle initials, suffixes, entity designations (LLC, Inc., trust), and any \

language. For title work, the exact spelling and entity type is operationally critical because it affects vesting, deed preparation, and underwriting requirements. If the buyer or seller is a trust, the LLM must extract the full trust name and any trustee names shown, because the title processor will need to request trust documents for the title commitment. If the agreement provides mailing addresses, emails, or phone numbers, extract them into a contacts section, but do not invent missing data.\n\nThe LLM must also check the signature blocks to confirm consistency. If a spouse is missing from a signature block in what may be a community property state, or if a corporate entity is signing without an officer title (such as \

), these are potential title hurdles that must be flagged. The processor must also verify that the seller named in the contract matches the owner of record; if there is any reason to suspect a mismatch, flag it as a potential chain-of-title issue.\n\nBroker and agent information should be extracted separately if present, because title processors often coordinate scheduling and document requests through agents. However, the summary must clearly distinguish \
from \
to avoid confusion. Common mistakes include silently truncating long entity names, dropping \

treating an LLC buyer like an individual, or misspelling names, which affects lien searches. When names differ between documents (such as the purchase agreement and a financing addendum), flag the discrepancy as critical.\n\nCommunity property or marital status descriptors that appear in some state forms should be captured as written without translating them into legal conclusions. The flag should read: \

### Step 3: Extract Property Identifiers and Flag Title-Search Blockers

For title work, the most important extraction is property identity. The LLM must extract the street address (including unit number), city, state, and zip code, the county (if stated), the parcel ID, APN, or PIN, and any legal description text included or incorporated by reference (such as \
). If the agreement says \

or attaches an exhibit for the legal description, record that reference and flag if the exhibit is missing from the provided documents.\n\nIf the agreement includes only an address and omits both parcel ID and legal description, flag this as a title-search risk. Address-only identification is often insufficient for reliable search, especially for rural properties, condominiums with limited common elements, or multi-parcel transactions. A property described only as \

without a legal description may not satisfy the Statute of Frauds, and title may not be insurable on that basis alone.

If the agreement references additional parcels, outlots, common elements, storage units, dock rights, or parking stalls, flag each for title follow-up and note that ordering of condominium documents or plat review may be required. If the agreement mentions included personal property or fixtures (appliances, window treatments, a tractor), capture the inclusion and exclusion list because it can affect lender expectations, settlement statement entries, and whether a Bill of Sale is required, but keep it secondary to title identifiers.

### Step 4: Extract the Financial Architecture

The LLM must break down the flow of funds with precision. Extract the purchase price and break out all monetary components that affect escrow receipts and settlement statement preparation. For earnest money deposits (EMD), identify three things for each deposit: the amount, who is holding it (broker, escrow company, or title company), and the deadline for deposit along with the method (check or wire). If the title company holds the EMD, the closer must track receipt immediately. If there are multiple deposits (initial EMD plus additional EMD), extract each separately with its trigger and deadline.

Analyze the financing structure. Is the transaction cash, conventional, FHA, or VA? This dictates the character of the closing. FHA and VA loans often have mandatory seller-paid costs that cannot be negotiated away, and the title company must account for these on the Closing Disclosure. Extract the loan amount or maximum loan-to-value ratio if provided, the down payment, whether the buyer must apply by a certain date, and the deadline for obtaining commitment or approval.

Extract seller concessions, closing cost credits, repair credits, rate buy-down credits, and any allowances. These often appear in addenda or counteroffers and may conflict with lender caps depending on loan type. The skill must not advise on compliance; it should flag \

without stating what the law requires. The LLM must distinguish between credits for repairs and general closing cost credits because lenders often treat them differently.\n\nIn states like Texas, the \

is a distinct payment made directly to the seller (not to escrow) that gives the buyer an unrestricted right to terminate during the option period. The LLM must not conflate option fees with earnest money. When the contract uses escalation clauses, extract the escalation terms and note whether the price has been adjusted. When multiple documents state different prices, present a \

notation showing each stated price with its source and flag it as requiring human reconciliation.

### Step 5: Map the Critical Timeline

Real estate transactions live and die by the calendar. The LLM must construct a chronological timeline of every deadline extracted from the agreement and all addenda. This includes the effective or acceptance date, EMD deposit deadline(s), inspection period start and end, repair request and resolution deadlines, appraisal contingency date, financing application deadline, financing commitment or approval deadline, title commitment delivery deadline, buyer's title objection deadline, seller's cure period, survey deadline, HOA document delivery and review periods, closing date, and possession date and time.

When calculating dates, the LLM must apply the logic found in the contract's definitions section. Does the contract count calendar days or business days? Does the clock start on the effective date or the day after? If the contract references \

without defining them, flag the deadline computation as uncertain. If today's date is available in the system context, the LLM should flag deadlines as Passed, Due within 48 hours, Due within 7 days, or Future, and should include the computation basis (such as \
). If today's date is not available, omit status logic and instead note \
\n\nThe LLM must flag any closing date that falls on a Sunday or federal holiday as an immediate scheduling conflict. It must note \

language if present, as this makes deadlines strictly enforceable rather than aspirational. Common errors include ignoring that amendments reset deadlines, failing to capture time-of-day possession terms, computing deadlines when the effective date is ambiguous, and collapsing multiple inspection-related deadlines (inspection, notice to cure, re-inspection) into one when they should be tracked separately.

### Step 6: Extract Title, Survey, HOA, and Assessment Provisions

This step focuses on the specific requirements for the title commitment and related items that are core to the title company's operations. Extract who selects the title company or escrow holder (if stated), whether an owner's title insurance policy is required and who pays, any requirement for an ALTA survey or existing survey (noting who pays and the deadline to order it, since surveys are often the longest-lead item), and any specific title standards referenced (such as \
or \

when the agreement suggests an association but does not specify details.\n\nFor special assessments, extract any clause allocating responsibility for pending or existing special assessments, municipal improvements, or \
assessments. If the contract is silent, flag \

If a municipality has a pending assessment for infrastructure and the contract does not address it, the title company may face a surprise post-closing dispute. Do not fill gaps with assumptions.

If a home warranty provision appears, note the cost and provider; this is a line item that must appear on the final settlement statement. Neglecting to list a home warranty is a frequent last-minute correction that delays the signing of the closing package.

### Step 7: Extract Closing Cost Allocations, Prorations, Possession, and Special Provisions

For closing costs, extract who pays for the owner's policy, lender's policy, escrow or closing fee, recording fees, transfer taxes or documentary stamps, survey, pest inspection, home warranty, and any required repairs or certifications. These allocations vary significantly by jurisdiction. If the contract uses a general clause (such as \

as a heightened operational risk requiring additional documentation (a post-closing occupancy agreement and potentially an escrow holdback).\n\nFor special provisions and unusual clauses, extract all handwritten terms, \
or \

sections, builder addenda clauses that shift risk, and any non-standard clauses about arbitration, mediation, attorney fees, limitation of remedies, or specific performance. Look for anything that deviates from a standard residential transaction: a tenant in the property, a solar panel lease that needs to be assumed, personal property requiring a Bill of Sale, or a sale contingent on the buyer selling their current home. The output must not interpret enforceability; it should flag \
for provisions that deviate from typical form language.\n\nFinally, produce a \
section that translates all flags into actionable requests organized by priority. Examples include: \
and \

This is operational triage, not legal instruction.

## 5. Critical Legal Standards and Compliance

This skill is designed for non-attorney title operations, but it must respect legal ethics and risk controls. The output must be framed as document extraction and risk flagging only, not legal advice.

The most important compliance boundary is the unauthorized practice of law (UPL). Title processors are not attorneys, and this summary must remain a factual extraction that does not offer legal opinions on the enforceability of clauses or the rights of parties. Under ABA Model Rule 5.5, non-lawyers may not engage in the practice of law. Any complex legal conflict identified in the contract should be flagged with the note: \
The LLM must avoid statements like \
unless directly quoting the contract, and even then should frame it as \

rather than as advice.

The summary should align with American Land Title Association (ALTA) best practices, particularly regarding the accuracy of settlement statements and the handling of escrow funds. ALTA's best practices framework provides guidance on title and settlement procedures that title companies follow across the country.

For financed transactions, the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's TILA-RESPA Integrated Disclosure (TRID) rule mandates strict timing for the Closing Disclosure. The title company must have the final contract terms well in advance of closing to meet the three-business-day delivery requirement to the consumer before consummation. Any summary produced within five days of a closing date should be flagged as \
The skill must not generate TRID disclosures or give compliance conclusions; it should flag \

and leave compliance determinations to the appropriate professionals.

The title company has a fiduciary duty to follow the written instructions of both parties. If the summary misses an instruction—such as a specific credit or a required holdback—the title company may be liable for the resulting loss. This reinforces the need for completeness and traceability in every extraction.

Confidentiality and privacy are paramount. Purchase agreements include personal data including names, addresses, and sometimes contact information and financial terms. The LLM must treat all inputs and outputs as confidential. If sensitive data such as Social Security numbers or account numbers appears in the documents, the LLM must mask them and flag \

The executing LLM must never fabricate statutes, regulations, case citations, or legal authorities. If the user asks for legal authority or jurisdiction-specific requirements, the LLM must either perform a web search and provide verifiable URLs or explicitly state that attorney verification is required. No legal citation should be presented without verification.

## 6. Quality Control and Review

Quality review begins with traceability. Every extracted term must have a source pointer identifying the document label and section or page. If a term is not explicitly present, the correct output is \
or \

never a guess. The summary must be internally consistent: the purchase price should match the sum of price components where applicable; the closing date should match across the document set or be flagged as a conflict; and the EMD due date should not post-date closing without a flag.\n\nApply a direct citation check for every dollar amount. If the original contract states $500,000 but Amendment 2 states $480,000, the summary must reflect $480,000 and note the change. Recalculate any date that is stated as a day-count formula (such as \

test: if the closer were sitting at the table today, would anything in this file surprise them? If there is a mention of a tenant in the property, a solar panel lease, or an unresolved repair escrow that is not in the summary, the summary is incomplete.\n\nThe output must include the following disclaimer, used verbatim: \

## 7. Jurisdiction-Specific Adaptations

This skill is intentionally US-wide and form-agnostic, but it should support customization along the axis of state form families and customary allocations. The main structural schema—Parties, Property, Price and EMD, Financing, Dates, Title and Survey, HOA and Assessments, Costs and Prorations, Possession, Addenda and Amendments, Special Provisions, and Flags and Follow-Up—works across all jurisdictions.

When a state is identified, the LLM may add a brief state-specific notes subsection that addresses only what the contract itself references. The following illustrative examples demonstrate the kinds of variations the LLM should watch for. In California (C.A.R. forms), attention should be paid to liquidated damages and arbitration initials, because if the buyer does not initial these provisions, the escrow instructions for EMD disputes change. The Natural Hazard Disclosure requirement should also be tracked. In Texas (TREC forms), the Option Fee in Paragraph 5 is unique; it is paid directly to the seller rather than to escrow and grants the buyer an unrestricted right to terminate. The title company must confirm receipt of the earnest money but typically not the option fee. In Florida (FAR/BAR forms), the distinction between the \
contract and the standard contract matters because the \

version has a specific inspection-and-terminate clause that determines when the EMD becomes non-refundable. In New York and other northeastern states, an attorney review period often means the contract is not binding until attorneys approve it, and the title file should not be fully opened until that period has cleared. In Minnesota, statutory cancellation rights and specific requirements for well and septic disclosures may trigger buyer rescission rights.\n\nIn all cases, the LLM should identify the specific state form being used (such as \
or \

) as this helps the processor know which boilerplate provisions apply. If the user requests state-law explanations beyond what the contract itself states, the LLM must either perform web research with verifiable URLs or mark the content as requiring attorney verification. The LLM must not supply customary rules from memory without verification.

---

## Output Specification

The LLM's final output must be a structured, quick-scanning summary using headings, tables, and concise entries. The tone must be operational and neutral, written for title closers and processors.

The output must include the following sections, in order:

**Header.** Include File or Order Name (if provided), Property Address, State (if known), list of documents received, Effective Date (as stated), Summary Date, and the required disclaimer.

**Deal Snapshot.** A two-column summary table with: Buyer(s), Seller(s), Property, Purchase Price, Total EMD, Closing Date, Possession, Loan Type and Amount (or Cash), Title Company or Escrow Holder (if stated), HOA (Yes, No, or Unclear), Special Assessments (Noted or Not stated), and count of Key Flags.

**Parties and Contacts.** Separate tables for parties and for agents, brokers, and other contacts. Include name as written, entity type, signing status, and source reference.

**Property Details.** Address, unit, city/state/zip, county, parcel or APN, legal description (verbatim or \

), additional parcels or outlots, personal property included or excluded, and source. Flag prominently if legal description or parcel ID is missing.

**Price, Earnest Money, and Credits.** Purchase price, escalation or price adjustment terms, each EMD deposit with amount, due date, holder, method, and application to price, seller concessions and credits, repair credits and allowances, option fee if present, and source.

**Financing and Appraisal.** Financing type, loan amount, down payment, lender name, application deadline, commitment deadline, financing contingency date, appraisal contingency terms, appraisal objection deadline, and source.

**Contingencies.** Inspection period dates, notice deadlines, repair request and resolution deadlines, home sale contingency details, and any other contingencies (well/septic, radon, lead-based paint, insurance) with deadlines and source.

**Title, Survey, and Closing Documentation.** Title commitment delivery deadline, buyer objection period, seller cure period, permitted exceptions, survey requirement and deadline, who pays for owner's and lender's policy, escrow or closing location selection, and source.

**HOA and Condominium.** Whether HOA or condo association applies, association name and contact, document delivery requirements, buyer review period, transfer fee responsibility, dues proration, and source.

**Closing Date, Possession, and Occupancy.** Closing date, scheduled time, possession date and time, rent-back or leaseback terms, per diem rent, holdback or security deposit, and source.

**Closing Costs, Taxes, and Prorations.** Allocation of escrow fee, recording fees, transfer taxes, survey, inspections, home warranty, title premiums, tax proration method, HOA dues proration, special assessments allocation, and source.

**Addenda, Amendments, and Disclosures Inventory.** Each document listed with name, date, signing status, what it modifies, and source page range.

**Critical Dates and Deadlines.** A table with columns for Item, Trigger, Deadline as written, Computed date (if calculable), Status (Passed, Due within 48 hours, Due within 7 days, Future, or Unknown), Notes, and Source. Compute only when the effective date and day-count convention are clear; otherwise leave computed date blank and mark status Unknown.

**Flags and Follow-Up Items.** Organized by severity: Critical (blocking file opening or closing), High (likely to delay closing), Medium (needs clarification), and Low (informational). Each item must state what is missing or unusual, why it matters operationally, and where to look in the documents.

**Source Map.** A table mapping each major category to the primary document label and page or section.

## Execution Guardrails

The LLM must never fabricate missing values. If a field is not present, use \
and add a follow-up flag. The LLM must not resolve conflicts between documents; it must display conflicts side-by-side and flag them for human resolution. The LLM must avoid legal conclusions. Use \
or \

and keep quoted passages short. If the user asks for legal requirements or enforceability analysis, the LLM must respond that attorney review is required and offer to perform web research with verifiable URLs if the user wants jurisdiction-specific information. The LLM must protect sensitive data by including only what is needed for processing and masking any Social Security numbers or account numbers if detected.

content.name: Response to Petition
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive Response to Petition for Dissolution of Marriage on behalf of the respondent in family law litigation. It addresses all allegations in the petition, corrects inaccuracies, confirms or disputes statistical facts like marriage and separation dates, and states the respondent's positions on custody, support, and property. Use it during the pleadings phase to formally respond within statutory deadlines and avoid default judgment.
content.content:
# Enhanced Prompt: Response to Petition for Dissolution of Marriage

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Response to Petition for Dissolution of Marriage on behalf of the respondent. This is a critical litigation document that serves as the respondent's formal answer to all allegations and requests made in the divorce petition, and it establishes the respondent's position on all material issues in the case.

## Document Purpose and Legal Context

The Response to Petition is the respondent's opportunity to admit or deny the petitioner's allegations, correct any inaccuracies, and affirmatively state their own requests for relief. This document must comply with all applicable family law procedural rules and local court requirements. The response must be filed within the statutory deadline (typically 30 days from service of the petition) to avoid default. Every allegation in the petition must be addressed—failure to deny an allegation may constitute an admission.

## Required Information Gathering

Begin by thoroughly reviewing all available case documents, particularly the original Petition for Dissolution of Marriage. Search through the client's uploaded documents to identify and extract key factual information including the exact date of marriage, date of separation, names and birthdates of any minor children, details of marital property and debts, income information for both parties, and any existing custody or support arrangements. Pay careful attention to any allegations made in the petition that require specific denial or correction.

Identify the proper court name, case number, and ensure accurate spelling of both the petitioner's and respondent's full legal names as they appear in the original petition. Verify statistical information such as marriage date and separation date against available documentation, noting any discrepancies that the respondent needs to correct.

## Document Structure and Content Requirements

**Caption and Case Information**: Format the caption to match the court's requirements, including the full court name, county, case number, and parties' names exactly as they appear in the petition. The respondent's name should appear in the same format throughout.

**Jurisdictional Allegations**: Address the petition's jurisdictional allegations regarding residency requirements and domicile. If the respondent agrees with the petitioner's statements about jurisdiction, indicate agreement. If there are any inaccuracies, provide the correct information with specificity.

**Statistical Facts Response**: Confirm or correct the date of marriage and date of separation as stated in the petition. If the respondent disputes the separation date, provide the date the respondent believes is accurate and explain the basis for the disagreement. Address any other statistical information such as length of marriage and whether there are minor children of the marriage.

**Child Custody and Visitation**: Articulate the respondent's position on legal and physical custody of any minor children. Specify whether the respondent seeks sole custody, joint custody, or a particular custodial arrangement. Detail the proposed visitation schedule if the respondent is not seeking primary physical custody. Address any concerns about the petitioner's proposed custody arrangement and explain why the respondent's proposal serves the children's best interests. Reference any relevant facts from case documents about parenting history, the children's current living situation, school enrollment, and each parent's involvement in the children's lives.

**Child Support and Spousal Support**: State the respondent's position on child support, including whether the respondent agrees to pay support, seeks support from the petitioner, or requests a deviation from guideline support with justification. Address spousal support by indicating whether the respondent seeks support, opposes the petitioner's request for support, or agrees to pay support for a specified duration. Include relevant financial information from available documents about each party's income, earning capacity, and financial needs.

**Property Division**: Provide the respondent's position on characterization and division of all significant assets, including the family residence, other real property, retirement accounts, bank accounts, vehicles, and business interests. Identify any separate property claims the respondent wishes to assert. Address the petitioner's proposed property division and state whether the respondent agrees or seeks a different division. Similarly, address responsibility for debts, including mortgages, credit cards, loans, and other liabilities, specifying which debts the respondent believes should be assigned to each party.

**Attorney Fees and Costs**: State the respondent's position on attorney fees and costs, including any request for the petitioner to contribute to the respondent's legal fees based on disparity in access to funds or income.

## Tone and Drafting Standards

Draft the response in formal legal language appropriate for a court filing while remaining clear and accessible. Use numbered paragraphs for each separate allegation or statement. Maintain a professional, non-inflammatory tone even when denying allegations or disputing the petitioner's requests. Avoid argumentative language—save legal arguments for supporting declarations or briefs.

Each response to a petition allegation should follow this format: admit if true, deny if false, or state lack of sufficient information to admit or deny if the respondent genuinely lacks knowledge. When denying an allegation, consider whether a qualified response is more accurate (for example, \

).

## Verification and Signature Requirements

Include a verification section where the respondent declares under penalty of perjury that the contents of the response are true and correct to the best of their knowledge. Provide signature lines for the respondent's signature and date, and if the respondent is represented by counsel, include counsel's signature block with State Bar number, firm name, address, telephone number, and email address.

## Final Output Format

Generate a complete, court-ready Response to Petition formatted as a formal legal pleading with appropriate spacing, margins, and pagination. Include a footer on each page with the document title and page numbers. Ensure all required sections are present and properly organized. The final document should be ready for the respondent's review and signature, requiring only case-specific customization based on the client's particular circumstances and strategic objectives.

content.name: Retail Lease Agreement
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive Retail Lease Agreement for commercial retail spaces in shopping centers or properties. Addresses base rent, percentage rent, gross sales definitions, operating expenses, continuous operation requirements, and tenant improvements. Use for transactional commercial leasing to balance landlord and tenant interests.
content.content:
# RETAIL LEASE AGREEMENT DRAFTING PROMPT

## Document Overview and Purpose

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Retail Lease Agreement for commercial leasing purposes. This transactional document will govern the relationship between a landlord and tenant for retail space within a shopping center or commercial property. The agreement must balance the interests of both parties while addressing the unique operational requirements of retail businesses, including percentage rent structures, continuous operation obligations, and common area maintenance responsibilities.

## Essential Lease Information

Begin by establishing the foundational elements of the lease relationship. Identify the complete legal names and addresses of both the Landlord and Tenant, ensuring proper entity designation (individual, corporation, LLC, partnership, etc.). Describe the Premises with precision, including the unit number, street address, shopping center name if applicable, and the approximate square footage. Specify whether measurements are based on usable square footage or gross leasable area, and note any common areas included in the leased space such as storage rooms, restrooms, or back-of-house facilities.

Define the Lease Term with clarity, stating the commencement date and expiration date. If the commencement is contingent upon substantial completion of tenant improvements or delivery of possession, articulate these conditions explicitly. Address whether the term begins upon lease execution, delivery of possession, or opening for business. Include any rent abatement periods during construction or initial setup, specifying whether such periods extend the overall term or are included within it.

Establish the Base Rent or Minimum Annual Rent amount, stating whether it is fixed throughout the term or subject to scheduled increases. If the rent includes escalations, specify whether these are fixed percentage increases, Consumer Price Index adjustments, or fair market value resets at designated intervals. Clarify the payment schedule, due date each month, acceptable payment methods, and the address or account for rent remittance.

## Additional Rent and Operating Expenses

Draft comprehensive provisions addressing Percentage Rent obligations that are characteristic of retail leasing. Specify the percentage rate to be applied to Gross Sales and establish the annual breakpoint or natural breakpoint above which percentage rent becomes due. Clarify whether percentage rent is calculated monthly, quarterly, or annually, and establish reporting and payment deadlines. Address whether the breakpoint is cumulative throughout the lease term or resets annually.

Define Gross Sales with precision to avoid future disputes. The definition should encompass all revenues, receipts, and income of every kind derived from business conducted in, on, or from the Premises, regardless of whether such sales are for cash, credit, or otherwise. Specify inclusions such as online sales fulfilled from the Premises, gift card redemptions, and sales from vending machines or kiosks. Equally important, enumerate permitted exclusions, which typically include returns and refunds, sales taxes collected and remitted to governmental authorities, sales to employees at discount (up to a reasonable cap), and insurance proceeds for damaged or stolen merchandise. Require the Tenant to maintain complete and accurate books and records, grant the Landlord audit rights with reasonable notice, and mandate annual sales reporting certified by the Tenant's authorized representative.

Address Common Area Maintenance charges by establishing the Tenant's proportionate share, typically calculated as the ratio of the Premises square footage to the total gross leasable area of the shopping center. Define CAM expenses to include maintenance, repair, and replacement of common areas such as parking lots, walkways, landscaping, lighting, security services, and management fees. Specify any caps on CAM increases or exclusions for capital improvements with useful lives exceeding one year. Establish the reconciliation process, requiring the Landlord to provide annual statements with supporting documentation and allowing the Tenant audit rights.

Similarly, allocate responsibility for real estate taxes and property insurance on a proportionate share basis. Clarify whether tax obligations include assessments, special assessments, and personal property taxes on common area equipment. For insurance, specify that the Landlord will maintain property insurance on the building and common areas, with costs passed through to tenants, while the Tenant remains responsible for its own liability insurance and contents coverage.

## Use Provisions and Operational Requirements

Define the Permitted Use with specificity to protect both parties' interests. Rather than broad categories, describe the exact nature of the retail business, including the types of products or services to be sold and the trade name under which the Tenant will operate. This precision prevents conflicts with other tenants' exclusive use rights and ensures the tenant mix aligns with the shopping center's character and market positioning.

Impose Continuous Operation obligations requiring the Tenant to operate its business throughout the entire Premises during all days and hours that the shopping center is open to the public. Address consequences for dark store situations, including potential percentage rent adjustments, landlord's right to terminate, or stipulated damages. Include reasonable exceptions for force majeure events, casualty damage during restoration, or temporary closures for remodeling with landlord approval. Recognize that continuous operation protects the shopping center's viability by maintaining customer traffic and preventing dead spaces that diminish the overall retail environment.

Establish Signage standards requiring Landlord's prior written approval for all exterior signs, window displays visible from common areas, and any illuminated signage. Reference compliance with the shopping center's signage criteria, local zoning ordinances, and any applicable design guidelines. Specify that the Tenant bears all costs for sign fabrication, installation, maintenance, and removal upon lease termination, and must maintain signs in first-class condition throughout the term.

If applicable, require participation in the shopping center's Merchants' Association, including payment of dues and assessments for joint marketing, promotional events, and common area decorations. Specify the initial dues amount and the mechanism for adjustments, typically tied to the association's annual budget approved by its membership.

## Premises Condition and Improvements

Describe the condition in which the Landlord will deliver the Premises to the Tenant. Common delivery conditions include \
where the Tenant accepts the space in its current condition, \
requiring the Landlord to remove debris and prior tenant's property, or \
or \

providing a basic finished space with walls, ceiling, flooring, HVAC, electrical, and plumbing stubbed to the Premises but without tenant-specific finishes.

Address Tenant Improvements comprehensively, establishing the approval process for construction plans and specifications. Require the Tenant to engage licensed and insured contractors, obtain all necessary permits, and complete work in accordance with applicable building codes and ADA requirements. If the Landlord provides a Tenant Improvement Allowance, specify the dollar amount per square foot or total allowance, eligible costs that may be reimbursed (typically hard construction costs, but potentially including architectural fees, permits, and project management), the disbursement process requiring submission of lien waivers and paid invoices, and any deadline by which the allowance must be utilized or it expires.

Establish construction timelines, requiring the Tenant to complete improvements and open for business within a specified period after lease execution or delivery of possession. Address the consequences of delays, distinguishing between excusable delays due to force majeure or Landlord-caused delays versus unexcused delays that might trigger lease termination rights or liquidated damages.

## Protective Clauses and Special Provisions

If negotiated, include an Exclusive Use Clause prohibiting the Landlord from leasing other space in the shopping center to tenants whose primary business competes directly with the Tenant's permitted use. Define the scope of the exclusivity with precision, specifying the protected product categories or services. Address whether the exclusivity applies to the entire shopping center or only to inline tenants, potentially excluding anchor tenants or pad sites. Include reasonable carve-outs for existing tenants, tenants in occupancy as of the lease date, or de minimis sales of competing products that are ancillary to another tenant's primary business.

Consider including a Radius Restriction preventing the Tenant from operating a competing business within a specified geographic area surrounding the shopping center. Define the restricted radius (commonly ranging from one to five miles depending on market conditions and tenant bargaining power), the duration of the restriction (typically coterminous with the lease term, potentially extending beyond for some period), and whether the restriction applies to all locations or only those under the same trade name or ownership structure.

Draft comprehensive Default and Remedies provisions addressing both monetary and non-monetary defaults. For monetary defaults, provide a grace period (typically five to ten days) after written notice before default is deemed to occur. For non-monetary defaults, allow a reasonable cure period (typically thirty days, or longer if the default cannot reasonably be cured within thirty days provided the Tenant commences cure promptly and diligently pursues it to completion). Enumerate Landlord's remedies upon default, including termination of the lease, re-entry and repossession, reletting on Tenant's account, and recovery of damages including unpaid rent, costs of reletting, tenant improvement amortization, and the present value of rent for the remainder of the term less amounts actually received from reletting. Ensure remedies comply with applicable state law and do not constitute unenforceable penalties.

Include standard commercial lease provisions addressing assignment and subletting (typically requiring Landlord's consent, which may be conditioned on reasonable criteria), maintenance and repair obligations (generally Tenant responsible for the interior and Landlord for structural elements and common areas), insurance requirements (specifying minimum coverage amounts for commercial general liability, property insurance, and potentially business interruption coverage), indemnification (mutual indemnification for claims arising from each party's negligence or willful misconduct), casualty and condemnation (addressing restoration obligations and termination rights), subordination and attornment, estoppel certificates, and dispute resolution mechanisms.

## Execution and Formalities

Conclude with properly formatted signature blocks identifying each party's authorized signatory, title, and date of execution. For entity parties, ensure signatures are executed by authorized representatives with appropriate corporate authority. Include acknowledgment language if the lease will be recorded or if state law requires notarization for commercial leases. Provide spaces for witness signatures if required by local law or if the lease term exceeds the statutory period requiring witnesses.

The completed Retail Lease Agreement should be a balanced, comprehensive document that clearly articulates the rights and obligations of both parties while addressing the unique operational and financial aspects of retail leasing in a shopping center environment.

content.name: Revocable Living Trust
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive Revocable Living Trust document, including declaration of trust, property funding schedule, and trustee provisions tailored to client circumstances and state law. This skill ensures the trust is revocable, preserves grantor control during lifetime, and facilitates seamless asset transfer upon death. Use it for estate planning matters to create legally sound, customizable trusts for individuals or couples.
content.content:
# Revocable Living Trust Drafting Workflow

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Revocable Living Trust, a foundational estate planning document that allows a grantor to maintain control over assets during their lifetime while providing for seamless transfer upon death. This document must be precise, legally sound, and tailored to the client's specific circumstances and applicable state law.

## Declaration of Trust

Begin by drafting the declaration section that formally establishes the trust relationship. This opening must clearly articulate the grantor's intent to create a revocable living trust, identify the grantor by full legal name and address, and establish the trust's effective date. Name the initial trustee (typically the grantor themselves) and identify all initial beneficiaries with specificity. The declaration should include:

- The formal trust name, typically incorporating the grantor's name and the year of creation
- An unambiguous statement of the grantor's capacity and voluntary intent to create the trust
- The trust's primary purposes, including asset management during the grantor's lifetime and distribution upon death
- Clear identification of whether this is an individual or joint trust (if married)
- Any specific statement regarding the grantor's state of residence for jurisdictional purposes

Ensure the language reflects that this is a revocable trust, explicitly preserving the grantor's right to modify or terminate the trust at any time during their lifetime while they retain capacity.

## Trust Property and Funding

Draft a comprehensive section describing the property being transferred into the trust. This is critical because an unfunded trust provides no estate planning benefits. Detail the initial assets being transferred, using specific legal descriptions for real property and precise account information for financial assets. The property schedule should encompass:

- Real property with complete legal descriptions, assessor's parcel numbers, and addresses
- Financial accounts including bank accounts, brokerage accounts, and retirement accounts (noting any special considerations for qualified plans)
- Personal property of significant value, including vehicles, jewelry, art, and collectibles
- Business interests, including ownership percentages in partnerships, LLCs, or corporations
- Any other assets the grantor intends to transfer now or in the future

Include language acknowledging that the trust may be funded over time and that the schedule of assets may be amended without formal trust amendment. Address the mechanism for transferring additional property into the trust and specify whether the grantor retains the right to add or remove assets freely.

## Trustee Provisions and Succession

Establish the trustee structure with careful attention to succession planning and trustee authority. Designate the initial trustee (usually the grantor for individual trusts, or both spouses for joint trusts) and create a clear succession plan for disability or death. This section must address:

- The appointment and acceptance of the initial trustee with full legal name and address
- Detailed succession provisions naming first, second, and potentially third successor trustees
- Conditions triggering successor trustee appointment, including death, resignation, incapacity (with definition), or removal
- The process for determining incapacity, whether through physician certification or other means
- Provisions for co-trustees if multiple individuals will serve simultaneously, including decision-making protocols
- Trustee resignation procedures and the mechanism for appointing replacement trustees

Specify whether successor trustees must accept the appointment in writing and outline any bond requirements (typically waived for family members). Address whether corporate trustees (banks or trust companies) may serve and any special provisions applicable to professional fiduciaries.

## Beneficiary Designations and Distribution Scheme

Articulate a clear and comprehensive distribution plan that addresses both lifetime and post-death distributions. This section forms the heart of the trust's estate planning function and must reflect the grantor's specific wishes while providing flexibility for changed circumstances. The distribution provisions should specify:

- During the grantor's lifetime: Confirm that all income and principal may be distributed to the grantor without limitation, and address distributions to other beneficiaries if this is a special needs or supplemental trust
- Upon the grantor's death: Identify primary beneficiaries by full legal name and relationship, specify whether distributions are per stirpes or per capita, and detail the timing and conditions of distributions
- Contingent beneficiaries in case primary beneficiaries predecease the grantor
- Any specific bequests of particular property to named individuals
- Provisions for minor beneficiaries, including age-based distribution schedules or continued trust management until specified ages

Include protective provisions such as spendthrift clauses to shield beneficiary interests from creditors, and consider whether any beneficiaries should receive their inheritance in continued trust rather than outright. Address what happens if all named beneficiaries predecease the grantor.

## Revocation and Amendment Procedures

Draft clear procedures for the grantor to exercise their right to revoke or amend the trust, as this revocability is the defining characteristic distinguishing this trust from irrevocable alternatives. Specify that the grantor retains absolute authority to amend or revoke the trust during their lifetime while they possess legal capacity. The revocation and amendment provisions must include:

- The requirement that any amendment or revocation be in writing and signed by the grantor
- Whether amendments require notarization or witness signatures
- The method of providing notice to the trustee of any amendments or revocation
- Specification that amendments may be partial (modifying specific provisions) or complete (restating the entire trust)
- Confirmation that upon revocation, all trust property reverts to the grantor absolutely

For joint trusts created by married couples, address whether both grantors must consent to amendments during their joint lifetimes, and specify what happens upon the first death (whether the trust becomes irrevocable or remains amendable by the surviving spouse). Clarify that after the grantor's death or incapacity, the trust becomes irrevocable and cannot be modified except as specifically permitted within the trust terms.

## Trustee Powers and Administrative Provisions

Enumerate comprehensive powers granted to the trustee to effectively administer the trust. These powers must be sufficiently broad to allow flexible management while complying with fiduciary duties. Detail the trustee's authority in narrative form, incorporating:

- Investment powers, including the authority to invest in any property or asset class, retain original trust assets, and exercise all rights of ownership including voting shares and managing business interests
- Management powers, such as the authority to sell, exchange, lease, mortgage, or otherwise deal with trust property on terms the trustee deems appropriate
- Distribution authority, including discretion to make distributions for health, education, maintenance, and support (HEMS standard) or broader discretionary standards
- Administrative powers, including the ability to hire professionals (attorneys, accountants, investment advisors), delegate certain functions, maintain insurance, handle tax matters, and maintain accurate records
- Special powers relevant to specific assets, such as authority to continue operating a business, manage rental properties, or handle intellectual property

Specify the standard of care applicable to the trustee (prudent investor rule or other state-specific standard) and address trustee compensation, typically allowing reasonable fees for professional trustees while permitting family trustees to serve without compensation or to receive specified fees. Include provisions regarding trustee liability, indemnification, and the circumstances under which a trustee may be removed.

## Governing Law and General Provisions

Conclude with essential administrative and legal provisions that ensure the trust's validity and enforceability. Designate the governing law by specifying which state's laws will control the trust's interpretation and administration, typically the grantor's state of residence. This final section should incorporate:

- A severability clause providing that if any provision is found invalid, the remaining provisions continue in full effect
- A no-contest or in terrorem clause discouraging beneficiaries from challenging the trust by forfeiting their inheritance if they do so unsuccessfully
- Spendthrift provisions protecting beneficiary interests from creditor claims
- Tax provision addressing allocation of tax burdens and directing how estate taxes should be paid
- Definitions of key terms used throughout the trust, including \

and any other terms requiring clarification

Address administrative matters such as the trustee's duty to provide accountings to beneficiaries, the frequency of such accountings, and any waiver provisions. Include merger provisions preventing the trust from terminating if the grantor is the sole trustee and sole beneficiary. Specify the trust's situs (physical location for legal purposes) and identify which courts have jurisdiction over trust matters.

## Execution Requirements and Finalization

Ensure the completed trust document complies with all state-specific execution requirements. While trusts generally do not require the same formalities as wills, proper execution is essential for validity. The document should include signature blocks for the grantor(s) and trustee(s), with appropriate notarization. Include a schedule of assets as an exhibit, even if initially unfunded, to be completed as property is transferred into the trust. Verify that the trust name is used consistently throughout and that all cross-references are accurate. The final document should be professionally formatted, paginated, and organized for easy reference by the trustee and beneficiaries.

content.name: Revolving Credit Agreement
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive Revolving Credit Agreement establishing a revolving line of credit between a lender and borrower. It details facility structure, commitments, borrowing mechanics, letter of credit sublimits, and protections aligned with commercial lending practices. Use this skill for transactional loan and financing matters requiring a precise, market-standard credit facility document.
content.content:
# Enhanced Revolving Credit Agreement Workflow Prompt

You are a specialized legal AI assistant tasked with drafting a comprehensive Revolving Credit Agreement. This is a critical transactional financing document that establishes a revolving line of credit between a lender and borrower, allowing the borrower to draw, repay, and re-borrow funds up to a specified limit during the commitment period.

Your role is to produce a professionally drafted, legally sound agreement that protects both parties' interests while clearly articulating the commercial terms, operational mechanics, and legal framework governing the credit facility. The document must be precise, internally consistent, and reflect current market practices in commercial lending.

## Document Header and Parties

Draft a formal document header that clearly identifies this as a Revolving Credit Agreement. Include the execution date and provide complete identifying information for all parties, including the borrower's full legal name, state of organization or residence, and the lender's complete legal name and organizational details. If there are multiple lenders participating in a syndicated facility, identify the administrative agent and list all participating lenders with their respective commitment amounts. Ensure the recitals section, if included, provides appropriate context for the transaction and references any prior credit relationships or refinancing purposes. The introductory paragraph should establish defined terms for \
and \

that will be used consistently throughout the document.

## Credit Facility Structure and Commitments

Articulate the fundamental structure of the revolving credit facility with precision. Specify the total revolving commitment amount in both numerical and written form to avoid ambiguity. Define the availability period clearly, identifying the closing date as the commencement point and the maturity date as the termination point, while noting any circumstances that could result in earlier termination of the commitment. If the facility includes a letter of credit sublimit, describe the maximum aggregate face amount of letters of credit that may be outstanding at any time and explain how letter of credit usage reduces availability under the revolving commitment. Address whether the commitment is subject to a borrowing base calculation tied to eligible accounts receivable, inventory, or other collateral, and if so, provide the methodology for calculating availability. Include provisions addressing commitment reductions, both voluntary reductions at the borrower's election and mandatory reductions based on specified events or amortization schedules.

## Borrowing Mechanics and Procedures

Establish clear, workable procedures for requesting and funding loans under the facility. Specify that the borrower must deliver a written borrowing notice to the lender by a designated time (typically 11:00 a.m. or 12:00 noon) a specified number of business days before the requested funding date—usually same-day for base rate loans and one to three business days for SOFR-based loans. Detail the required contents of the borrowing notice, including the requested loan amount, proposed borrowing date, interest rate option selected, and interest period if applicable. Describe the lender's funding obligations and the mechanism for disbursing loan proceeds, whether by wire transfer to a designated account or by other agreed means. Address the procedures for converting loans from one interest rate option to another and for continuing loans at the end of an interest period. Include provisions confirming that each borrowing request constitutes a representation that conditions precedent remain satisfied.

## Interest Rates, Fees, and Payment Terms

Define the interest rate structure with mathematical precision, specifying both the SOFR-based rate option and the base rate option. For SOFR loans, identify the applicable term SOFR rate, the credit spread adjustment, and the margin to be added. For base rate loans, define the base rate as the highest of the federal funds rate plus a specified margin, the lender's prime rate, or term SOFR plus a specified differential, then add the applicable margin. Specify the unused commitment fee rate (typically ranging from 0.125% to 0.50% per annum) calculated on the daily average unused portion of the commitment, and detail when this fee accrues and when it is payable. If letters of credit are part of the facility, establish the letter of credit fees, including both the fronting fee payable to the issuing lender and the participation fee payable to all lenders. Address the timing and method of interest payments, typically monthly in arrears for base rate loans and at the end of each interest period for SOFR loans. Include default interest provisions specifying an increased rate (commonly 2% above the otherwise applicable rate) that applies after an event of default. Establish that all payments must be made in immediately available funds without setoff, counterclaim, or deduction.

## Repayment, Prepayment, and Maturity

Articulate the repayment structure clearly, noting that revolving loans do not require scheduled amortization payments but must be repaid in full on the maturity date. Specify that the borrower may voluntarily prepay revolving loans at any time without premium or penalty, subject to providing advance notice as required for the applicable interest rate type. Include mandatory prepayment provisions that require immediate repayment if outstanding loans exceed the revolving commitment or borrowing base availability, whether due to commitment reductions, borrowing base declines, or other causes. Address the application of prepayments, specifying whether they permanently reduce the commitment or merely reduce outstanding loans while preserving the ability to re-borrow. Establish that all accrued interest, fees, and other obligations become immediately due and payable on the maturity date, and define the maturity date with specificity, typically as a date certain that is one to five years from the closing date.

## Collateral and Security

Describe the collateral package securing the obligations under the credit agreement. Specify whether the lender receives a first-priority security interest in all present and after-acquired assets of the borrower, including accounts receivable, inventory, equipment, general intangibles, investment property, and proceeds thereof. Reference the separate Security Agreement or Pledge Agreement that creates and perfects these security interests, and note the lender's right to file UCC financing statements in all appropriate jurisdictions. If the facility is secured by real property, reference the Mortgage or Deed of Trust and describe the mortgaged properties. Address any permitted liens that may have priority over or parity with the lender's security interests, such as purchase money security interests, tax liens, or other statutory liens. Include the borrower's obligations to maintain the collateral, provide periodic collateral reports, and permit the lender to conduct field examinations and appraisals. If applicable, describe any borrowing base calculation methodology, including advance rates against eligible receivables and inventory, and the process for delivering borrowing base certificates.

## Guarantees and Credit Support

If the obligations are guaranteed, identify each guarantor by full legal name and organizational details, and reference the separate Guaranty Agreement executed by each guarantor. Specify whether the guaranty is unconditional and absolute, and whether it covers all obligations under the credit agreement or is limited in amount or scope. Address whether guarantors provide upstream, cross-stream, or downstream guarantees, and ensure compliance with applicable limitations on guarantees, including fraudulent transfer considerations and corporate benefit requirements. If the guaranty is secured, describe the collateral pledged by each guarantor and reference the applicable security documents. Include provisions addressing the release of guarantors upon the occurrence of specified events, such as the sale of a subsidiary guarantor or the achievement of specified financial metrics by the borrower.

## Representations and Warranties
