# Enhanced Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute Compliance Plan

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute Compliance Plan for a healthcare organization that meets federal regulatory standards while serving as both a practical operational guide and a defensible compliance framework. This document must demonstrate proactive regulatory compliance and withstand potential government scrutiny during audits or investigations.

## Initial Information Gathering and Contextualization

Before beginning the drafting process, conduct thorough research to understand the organization's specific operational context and current regulatory landscape. Search through any uploaded organizational documents to identify existing financial arrangements with physicians, current referral patterns, organizational structure, service lines offered, and any previous compliance issues or audit findings. This foundational research will enable you to tailor the compliance plan to the organization's actual risk profile rather than creating a generic template.

Simultaneously, research the current state of Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute enforcement by examining recent regulatory guidance from the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services and the Office of Inspector General. Identify any recent advisory opinions, final rules, or enforcement actions that may impact the organization's compliance obligations. Pay particular attention to regulatory changes implemented in the past two years, as healthcare fraud and abuse laws undergo periodic updates that must be reflected in the compliance plan. When citing legal authorities, ensure all statutory references, regulatory provisions, and official guidance documents are current and properly formatted according to legal citation standards.

## Foundational Framework and Regulatory Architecture

Draft an introduction that establishes the compliance plan as a cornerstone of the organization's commitment to ethical healthcare delivery and regulatory adherence. The opening section should articulate not merely that the organization has implemented this framework, but why such implementation reflects core institutional values and risk management priorities. Define the scope with precision, specifying which legal entities within the healthcare system are covered, which categories of personnel must comply, which types of business relationships fall under the plan's purview, and which designated health services trigger Stark Law obligations. The authority section should reference the specific board resolution, executive directive, or regulatory mandate that empowers the compliance program, including the date of adoption and any subsequent amendments.

Develop a substantive regulatory framework section that provides more than superficial summaries of the applicable laws. For the Stark Law, explain the prohibition on physician self-referrals for designated health services when financial relationships exist, but go deeper into what constitutes a \

under the regulatory definition, encompassing both ownership interests and compensation arrangements. Detail each category of designated health services with specific examples relevant to the organization's operations, such as clinical laboratory services including blood work and pathology, physical and occupational therapy services, radiology and imaging services including MRI and CT scans, radiation therapy services, and home health services. Address the strict liability nature of Stark Law violations, emphasizing that intent is irrelevant and that technical violations can result in significant penalties even when no improper purpose existed.

For the Anti-Kickback Statute, explain the criminal prohibition on offering, paying, soliciting, or receiving any remuneration to induce or reward referrals for items or services reimbursable by federal healthcare programs. Distinguish this from Stark Law by emphasizing the intent requirement—that one purpose of the remuneration must be to induce referrals—and the criminal nature of violations, which can result in imprisonment in addition to monetary penalties. Provide detailed analysis of the safe harbors most relevant to the organization's operations, explaining not just their existence but their specific requirements. For the employment safe harbor, detail the requirements that the employee be engaged for at least one year, that compensation be consistent with fair market value, that compensation not be determined in a manner that takes into account the volume or value of referrals, and that the services performed are commercially reasonable. Apply similar analytical depth to personal services arrangements, space and equipment rental safe harbors, and any other safe harbors relevant to the organization's business model.

## Risk Assessment Methodology and Identification

Establish a systematic approach to identifying and evaluating compliance risks specific to the organization's operations. Begin by examining all existing financial relationships with physicians and other potential referral sources, creating a comprehensive inventory that includes employed physicians and their compensation structures, independent contractor physicians providing services under professional services agreements, medical directors and consultants receiving stipends or hourly compensation, physicians with ownership interests in joint ventures or the organization itself, physicians leasing space or equipment from the organization, and physicians receiving recruitment incentives or relocation assistance. For each category of relationship, analyze whether the arrangement satisfies applicable Stark Law exceptions and Anti-Kickback Statute safe harbors.

Develop a risk-scoring methodology that assigns quantitative values to various risk factors, enabling the organization to prioritize compliance resources toward the highest-risk areas. Consider factors such as the volume of referrals generated by physicians in financial relationships, the dollar value of designated health services referred, whether compensation formulas contain any elements that vary with referral volume or value, whether fair market value has been independently verified within the past twelve months, and whether arrangements are documented in written agreements that satisfy regulatory requirements. Create risk categories—such as high, medium, and low—with specific criteria for each classification and corresponding monitoring frequencies.

Analyze referral patterns using quantitative methods to identify statistical outliers or unusual concentrations that may suggest compliance concerns. Examine whether certain physicians refer disproportionately high volumes compared to similarly situated practitioners, whether referral patterns changed significantly after entering into financial arrangements, whether physicians refer exclusively or predominantly to the organization despite having clinical privileges at multiple facilities, and whether designated health services are being ordered at rates inconsistent with clinical norms or patient populations. Document the analytical methodology used for referral pattern analysis, including data sources, statistical techniques, and thresholds for triggering compliance review.

## Operational Policies and Procedural Controls

Establish detailed policies that translate regulatory requirements into actionable operational procedures. Require that all financial arrangements with physicians and referral sources be reduced to writing before any services are performed or compensation is paid, with written agreements containing specific elements including a detailed description of services to be provided, the time commitment required, the compensation methodology with specific dollar amounts or formulas, the term of the arrangement with specific start and end dates, and termination provisions that comply with regulatory requirements. Implement a mandatory pre-approval process requiring that proposed arrangements be submitted to the compliance department at least thirty days before the intended effective date, allowing sufficient time for legal review, fair market value assessment, and necessary revisions.

Create a fair market value assessment protocol that provides objective verification of compensation levels. Establish thresholds requiring third-party valuation for arrangements exceeding specified dollar amounts annually, such as fifty thousand dollars, or for any arrangement with physicians who generate significant referral volume regardless of compensation level. Specify the qualifications required for valuation experts, such as relevant healthcare experience, familiarity with the geographic market, and independence from both the organization and the physician. Require that fair market value assessments consider multiple data sources including national and regional compensation surveys, local market conditions and competitive factors, the physician's qualifications and experience, the time commitment and responsibilities required, and the commercial reasonableness of the arrangement independent of referral value.

Implement referral tracking and monitoring systems that provide ongoing visibility into potential compliance risks. Establish automated reporting mechanisms that flag arrangements for compliance review when referral volumes exceed predetermined thresholds, when referral patterns change significantly from historical baselines, when new designated health services are added to the organization's offerings, or when physicians enter into new financial relationships. Create periodic review requirements mandating that all existing arrangements be reassessed at least annually to verify continued compliance as circumstances evolve, with more frequent reviews for high-risk arrangements or those approaching renewal dates.

Provide explicit guidance on prohibited practices with specific examples tailored to the organization's operations. Prohibit compensation formulas that include any component based on the volume or value of referrals, such as productivity bonuses calculated on designated health services ordered, per-click lease payments that vary with equipment usage for referred patients, or medical director stipends that increase when referral volumes rise. Forbid rental arrangements at rates that deviate from fair market value, whether above-market rates that may constitute disguised remuneration or below-market rates that provide improper benefits to referring physicians. Prohibit providing free or discounted services to physicians in positions to refer, such as complimentary laboratory testing, free medical records services, or below-cost billing and coding assistance. Establish clear restrictions on recruitment incentives, specifying maximum income guarantees, permissible relocation assistance, and documentation requirements to satisfy regulatory safe harbors.

## Education and Training Infrastructure

Design a comprehensive training program that ensures all personnel understand their specific compliance obligations and can recognize potential violations in their daily work. Require initial training for all new employees within thirty days of hire, with role-specific content tailored to job responsibilities. Provide enhanced training for personnel in high-risk functions, including physician contracting staff who negotiate and structure financial arrangements, business development personnel who identify and pursue new physician relationships, billing and coding staff who submit claims for designated health services, and compliance personnel who monitor and audit arrangements. Develop separate training modules for physicians, emphasizing their personal liability under these statutes and their obligation to disclose financial relationships that may affect referral decisions.

Structure training content to progress from foundational concepts to practical application. Begin with the basic legal framework, explaining why these laws exist and the policy concerns they address, such as overutilization of services, increased healthcare costs, and compromised medical judgment. Progress to the specific prohibitions and requirements of Stark Law and the Anti-Kickback Statute, using case studies and examples drawn from the organization's actual operations or relevant enforcement actions. Teach participants how to identify potential compliance issues in common scenarios, such as recognizing when a proposed arrangement may not satisfy an exception or safe harbor, identifying compensation formulas that improperly account for referral value, or spotting unusual referral patterns that warrant further inquiry.

Incorporate interactive elements that test comprehension and reinforce learning, such as scenario-based assessments requiring participants to analyze hypothetical arrangements, case study discussions examining real enforcement actions and their lessons, and role-playing exercises where participants practice responding to compliance concerns. Maintain detailed training records documenting participant names and roles, training dates and duration, topics covered and materials provided, assessment results demonstrating comprehension, and any follow-up training required for participants who did not achieve passing scores. Update training materials at least annually to incorporate regulatory changes, new OIG guidance, recent enforcement actions, and lessons learned from internal audits or investigations.

## Monitoring, Auditing, and Verification Systems

Establish ongoing monitoring procedures that provide continuous oversight of compliance with Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute requirements. Implement automated monitoring systems that track key compliance indicators in real-time, such as referral volumes by physician and service type, compensation payments to physicians in financial relationships, utilization rates for designated health services, and contract expiration dates requiring renewal or termination. Configure alerts that notify compliance personnel when monitoring thresholds are exceeded, enabling prompt investigation and corrective action before violations occur or escalate.

Develop comprehensive internal audit protocols that systematically examine compliance with regulatory requirements and organizational policies. Create annual audit work plans that specify the scope of review, including which arrangements will be audited, which time periods will be examined, which compliance elements will be tested, and which documentation will be reviewed. Employ risk-based sampling methodologies that focus audit resources on the highest-risk arrangements while maintaining sufficient coverage of lower-risk areas to verify overall program effectiveness. For each audited arrangement, verify that written agreements contain all required elements and satisfy applicable exceptions or safe harbors, that compensation reflects fair market value supported by appropriate documentation, that services are actually being performed as documented through time records or deliverables, that referral patterns do not suggest improper influence on medical decision-making, and that billing for designated health services complies with regulatory requirements.

Engage external auditors or specialized healthcare legal counsel periodically to provide independent assessment of the compliance program's effectiveness. External reviews should occur at least every three years, or more frequently if significant compliance issues have been identified, major regulatory changes have occurred, or the organization has undergone substantial operational changes such as mergers or acquisitions. External reviewers should assess whether policies and procedures adequately address regulatory requirements, whether monitoring and auditing activities are sufficient in scope and frequency, whether training programs effectively educate personnel on compliance obligations, whether investigation and corrective action processes function appropriately, and whether the compliance program compares favorably to industry standards and regulatory expectations.

Document all audit findings in written reports that specify the arrangements or practices examined, the compliance deficiencies identified with specific regulatory citations, the potential risk level of each finding, the recommended corrective actions with implementation timelines, and the responsible individuals or departments for remediation. Track corrective action implementation through completion, conducting follow-up verification to ensure that deficiencies have been fully remediated and that similar issues have not recurred in other areas. Create compliance dashboards that provide senior management and the board of directors with ongoing visibility into key metrics such as the number and severity of audit findings, the status of corrective action plans, training completion rates, and the volume and nature of compliance reports received through reporting mechanisms.

## Reporting Infrastructure and Non-Retaliation Protections

Establish multiple confidential reporting channels that enable employees, physicians, contractors, patients, and other stakeholders to report suspected violations or compliance concerns without fear of retaliation. Implement a compliance hotline operated by an independent third-party vendor, available twenty-four hours per day and seven days per week, with multilingual capabilities to accommodate diverse workforces. Provide alternative reporting methods for individuals who prefer different communication channels, including a dedicated compliance email address monitored by compliance personnel, a physical mailing address for written correspondence sent directly to the Compliance Officer, an online reporting portal accessible through the organization's intranet, and the option to report in person to designated compliance personnel or human resources representatives.

Communicate clearly and repeatedly that the organization strictly prohibits retaliation against anyone who reports suspected violations in good faith, regardless of whether the report is ultimately substantiated. Define retaliation broadly to include any adverse action taken because of reporting activity, such as termination or demotion, reduction in compensation or benefits, unfavorable work assignments or schedule changes, exclusion from meetings or communications, or creation of a hostile work environment. Establish disciplinary consequences for retaliatory conduct up to and including termination of employment, and ensure that managers and supervisors receive specific training on non-retaliation obligations. Publicize reporting mechanisms and non-retaliation protections through multiple channels including initial and annual training programs, posted notices in employee areas and on organizational intranets, employee handbooks and policy manuals, and periodic communications from senior leadership emphasizing the importance of speaking up.

Implement procedures for receiving, logging, and triaging compliance reports to ensure prompt and appropriate response. Require that all reports be immediately documented in a centralized compliance log capturing the date and time of the report, the reporting channel used, the identity of the reporter if disclosed, a summary of the allegations or concerns, and the initial risk assessment and triage decision. Establish criteria for assessing report severity and determining appropriate response, such as immediate investigation for reports alleging ongoing violations with significant financial or patient safety implications, expedited investigation for reports suggesting systemic compliance failures, standard investigation for reports of isolated potential violations, or referral to other departments for reports involving non-compliance matters such as human resources or operational issues.

## Investigation Protocols and Remediation Procedures

Define comprehensive procedures for investigating reported compliance concerns or audit findings to ensure thorough, objective, and timely resolution. Begin each investigation with an immediate assessment to determine whether interim protective measures are necessary, such as suspending questionable arrangements pending investigation, restricting access to systems or information, or placing individuals on administrative leave when circumstances warrant. Assign investigations to qualified personnel with appropriate expertise and independence, engaging external legal counsel for matters involving potential criminal violations, significant financial exposure, or situations where internal conflicts of interest may compromise objectivity.

Conduct investigations according to established protocols that ensure thoroughness and consistency. Develop investigation plans that specify the scope of inquiry, the information and documentation to be gathered, the individuals to be interviewed, the timeline for completion, and the standards for evaluating findings. Gather relevant documentation systematically, including written agreements and amendments, compensation records and payment histories, referral data and utilization reports, fair market value assessments and supporting analyses, and correspondence related to the arrangement. Interview witnesses using structured protocols, documenting their statements contemporaneously and providing opportunities to review and correct interview summaries. Analyze findings against applicable legal requirements, determining whether violations of Stark Law, the Anti-Kickback Statute, or organizational policies have occurred.

Document investigation findings in written reports that provide sufficient detail to support conclusions and recommended actions. Investigation reports should summarize the allegations or concerns that triggered the investigation, describe the investigative methodology and information sources, present factual findings supported by documentary evidence and witness statements, analyze whether violations occurred with specific regulatory citations, assess the severity and scope of any violations identified, and recommend specific corrective actions with implementation timelines. Present investigation reports to appropriate decision-makers, such as the Compliance Officer, senior management, or the board of directors, depending on the severity and nature of findings.

Implement corrective actions that are proportionate to the violations identified and designed to prevent recurrence. When violations are substantiated, consider the full range of remedial measures including terminating non-compliant arrangements immediately or restructuring them to satisfy regulatory requirements, recovering overpayments or improper remuneration through repayment demands or offset against future compensation, disciplining responsible individuals through counseling, suspension, termination, or referral for professional sanctions, enhancing policies or controls to address systemic weaknesses that contributed to violations, and self-disclosing to government authorities when required by law or when voluntary disclosure may mitigate penalties. Develop corrective action plans that specify each remedial step to be taken, assign responsibility for implementation to specific individuals or departments, establish deadlines for completion of each action, and define metrics for measuring effectiveness. Conduct follow-up monitoring to verify that corrective actions have been fully implemented and that similar violations have not recurred, documenting verification activities and results in the compliance files.

## Documentation Standards and Record Management

Establish comprehensive documentation requirements that create a complete compliance record for all financial arrangements with physicians and referral sources. Require that every arrangement be supported by a written agreement executed before services commence or compensation is paid, containing specific mandatory elements including the identities of the parties with complete legal names and addresses, a detailed description of the services to be provided with specific deliverables or responsibilities, the time commitment required expressed in hours per week or month, the compensation methodology with specific dollar amounts or objective formulas, the term of the arrangement with specific start and end dates, termination provisions that comply with regulatory requirements such as notice periods, and attestations that compensation reflects fair market value and is not determined based on referral volume or value.

Maintain centralized compliance files for each arrangement containing all relevant documentation in organized, readily accessible format. Compliance files should include the executed agreement and all amendments or modifications, fair market value analyses with supporting data sources and methodologies, board or committee approvals with meeting minutes reflecting the approval decision, compliance reviews and certifications documenting regulatory analysis, evidence of services actually rendered such as time records, reports, or deliverables, compensation records showing all payments made, and correspondence related to the arrangement including negotiation communications and annual review documentation. Implement version control procedures that track changes to agreements over time, maintaining superseded versions to provide complete historical records.

Establish document retention policies that comply with federal requirements and support the organization's ability to defend against potential government investigations or qui tam actions. Retain all compliance-related records for at least ten years from the date of last service or payment, or longer if required by state law or if litigation or investigation is pending or reasonably anticipated. Implement secure storage systems with appropriate access controls that protect confidential information while ensuring availability for legitimate compliance purposes, such as password-protected electronic repositories with role-based access permissions, locked physical storage for paper records with sign-out logs, and backup systems that prevent loss due to technical failures or disasters. Create document management protocols that facilitate efficient retrieval when needed for compliance monitoring, internal audits, external reviews, or government inquiries, such as standardized naming conventions, indexed filing systems, and search capabilities for electronic records.

## Governance Structure and Continuous Improvement

Designate a Compliance Officer with appropriate authority, resources, and organizational positioning to implement and oversee this compliance plan effectively. The Compliance Officer should possess relevant expertise in healthcare regulatory compliance, including knowledge of Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute requirements, and should have sufficient seniority and independence to challenge business decisions that pose compliance risks. Establish reporting lines that provide the Compliance Officer with direct access to senior management and the board of directors, enabling escalation of significant compliance issues without interference from operational leadership who may have conflicting interests. Allocate adequate resources to the compliance function, including sufficient staffing to conduct monitoring and auditing activities, budget for external consultants and legal counsel when needed, and technology systems to support compliance activities.

Create a Compliance Committee that provides oversight and strategic direction for the compliance program, comprising representatives from key organizational functions such as legal counsel, finance, operations, medical staff leadership, and human resources. The Compliance Committee should meet at least quarterly to review compliance program activities, assess audit findings and investigation results, evaluate the effectiveness of corrective actions, consider regulatory developments and their implications, and recommend program enhancements. Document all Compliance Committee meetings through detailed minutes that record attendance, matters discussed, decisions made, and action items assigned, maintaining these records as part of the compliance program documentation.

Conduct comprehensive annual reviews of the compliance plan to assess its effectiveness and identify opportunities for improvement. Annual reviews should evaluate whether policies and procedures remain current with regulatory requirements, whether monitoring and auditing activities are detecting compliance issues effectively, whether training programs are achieving desired learning outcomes, whether reporting mechanisms are being utilized and producing actionable information, and whether the compliance program compares favorably to industry standards and regulatory expectations such as OIG compliance program guidance. Analyze compliance metrics and trends to identify systemic issues or emerging risks, such as increasing audit findings in particular areas, recurring types of compliance reports, or changes in referral patterns that may indicate program weaknesses.

Update the compliance plan promptly when significant regulatory developments occur, such as new or revised Stark Law exceptions or Anti-Kickback Statute safe harbors, final rules or regulations from CMS or OIG, advisory opinions or other guidance addressing novel arrangements, or enforcement actions that clarify regulatory interpretation or establish new compliance expectations. Establish a regulatory monitoring process that tracks relevant legal developments through subscriptions to regulatory updates, participation in industry associations, and consultation with specialized healthcare legal counsel. When plan updates are necessary, follow formal amendment procedures that include drafting revised provisions, obtaining legal review to ensure regulatory compliance, securing approval from the Compliance Committee and board of directors, and communicating changes to all affected personnel through training and policy distributions.

Benchmark the organization's compliance program against industry standards and regulatory expectations to ensure it reflects best practices and evolving compliance norms. Compare program elements to OIG compliance program guidance for healthcare organizations, industry standards published by professional associations such as the Health Care Compliance Association, and compliance programs of peer organizations to the extent information is available. Consider engaging external consultants periodically to conduct gap analyses that identify areas where the program could be strengthened, providing objective assessment and recommendations for enhancement. Document all benchmarking activities and resulting program improvements, demonstrating ongoing commitment to compliance excellence and continuous improvement.

## Drafting Execution and Quality Standards

Throughout the document, maintain a professional tone appropriate for a regulatory compliance document that may be reviewed by government auditors, enforcement attorneys, or judicial officers in the event of litigation. Use precise legal terminology that accurately reflects statutory and regulatory language, while ensuring the document remains accessible to non-lawyer personnel who must implement its requirements in daily operations. Avoid vague or aspirational language in favor of specific, actionable requirements that enable personnel to understand exactly what is expected of them, such as \
rather than \

Cite to specific legal authorities throughout the document to demonstrate the regulatory foundation for each requirement and to facilitate future updates when laws change. Include complete citations to statutory provisions such as 42 U.S.C. § 1395nn for Stark Law and 42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b) for the Anti-Kickback Statute, regulatory provisions such as 42 C.F.R. § 411.357 for Stark Law exceptions and 42 C.F.R. § 1001.952 for Anti-Kickback safe harbors, and official guidance such as OIG advisory opinions, CMS frequently asked questions, and preambles to final rules. Ensure all legal references reflect the most current versions of laws and regulations, verifying currency through authoritative sources.

Ensure internal consistency across all sections of the compliance plan, with cross-references where policies in one section relate to procedures described elsewhere. For example, when the risk assessment section identifies high-risk arrangements requiring enhanced monitoring, cross-reference the specific monitoring procedures described in the auditing section. When the training section requires role-specific education, cross-reference the operational procedures that define those roles and their compliance obligations. Create a table of contents that facilitates navigation and enables users to quickly locate relevant provisions, and consider including an index of key terms and concepts for complex or lengthy plans.

The final document should serve multiple purposes simultaneously: as a practical operational guide that personnel can consult when questions arise in daily work, as a training resource that educates stakeholders on compliance obligations, as an audit tool that provides standards against which compliance can be measured, and as a demonstration of good faith compliance efforts that may mitigate penalties in the event of government investigation or enforcement action. Structure the document to support these varied uses through clear organization, comprehensive coverage of regulatory requirements, specific operational procedures, and evidence of thoughtful risk assessment and program design.

content.name: State Charity Filing Threshold Research
content.summary: Guides legal professionals and compliance teams through a repeatable, citation-backed research protocol to identify state-specific charitable solicitation filing requirements keyed to gross revenue. Extracts and normalizes audit and financial-statement thresholds, sliding-scale filing fees, and fiscal-year-based due dates across all target jurisdictions, producing a structured state-by-state compliance matrix with full source documentation.

# State Charity Filing Threshold Research

**Skill slug:** @state-charity-filing-threshold-research
**Version:** 1.0
**Audience:** Attorneys, paralegals, and compliance teams supporting charitable solicitation registrations and renewals
**Use case:** Build or update a state-by-state matrix of financial-statement requirements and filing fees driven by gross revenue and fiscal year end

---

## Assumptions Used

1. **Filing type in scope:** Charitable solicitation **registration/renewal** filing (not corporate annual report; not IRS filings). If a state couples these, we capture solicitation-related requirements and note cross-links.
2. **Entity type in scope:** A **501(c)(3) charitable organization** (not a professional fundraiser, professional solicitor, or commercial co-venturer). Those regimes are out of scope unless added at Checkpoint B.
3. **Revenue driver:** Thresholds are keyed to a revenue concept that varies by state (e.g., \

). **Default approach:** capture the state's defined term verbatim and map it to a standardized field.
4. **Financial basis:** Thresholds are calculated based on the organization's most recent completed fiscal year financials.
5. **Currency standard:** Rules are treated as current if **verified within the last 90 days**. Older verification is flagged.
6. **No legal advice:** This skill supports research and drafting; it does not replace jurisdiction-specific legal counsel.

---

## Open Items / Needed Inputs

If you do not provide these, the skill proceeds using defaults in Phase 0.

- [ ] Jurisdictions in scope (one state, a list, or all registration states)
- [ ] Organization's gross revenue / total contributions (per Form 990)
- [ ] Fiscal year end date
- [ ] Entity category (public charity, private foundation, religious organization, educational institution)
- [ ] Revenue basis preference for modeling (GAAP total revenue vs. contributions vs. total support)
- [ ] Desired output format (memo, spreadsheet, CSV, JSON)
- [ ] Whether to include: exemptions, extensions, penalties/late fees, filing portals, professional fundraiser rules

---

## Phase 0: Minimum-Input Alignment

### Checkpoint A: Pre-Draft Intake Snapshot

**Confirm or edit these parameters (defaults provided):**

| # | Parameter | Default | Assumption |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Jurisdictions** | All 41 registration states + DC | Comprehensive national compliance map |
| 2 | **Filing scope** | Charitable solicitation annual renewal/financial report | Not initial registration |
| 3 | **Entity scope** | 501(c)(3) charitable organization | Not professional fundraiser/solicitor |
| 4 | **Gross revenue** | $1,000,000 | Illustrative; triggers audit requirements in many major jurisdictions |
| 5 | **Fiscal year end** | December 31 | Calendar year |
| 6 | **Revenue basis** | Capture state-defined measure verbatim; map to Form 990 Part VIII where possible | Preserves legal nuance |
| 7 | **Output mode** | Mode 1: Full Compliance Package | Includes matrix, citations, normalization, memo |

**Proceeding assumptions if no response:** Use the defaults above and produce templates plus illustrative completed records for CA, NY, IL, FL, PA, and MA.

**Related skills:**
- @legal-research-primary-source-citation-check — primary source validation
- @statutory-definition-mapping — align \

definitions across jurisdictions
- @charity-registration-master — actual filing process and forms
- @nonprofit-governance-audit-committee — board-level audit policies that may impose lower thresholds than state mandates

---

## Phase 1: Source Scoping & Research Plan

### Objective
Identify authoritative sources and a repeatable search path for each state so extraction is consistent and defensible.

### Deliverables
1. Per-State Source Map
2. Reusable Search Query Set
3. Document Capture Plan (audit trail)

### 1.1 Per-State Source Map

For each state, identify the regulator, controlling law, and key documents.

| Field | Entry (per state) |
|---|---|
| **State** | |
| **Regulator / Agency** | (e.g., Attorney General Charities Bureau; Secretary of State) |
| **Statute citation** | (code + section) |
| **Regulation citation** | (admin code title + section, if any) |
| **Filing form(s)** | (name/number + link) |
| **Instruction booklet** | (link) |
| **Fee schedule page** | (link) |
| **Due date authority** | (statute/reg or instructions) |
| **Last verified (date)** | YYYY-MM-DD |
| **Notes** | (exemptions, special categories, unified filing portals) |

### 1.2 Reusable Search Queries

Use jurisdiction name + key phrases:
- `[State] charitable solicitation renewal audit requirement gross revenue`
- `[State] financial statement review compilation threshold charitable organization`
- `[State] charitable organization annual report filing fee schedule`
- `[State] due date fiscal year end charitable solicitation annual report extension`

**Primary-source-first rule:** Prefer code/regulation text over FAQ summaries. If only an agency FAQ states a threshold, capture it but flag as \

### 1.3 Document Capture Plan

- Save **PDF copies** of instructions and fee schedules.
- Record **URLs + access date** for every source.
- Capture **quoted excerpts** for each threshold and fee tier.

### Phase 1 Checklist
- [ ] Regulator and official program page identified for each state
- [ ] Controlling statute(s) located
- [ ] Controlling regulation(s) located, if any
- [ ] Current renewal/annual report form and instructions located
- [ ] Fee schedule authority and current schedule located
- [ ] Last verified date and effective date recorded

---

## Phase 2: Primary-Source Extraction

### Objective
Extract four required rule categories—audit thresholds, review/compilation thresholds, filing fees, and due dates—with precise citations and definitional notes.

### Deliverables
1. State Revenue Definition Comparison Table
2. Per-State Rule Record (audit, review, compilation, fees, due dates)

### 2.1 Revenue Definition Comparison

Not all states define \

the same way. This table captures critical definitional differences.

| State | Revenue Definition Trigger | Exclusions / Inclusions | Form 990 Line Reference | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **California** | Gross Revenue ($2M+) | Excludes grants from gov. agencies and certain trust funds | Part VIII, Line 12 | RRF-1 instructions define \

|
| **New York** | Total Revenue ($1M+) | Includes all support and revenue | Part VIII, Line 12 | CHAR500 instructions; specific triggers for Public Support |
| **Illinois** | Contributions ($300K+) | Focuses on contributions only, not total revenue | Part VIII, Line 1h | AG-990-IL |
| **Florida** | Contributions ($500K+) | Sliding scale based on contributions only | Part VIII, Line 1h | CH-1 instructions |
| **Massachusetts** | Gross Support & Revenue ($500K+) | One of the lower thresholds nationally | Part VIII, Line 12 | Form PC |
| **Pennsylvania** | Total Revenue ($750K+) | Compiled statements below $250K | Part VIII, Line 12 | BCO-10 instructions |
| **Georgia** | Total Revenue ($1M+) | Review required $500K–$1M | Part VIII, Line 12 | C-100 instructions |

> **Action:** Map your Form 990 Part VIII (Revenue) figures to each state's specific definition. Do not assume \

means the same thing across states.

### 2.2 Per-State Rule Record Template

Complete this table for each state in scope.

### 2.3 Illustrative Audit Threshold Matrix

| Jurisdiction | Independent Audit Threshold | Review Threshold | Compilation / Unaudited | Key Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **California** | ≥ $2,000,000 | N/A (no review tier) | Below $2M: unaudited OK | Audit by independent CPA; uses \

|
| **New York** | ≥ $1,000,000 | $250K – $1M | Below $250K: unaudited OK | Thresholds updated recently; CHAR500 |
| **Georgia** | ≥ $1,000,000 | $500K – $1M | Below $500K: compilation OK | C-100 |
| **Massachusetts** | ≥ $500,000 | $200K – $500K | Below $200K: unaudited OK | Among lowest national thresholds |
| **Pennsylvania** | ≥ $750,000 | $250K – $750K | Below $250K: compiled OK | BCO-10 |
| **Illinois** | ≥ $300,000 (contributions) | $25K – $300K | Below $25K: unaudited OK | Uses \

content.name: State Merit Review Analysis
content.summary: This skill guides the analysis of state merit review for securities offerings that are not covered securities under NSMIA, focusing on NASAA-influenced scrutiny of cheap stock, promoter's equity investment, inequitable voting rights, and promoter compensation. It provides a structured workflow for confirming merit review applicability, mapping state-specific standards, performing quantitative and qualitative analyses of capitalization and governance terms, and drafting examiner-ready comment responses. The skill embeds anti-hallucination guardrails requiring verified legal citations and emphasizes professional responsibility duties and attorney supervision for all regulator-facing submissions.
content.content:
# State Merit Review Analysis: Navigating NASAA Statements of Policy for Non-Covered Securities

## 1. Opening Context

This skill provides the analytical framework and drafting guidance necessary to navigate state \
during a securities offering. In the United States, securities offerings that are not \

under the National Securities Markets Improvement Act of 1996 (NSMIA), codified at 15 U.S.C. § 77r, are subject to the concurrent jurisdiction of state securities regulators under what is commonly called \
law. Unlike the SEC's primarily disclosure-based regime—ensuring that all material facts are told—many states exercise \
jurisdiction. This means the state administrator has the statutory authority to deny, condition, or delay a securities registration if the substantive terms of the deal are deemed \

to investors. Offerings commonly subject to merit review include Regulation A (Tier 1 and Tier 2) offerings marketed to non-accredited investors in merit states, Rule 504 offerings, intrastate offerings, and direct public offerings not listed on a national exchange.\n\nExecuting this work poorly can result in a stop order, forced restructuring, or withdrawal from key jurisdictions—effectively killing or delaying a capital raise. A competent attorney must do more than provide adequate disclosure; they must proactively analyze the issuer's capital structure against the North American Securities Administrators Association (NASAA) Statements of Policy (SOPs), which function as the shared analytical vocabulary—though not a uniform rulebook—of state merit review. High-quality execution involves identifying \

early in the drafting process, such as excessive cheap stock, inequitable voting rights, or inadequate promoter investment, and either restructuring the deal or preparing persuasive responses that justify the terms. This skill transforms the raw data of a capitalization table and corporate charter into a sophisticated Blue Sky compliance and negotiation strategy.

The work product serves three core objectives. First, it helps counsel determine whether to restructure the offering to avoid or minimize merit review exposure. Second, it allows counsel to pre-empt examiner objections by aligning terms with state expectations at the outset. Third, it enables efficient, persuasive comment responses that protect the issuer's economics without triggering new issues or inconsistencies across the disclosure package.

This workflow is governed by the state securities statute and regulations in the relevant jurisdiction(s), NASAA SOPs to the extent adopted or used as guidance by those states, the offering exemption or registration pathway selected, and professional responsibility duties including competence, candor to regulators, and confidentiality. Because state merit review is inherently jurisdiction-specific and policy-driven, this skill embeds anti-hallucination guardrails: any citation to a statute, regulation, order, NASAA policy text, or state guidance must be verified via web research or explicitly flagged for attorney confirmation before use. Under no circumstances should the output include invented case citations, fabricated policy quotations, or unverified statutory section numbers.

## 2. Understanding the Context and Purpose

State merit review exists to protect retail investors from \

deals where insiders take minimal risk while the public bears the brunt of the capital requirements. While the SEC ensures the investor knows the terms through disclosure, merit states aim to prevent substantively unfair terms from occurring in the first place. The work product typically manifests during the pre-effective phase of an offering, often in response to a comment letter from a state examiner, though the most effective practice is to conduct the analysis before filing to shape the offering terms proactively.

The strategic objective is to secure clearance in as many target jurisdictions as possible without compromising the issuer's fundamental business goals. The primary external audience is the state securities examiner, a regulatory attorney whose mandate is consumer protection. To succeed, counsel must speak the language of the NASAA SOPs, which function as the common analytical framework of state merit review. The immediate internal audience is the deal team—partner, issuer counsel, and sometimes underwriter counsel—who needs a candid risk assessment and a plan to get cleared.

Strategically, remember that merit review is negotiation. Your response to an examiner should be credible and transparent, solution-oriented, and disciplined—offering only the concessions necessary and avoiding \

in ways that impair the issuer or set adverse precedents for other states. Failing to account for NASAA standards early can lead to costly pivots, such as being forced to place founder stock in escrow or amend the company's bylaws to eliminate disparate voting rights days before a planned launch.

Scope boundary: this skill covers merit review analysis and drafting of written responses to examiner comments focused on cheap stock, voting rights, and promoter's equity and compensation. It does not cover full Blue Sky registration form preparation, federal securities law drafting beyond what is needed to contextualize covered versus non-covered status, broker-dealer or agent licensing analysis, or oral advocacy in calls with examiners—though the negotiation strategy section can inform those activities.

## 3. Prerequisites and Information Gathering

Before beginning the substantive analysis, the LLM must collect and review the following materials. The LLM should explicitly prompt the user for any item that is missing before proceeding, because state examiners will cross-check numbers and terms across the full package.

The core document set includes: the most recent draft of the offering document (prospectus, offering circular on Form 1-A, or private placement memorandum) and all exhibits; the issuer's charter documents (certificate or articles of incorporation, any certificates of designation, bylaws or operating agreement) and amendments; a detailed capitalization table showing all issuances of equity, options, warrants, SAFEs, and convertible instruments since inception, including dates, prices paid, consideration type, vesting terms, and holder identity categorized as \
or \

; a chronology of issuances with supporting documentation (board consents, subscription agreements, service agreements for equity grants); all promoter, founder, and insider compensation arrangements including cash compensation, equity grants, consulting agreements, related-party contracts, loans, and reimbursements; selling compensation terms (underwriter agreement, placement agent agreement, finder agreements, warrants, expense reimbursement); and historical financials (audited or reviewed balance sheets) to determine the equity investment of promoters.

Additional required information includes: the list of target states and the filing pathway in each (registration by qualification, coordination, or notification, or exemption notice), with expected timelines and any known examiner pre-clearance practices; any prior examiner correspondence, deficiency letters, or comment letters; the federal exemption or registration being used (Reg A Tier 1 or 2, Reg D Rule 504, intrastate offering, direct registration, or other); and the type of issuer entity (corporation, LLC, or other).

The LLM should also ask targeted questions to surface merit triggers that are often not obvious from the offering document alone: whether any shares were issued for nominal cash or services (\

), whether promoters received equity disproportionate to their cash or tangible asset contributions, whether any voting or control rights deviate materially from economic ownership, whether offering proceeds will repay insiders, whether there are contingencies (reverse splits, conversions) that change the economics at closing, and whether any state has already informally flagged issues.\n\nCritically, if the LLM cannot confirm whether the securities are \

under NSMIA, it should pause and request attorney direction rather than assume. The covered-security determination is the threshold question that controls whether this entire analysis is necessary.

## 4. Step-by-Step Process

### Step 1: Confirm the Filing Posture and Whether Merit Review Applies

The first step is to determine definitively whether merit review applies. Under 15 U.S.C. § 77r, \

are exempt from state substantive review (though states retain anti-fraud authority and may require notice filings with fees). The LLM must analyze whether the offering qualifies as covered—for example, because the securities are listed on a national exchange (NYSE, NASDAQ), sold only to \

as defined by the SEC, or issued under a federal exemption that preempts state law such as Rule 506(b) or 506(c) of Regulation D.

If the offering is not a covered security—as is typically the case for Regulation A offerings seeking broad state clearance, Rule 504 offerings, intrastate offerings, and direct public offerings not listed on a national exchange—the LLM must then categorize the target states into merit review jurisdictions and disclosure-only jurisdictions. Do not rely on memory for this classification; verify via the state regulator's website or NASAA resources and include source URLs in the analysis.

If the offering is intended to be covered but is at risk of losing that status due to a technical defect—such as general solicitation issues for Rule 506(b), bad actor disqualification under Rule 506(d), or integration problems—flag that as a gating risk because losing covered status mid-process can trigger sudden merit review exposure in states where notice-only filings had been planned.

The LLM should produce a short posture memo paragraph for the file stating the assumed pathway and why merit review applies, with verified citations. For example: \

### Step 2: Map the States and Identify Controlling Merit Standards and NASAA Policy Touchpoints

Once merit review is confirmed, treat the task as a jurisdictional mapping exercise. States vary significantly in how directly they incorporate NASAA SOPs, and many have idiosyncratic \

communicated through examiner practice, interpretive guidance, or conditioning orders. The goal is to produce a state-by-state assessment identifying what each state prioritizes, what standards it cites (statute, regulation, or NASAA policy), and what remedies it commonly requires.\n\nFor each target state, verify: the statutory standard for denial or conditioning (commonly \

or similar language, often found in the state's version of the Uniform Securities Act at Section 306 or its equivalent); the registration method and its typical merit review intensity; and any explicit adoption of or reference to the NASAA SOPs relevant here—particularly the NASAA Statement of Policy Regarding Promotional Shares (Cheap Stock), the NASAA Statement of Policy Regarding Promoter's Equity Investment, and the NASAA Statement of Policy on Unequal Voting Rights.

The coordinated review process is an important procedural tool. If available for the offering type, the NASAA Coordinated Review program (such as the CR-3(b) process for Regulation A offerings) allows one lead merit state to negotiate on behalf of all participating states, preventing the issuer from fighting separate battles in twenty jurisdictions simultaneously. The LLM should identify whether coordinated review is available and recommend its use where appropriate.

Be aware of key state-specific divergences. California, for example, does not strictly follow all NASAA SOPs but instead applies its own standards under the California Corporate Securities Law of 1968, with specific provisions such as those in California Code of Regulations Title 10, Section 260.140 and related subsections addressing promoter's equity. Texas is known as a strict merit state that pays particular attention to affiliated transactions, requiring demonstration that related-party transactions are on terms as favorable as those available from unaffiliated third parties. Washington State applies specific scrutiny to developmental-stage companies and may require impoundment of proceeds (escrowing funds raised until a minimum threshold is met) if the company has no revenue or near-term path to profitability.

When citing any NASAA SOP or state-specific standard, the LLM must verify the text via web research and include a URL to the authoritative source. If the LLM cannot find an authoritative source after reasonable research, it must flag the point for attorney verification and recommend contacting the examiner or engaging local counsel.

### Step 3: Perform the Cheap Stock Analysis

Cheap stock is one of the most frequent merit review flashpoints. NASAA defines cheap stock as equity issued to promoters for a price substantially lower than the proposed public offering price, typically within a 36-month look-back period preceding the filing. The concern is that insiders are getting a \
on the capital provided by the public, creating unfair dilution.\n\nThe analysis must be both quantitative and qualitative. On the quantitative side, identify all \

as defined for merit review purposes—officers, directors, holders of 5% or more of the outstanding securities, or anyone providing services in exchange for equity. Calculate the dilutive effect by comparing the price paid by promoters to the public offering price. Reconstruct a clean chronology of issuances and compute effective prices per share or unit, including any built-in discounts via conversion terms, warrants, or liquidation preferences. Tie this to the anticipated offering price and post-money ownership percentages.\n\nOn the qualitative side, assess whether the issuer can justify the price disparity—through early-stage risk borne at the time of issuance, services actually rendered and documented, vesting schedules and lock-up restrictions, repurchase rights, or performance milestones. The key examiner question is: \
\n\nRemedies commonly requested in merit review practice include: escrow of promotional shares until performance milestones are met (the \

typically lasting until the company hits specific earnings milestones or for a period of several years); contractual lock-ups restricting resale for a defined period; cancellations or reverse splits to reduce promotional overhang; conditioning that a portion of proceeds be used for business operations rather than insider repayment; and enhanced dilution disclosure quantifying the impact on new investors. The LLM should not assert that any specific remedy is \

unless verified for the particular state; instead, describe remedies as commonly requested and flag specific state requirements for verification.\n\nA common mistake is failing to include shares issued for intangible property or past services in the cheap stock calculation. Examiners will look through consulting agreements and advisory arrangements to find hidden cheap stock. Another common error is presenting capitalization tables that do not reconcile to charter authority, omitting derivative securities, or relying on conclusory \

explanations without supporting evidence such as board consents, subscription agreements, and service descriptions.\n\nWhen responding to an examiner's cheap stock comment, the most effective approach combines transparency with targeted mitigation. For example: \

This is illustrative; the specific remedy must be confirmed as acceptable under the applicable state's practice.

### Step 4: Analyze Promoter's Equity Investment

The NASAA Statement of Policy on Promoter's Equity Investment requires that founders have sufficient \

The standard is generally that promoters' equity—calculated as cash and tangible assets contributed minus liabilities—should represent a meaningful percentage of the total aggregate offering price. While the specific threshold can vary by state and offering type, a commonly referenced benchmark is that promoter investment should be at least 10% of the total aggregate offering price.

For example, if a company is raising $10 million, the promoters should generally have at least $1 million in hard equity in the company. If their cash investment is only $100,000, the examiner will likely issue a comment regarding inadequate promoter investment. Beyond mere identification of the shortfall, the analysis should calculate the promoter's equity using the NASAA methodology (not general accounting principles), which focuses on cash and tangible assets rather than imputed value of services or goodwill.

Strategic responses to inadequate promoter investment comments should emphasize tangible assets contributed (equipment, inventory, proprietary software with a formal third-party valuation) rather than relying solely on the cash figure reflected on the balance sheet. If the promoter has personally guaranteed significant corporate debt, that fact should be presented as additional evidence of economic alignment, though states vary in whether guarantees count toward the equity calculation. The LLM should verify the specific state's position on what counts toward the promoter's equity calculation before making this argument.

This analysis connects directly to the cheap stock analysis: excessive cheap stock combined with inadequate promoter cash investment is the combination most likely to generate serious examiner resistance, because it signals that insiders are taking economic value without bearing commensurate risk.

### Step 5: Evaluate Voting Rights, Control Features, and Governance Terms

Merit review frequently focuses on governance as a fairness issue, especially when the offering is marketed to retail investors. State regulators are skeptical of dual-class voting structures where the public receives non-voting or limited-voting shares while founders retain control through super-voting shares. The NASAA SOP on Unequal Voting Rights generally provides that offerings should not involve voting rights that are not proportionate to equity interest, unless the issuer can demonstrate a compelling business justification.

The analysis should proceed by reviewing the charter documents for any weighted voting provisions, provisions allowing a minority of shareholders to elect a majority of the board, \

preferred stock provisions that allow the board to create new classes with superior rights without shareholder approval, and negative covenants (or the absence thereof) ensuring the public has the right to vote on fundamental changes such as mergers, liquidations, and asset sales.

A critical mistake is assuming that because the SEC and major exchanges permit dual-class structures (as is common in Silicon Valley technology companies), merit states will accept them. They generally will not for small issuers in retail offerings. The analysis must assess what a state administrator could deem inequitable and then propose drafting or structural changes to reduce that risk.

Mitigation strategies include: drafting sunset provisions that convert super-voting shares to common shares upon certain events (e.g., the founder's departure, a specified number of years post-offering, or a transfer to a non-permitted holder); adding independent director requirements; ensuring class votes on major transactions; and providing enhanced plain-English disclosure of the governance structure and its implications for public investors. These mitigations should be presented to the examiner as affirmative protections, not grudging concessions.

The offering document's \

section must align precisely with the actual charter and bylaws. Examiners will compare them, and any discrepancy will undermine credibility.

### Step 6: Assess Promoter Compensation and Related-Party Transactions

Promoter compensation analysis extends beyond founder equity to encompass the full picture of insider economic extraction: consulting fees, employment compensation, transaction bonuses, loans from the company, related-party leases, IP assignment payments, and reimbursements. The question is whether insiders are extracting value in ways that a state may deem excessive relative to investor capital and business needs.

Build a comprehensive schedule of promoter and insider benefits, then connect these to the use of proceeds. If offering proceeds will repay insiders—whether through loan repayment, deferred compensation, or related-party transaction payments—that must be prominently disclosed and may require conditioning or caps under some states' merit practices. Texas, for example, requires demonstration that affiliated transactions are on terms as favorable as arm's-length transactions with unrelated parties.

The most persuasive response framework quantifies the total promoter take in both absolute dollars and as a percentage of capitalization, justifies it with concrete contributions and restrictions, and offers targeted concessions if needed—such as deferring consulting fees until minimum proceeds are raised, capping reimbursements, or escrowing promotional shares. Avoid agreeing to broad conditions (such as blanket escrow of all insider shares) without assessing downstream effects on employee incentives, future financing rounds, and tax consequences.

Be aware that the definition of \

for merit review purposes can be broader than expected. Examiners may view any control person, significant consultant, or paid finder as a promoter depending on the facts. The LLM should identify all persons who could arguably be classified as promoters and ensure their compensation is fully disclosed and analyzed.

### Step 7: Draft the Examiner-Ready Comment Response Package

The response letter is both advocacy and negotiation. It should be organized, respectful, and grounded in the record. It should not read like a litigation brief, but it must be legally literate and precise. The package typically includes: a cover letter responding point-by-point to each examiner comment, a redline of the offering document showing all revisions, and supporting exhibits (revised charter provisions, escrow or lock-up agreements, updated capitalization table, selling compensation details).

The response should open with a short global paragraph acknowledging the jurisdiction's authority and summarizing the overall approach to the comments. Then address each examiner comment by quoting it verbatim and responding beneath it. The response structure for each comment should: cite the specific NASAA SOP or state administrative code section that establishes the legal standard; explain how the issuer's facts meet the requirement or why a deviation is justified; and describe the proposed remedy, specifying precisely what change was made and where in the offering document (with page and section references).

Where the issuer agrees to a change, the redline must reflect it and any required agreements must be attached in final or near-final form. Where the issuer disagrees or proposes an alternative, provide a reasoned explanation tied to investor protection and fairness, and offer an intermediate position—such as enhanced disclosure rather than restructuring, or a narrower lock-up rather than full escrow.

Every factual assertion must be supported by a cite to the record (capitalization table, agreements, board minutes) and every legal assertion must have a verified citation or be flagged for attorney verification. The response letter is the external-facing document; keep negotiating positions, candid risk assessments, and privileged strategy in internal memoranda.

Adversarial awareness is paramount: the examiner will test internal consistency across all documents. If the response says promotional shares are restricted, the restriction must appear in a binding agreement and be described consistently in the offering document. If the response says no selling compensation is paid, there cannot be a consulting arrangement that functions as disguised selling compensation.

### Step 8: Develop a Negotiation Plan with Fallback Positions

Merit review frequently involves iterative bargaining. A skilled lawyer enters that negotiation with a prioritized list of what terms are non-negotiable for the business, what concessions are acceptable, and what alternative structures could satisfy the examiner without undermining the capital raise.

For each major issue area (cheap stock, promoter investment, voting rights, promoter compensation), the LLM should recommend a primary position and one or two fallbacks. Anchor each position in an investor-protection narrative, market practice for comparable offerings (flagging assertions about market norms for verification unless a credible source can be cited), and practical enforceability. For example, if asked to escrow founder shares, a fallback might be a time-based lock-up plus a contractual repurchase right upon bad acts, combined with enhanced dilution disclosure. If asked to eliminate super-voting, a fallback might be a sunset clause and independent director covenant.

Critical considerations for the negotiation plan include: cross-state consistency, because a concession in one state may require updating disclosures for all states and investors; the risk that conceding early without knowing other states' positions may create unnecessary constraints; and the practical reality that agreeing to conditions conflicting with charter law or that are operationally impossible to administer will create problems rather than solve them.

## 5. Critical Legal Standards and Compliance

This work implicates several professional responsibility obligations. Under Model Rule 1.1 (Competence), an attorney must understand the interplay between federal preemption and state jurisdiction; filing in a merit state without conducting a NASAA SOP audit may violate the duty of competence. Model Rule 1.3 (Diligence) requires timely responses to examiner comments, as delays can trigger automatic withdrawal in some states. Model Rule 1.4 (Communication) requires ensuring the client understands the business impact of proposed concessions before agreeing to them. Model Rule 1.6 (Confidentiality) protects drafts, capitalization tables, and internal regulator strategy. Rules 1.7 through 1.9 on conflicts of interest are implicated where counsel represents the issuer and also has relationships with promoters, placement agents, or other parties whose interests may diverge during the merit review negotiation. Model Rule 3.3 (Candor) applies by analogy to regulator-facing submissions—while state examiners are not courts, all representations made to examiners regarding the capitalization table and value of assets must be truthful, and misrepresentation can lead to fraud charges under state Blue Sky laws. Model Rule 4.1 (Truthfulness in Statements to Others) applies directly.

The Uniform Securities Act (Section 306 or its state equivalent) provides the statutory basis for a stop order. The commissioner may issue a stop order if the offering involves unreasonable amounts of underwriters' and sellers' discounts, commissions, or other compensation, or promoters' profits or participation, or unreasonable amounts or kinds of options. Understanding this statutory language helps frame responses that address the examiner's specific statutory mandate.

Regarding privilege, while communications with the client are privileged, responses to examiners are public records in many states. The LLM should avoid embedding privileged internal assessments, candid risk analyses, or negotiating positions in response letters. Maintain a clear separation between the internal strategy memorandum and the external response package.

The anti-fraud overlay remains operative even in merit review. Do not attempt to \

a merit issue by obscuring it. If cheap stock exists, disclose it. If promoters are receiving compensation, disclose it. If voting rights are unequal, explain them plainly. Any attempt to downplay or omit material facts can become an enforcement issue under both state and federal anti-fraud provisions.

The highest-risk malpractice failure modes in this practice area are: misclassifying an offering as covered and failing to make required state filings; providing incorrect or inconsistent capitalization table and cheap stock disclosures; promising restrictions (escrow, lock-ups) not actually implemented in binding agreements; misstating the terms of voting rights or promoter compensation; and citing fabricated or inaccurate NASAA policy text or state law. Mitigate these risks by requiring document-backed factual assertions, maintaining a single source-of-truth capitalization table, and verifying all legal authorities through web research before submission.

## 6. Quality Control and Review

Before submitting any filing or response to a state regulator, quality control must address the following. First, confirm the preemption determination: has it been verified that the security is not a covered security? Performing a merit analysis on a preempted security is not only unnecessary but potentially harmful, as it may invite scrutiny the offering is entitled to avoid. Second, verify mathematical accuracy: are the cheap stock and promoter investment percentages calculated using the specific NASAA methodologies rather than general accounting principles? Third, check consistency across all documents: does the data in the capitalization table match the disclosure in the \
and \

sections of the offering document? Fourth, verify all citations: are NASAA SOPs cited to their current versions with accessible URLs, and are state statute and regulation citations accurate? Fifth, apply an adversarial scrub: if you were a state examiner looking to protect a retail investor, what part of this deal would you find unfair? Has that specific vulnerability been addressed?

All citations to legal authorities must either provide verified URLs or be clearly flagged for attorney confirmation. The LLM must flag uncertainties and decision points for attorney review—such as whether a particular state will accept a lock-up in lieu of escrow, whether the promoter definition captures a particular consultant, or whether a governance change triggers charter amendment and stockholder approval requirements.

All output from this skill requires review by a licensed securities attorney before use. The analysis does not constitute legal advice and is intended to assist legal professionals in their work.

## 7. Jurisdiction-Specific Adaptations

This skill is intentionally multi-jurisdictional because Blue Sky merit review is state-specific. The adaptation principle is to treat NASAA Statements of Policy as a starting vocabulary and shared analytical framework, not a uniform rulebook. Some states adhere closely to NASAA positions; others apply their own interpretive standards or focus on particular investor-protection themes.

When adapting to a specific state, the LLM must verify whether the state applies merit review for the chosen filing pathway, identify any published conditioning guidelines, interpretive orders, or administrative rules addressing promotional shares, voting rights, and promoter compensation, and confirm whether the state has adopted, modified, or rejected the relevant NASAA SOPs. For each finding, include URLs to the state regulator's website or other authoritative sources. If the LLM cannot locate an authoritative source after reasonable web research, it must flag the point for attorney verification and recommend contacting the examiner or engaging local counsel.

Key state-specific considerations that practitioners should verify include: California does not strictly follow all NASAA SOPs but applies its own standards under the California Corporate Securities Law of 1968, with provisions such as California Code of Regulations Title 10, Section 260.140 and related subsections addressing promoter's equity and underwriter compensation. Texas is a strict merit state that focuses heavily on affiliated transactions, requiring demonstration that related-party transactions are on arm's-length terms. Washington State applies specific scrutiny to developmental-stage companies and may require impoundment of proceeds until minimum thresholds are met. New York is traditionally a notice-filing state for most offerings but has specific requirements under the Martin Act that may affect certain offering types.

Two common areas of interstate divergence to address explicitly are: differences in how states treat escrow, impound, and minimum offering proceeds conditions (some require third-party escrow under specific terms while others allow attorney trust accounts or different release triggers); and differences in tolerance for dual-class or non-voting securities, which may be acceptable with strong disclosure in some states but treated as inequitable in others. These divergences reinforce the need for state-specific verification of every substantive standard before filing or responding to comments.

content.name: State Qualification to Do Business
content.summary: Drafts a comprehensive Application for Certificate of Authority to qualify a foreign corporation to conduct business in a target U.S. state. Incorporates jurisdictional research, name availability verification, and details from corporate foundational documents like articles of incorporation and officer information. Use this skill for ensuring corporate compliance during interstate expansion to avoid penalties and maintain legal standing.
content.content:
# Enhanced Prompt: State Qualification to Do Business Application

## Objective and Scope

You are tasked with drafting a comprehensive Application for Certificate of Authority to enable a corporation incorporated in one state to lawfully conduct business in another state. This foreign qualification process is a critical corporate compliance requirement that protects the corporation's ability to enforce contracts, maintain standing in courts, and avoid substantial penalties for conducting unauthorized business activities. The application must satisfy all statutory requirements of the target state while accurately reflecting the corporation's current organizational structure and legal status.

## Initial Information Gathering and Document Review

Begin by searching through all available documents in the matter to locate the corporation's foundational documents, including the articles or certificate of incorporation, current bylaws, recent board resolutions, and any existing certificates of good standing from the home state. Extract the corporation's exact legal name as it appears in the formation documents, paying careful attention to punctuation, spacing, and required corporate designators such as \
or \

Identify the state or country of incorporation, the precise date of incorporation, and whether the corporation has perpetual duration or a specified term of existence.

Review any available corporate records to identify the current officers and directors, including their full legal names, titles, and business addresses. If organizational charts, annual reports, or recent filings are available in the documents, extract this governance information to ensure accuracy and currency. Search for any existing registered agent agreements or correspondence that might indicate the corporation's preferred registered agent in the target state.

## Jurisdictional Research and Name Availability

Determine the specific requirements of the foreign state where the corporation seeks to qualify by researching that state's business corporation act and the filing procedures of its secretary of state or equivalent authority. Identify whether the state provides a mandatory official form for foreign qualification or whether a custom application must be drafted to satisfy statutory requirements. Note any unique requirements such as notarization, authentication of supporting documents, or specific formatting requirements.

Verify whether the corporation's legal name is available for use in the foreign state or whether a conflict exists with an existing entity. If the exact corporate name is unavailable, determine what alternative name or fictitious name the corporation will use to conduct business in that jurisdiction, ensuring compliance with the state's assumed name statutes. Document any name reservation or fictitious name filing that may be required as a prerequisite to the qualification application.

## Drafting the Application Document
